title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived in the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit rules sit inside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and the Act says a landlord and tenant may not agree to waive or give up any right, duty or remedy under it, in an oral or written rental agreement, unless the Act itself allows it. The deposit section allows no waiver. So a lease cannot make the deposit nonrefundable, let you keep it for reasons beyond unpaid rent, tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, end-of-tenancy cleaning and other reasonable expenses from the tenant's default, excuse the itemized written notice, extend the 45-day return period, or remove the tenant's bad-faith remedy (up to $200 plus actual damages). Leave such clauses out. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies covered by the Act (rental agreements entered into after July 1, 1991, other than the Act's excluded arrangements, such as transient hotel or motel stays).

title: Selling a Rental: The Transferee Can Owe the Deposit Penalty
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit statute reaches whoever takes over the deposit: a landlord or a transferee who keeps a deposit in violation of the statute and without good faith can owe the tenant up to $200 plus actual damages. A buyer of the property also steps into the seller's rights under existing leases and is bound by the leases' covenants to the tenants, and a tenant who paid rent to the seller before learning of the sale is protected. The statute does not say whether the seller is released, how the deposit must move at closing, or that the tenant must be told. So when you sell, transfer each tenant's deposit (or a credit for it) to the buyer, get the buyer's written assumption of the deposit duties, and tell each tenant in writing who now holds the deposit and where to pay rent. When you buy, insist on receiving the deposits. The rules are the same for every tenancy type covered by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: No Statutory Order for Applying a Tenant's Payment
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that sets the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment among rent, late fees and other charges, so the lease may set the order. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, rent means all payments the rental agreement requires, including late fees the agreement requires a defaulting tenant to pay, so an unpaid late fee or other lease charge is unpaid rent for the three-day nonpayment notice. In an eviction based only on nonpayment, the tenant can stop removal by paying all unpaid rent and other sums in the judgment by the court-ordered move-out date, and you must in good faith accept full payment tendered by then. Apply payments to the oldest rent first and state the order in the lease so your ledger matches the notice. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that specifically bars charging a tenant for a service you do not provide. Two general rules still matter. Every duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and every step you take to enforce a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith, meaning honesty in fact and reasonable community standards of fair dealing. And because every payment the lease requires counts as rent, a fee for a service that is never delivered can end up in a nonpayment notice or eviction claim where a judge will look at the rental agreement. Charge only for services you actually provide, describe each one and its fee in the lease, and stop or credit the fee if the service stops. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Every Payment the Lease Requires Counts as Rent
bodyText: Under Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, rent means all payments the tenant must make to you under the rental agreement, including late fees the agreement requires a defaulting tenant to pay. So a pet fee, utility charge, repair charge or other fee is rent if the lease requires the tenant to pay it to you, and you do not need to label it additional rent. That matters for nonpayment: you may give written notice that the rental agreement will end if the rent is not paid within three days, not counting intermediate weekends and legal holidays (e-mail or text counts only if the tenant agreed in writing to it, and deliver a paper copy too, because Mississippi's electronic-transactions law excludes eviction and default notices for a primary residence), and your eviction affidavit states the rent and any additional fees owed. A charge the lease does not require is not rent; collect it only by agreement or in court. In a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement, so state every fee, its amount and when it is due. The rule applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Passing Local Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that allows or forbids passing a local government fee, such as a rental registration, inspection or permit fee, on to a tenant. It is a lease term like any other: you may recover it only if the lease requires the tenant to pay it, and once the lease requires it, the charge counts as rent under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. During a fixed term you cannot add it unless the lease already provides for it. For a month-to-month tenancy you can add it for the future only by ending the tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice and offering new terms; for a week-to-week tenancy, 7 days. State the fee, its amount and when it is billed. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bars, or expressly allows, passing to a tenant a fine a city, county or agency imposes on you as owner. So it is a lease term: you may require the tenant to reimburse a fine caused by the tenant's own conduct or that of the household or guests (for example a trash, noise, parking or animal citation), but only if the lease says so. The tenant already owes you a statutory duty to keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of waste properly, and, to the extent of the tenant's legal obligation, comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. Fines for conditions that are your duty, such as code compliance and repairs you must make, stay with you; a lease cannot waive the Act's duties. A required reimbursement counts as rent once the lease requires it. The same rules apply to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Rule Comparing Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bars terms more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or that caps the rent difference between lease types. You may charge different rent or set different terms for different lease lengths. If the rental agreement fixes no definite term, the tenancy is week to week when the tenant pays weekly rent and month to month in all other cases. Either side may end a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 7 days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before; no notice period is needed where the other side has committed a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety (a landlord's eviction complaint must still attach a written notice). A fixed term simply expires on the date stated. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Rent Concessions
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on rent concessions such as free months, move-in credits or discounts. A concession is a lease term: write it into the lease, saying which periods are free or reduced, the full rent that otherwise applies, and whether any part must be repaid if the tenant leaves early or breaches. Be precise, because rent under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is whatever payments the rental agreement requires, and in a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement, so an unclear concession can leave you unable to prove what rent was owed. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Rent Installments Are a Lease Choice
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on splitting rent into installments, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets no default due date, payment place or installment schedule. The only statutory tie is the tenancy type: if there is no definite term, a tenant who pays weekly rent has a week-to-week tenancy and every other tenant has a month-to-month tenancy, which changes the termination notice (7 or 30 days). So set the schedule in the lease. If you split monthly rent into two payments, say that the tenancy is still month to month, that each payment is a scheduled installment and not a partial payment, and when a late fee applies to each. A missed installment is unpaid rent for the three-day nonpayment notice. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Rent-Reporting Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires you to offer positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, requires a lease election for it, or restricts reporting a tenant's rent payment history. If you or a service you hire reports rent payments or unpaid balances, federal consumer-reporting law governs accuracy, notices and disputes. If you use a reporting program, describe it in the lease, say whether it is optional and whether it reports on-time payments, late payments or both, and keep records that match what is reported. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Government-Shutdown Rent Protection in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for federal or state workers affected by a government shutdown or furlough. The ordinary rules apply: unpaid rent, including any late fee the lease requires, supports a written three-day nonpayment notice, and in an eviction based only on nonpayment the tenant can stop removal by paying everything in the judgment by the court-ordered move-out date. If a tenant tells you a shutdown has stopped their pay, consider a written payment plan that says whether late fees are waived and that accepting partial payments does not waive the rest. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Passing Property-Tax Increases to Tenants
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that permits, forbids or regulates a residential lease clause passing real estate tax increases to the tenant. It is a contract term. During a fixed term you may pass on an increase only if the lease says so, stating how the tenant's share is figured, when it is billed and whether a tax reduction is credited back; once the lease requires the payment, it counts as rent. For a month-to-month tenancy you can raise rent for the future by ending the tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice and offering new terms; for week to week, 7 days. After a fixed term expires you may demand an increase, but not with the dominant purpose of retaliating against the tenant for actions the Act authorizes. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Rule Requiring Fees to Be Listed in the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires a residential lease to list every fee, or that sets a notice period before you add one. In practice the lease controls: rent under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is whatever payments the rental agreement requires, including late fees it requires of a defaulting tenant; your eviction affidavit must state the rent and any additional fees owed; and in a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement. A fee not in the lease is hard to collect. You cannot add a fee during a fixed term unless the lease allows it; for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, add it for the future only with the 30-day or 7-day written termination notice and new terms. List each fee, its amount, purpose and due date. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Statutory Late-Fee Limit in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that limits the amount of a residential late fee, whether as a dollar cap, a percentage of rent, a daily fee or a grace period. The late-charge limit in Mississippi's consumer-credit law applies to late payments on loans and other extensions of credit, and the Code's other late-fee rules concern self-storage and rental-purchase of goods, not a lease of a home. A late fee is enforceable as a term of the rental agreement, but a court can refuse a fee that is a penalty rather than a fair estimate of your loss, so keep it modest and charge it once per late payment. See the late-fee row for how a required late fee counts as rent. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Algorithmic Rent-Setting Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bans or regulates setting rents with algorithmic pricing or revenue-management software. Federal antitrust law still applies to any agreement among competing landlords to coordinate rents, and Mississippi's general antitrust statutes were not reviewed here, so do not share nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease data with competitors through a pricing service, keep the final rent decision your own, and keep a record of how you set each rent. Mississippi has no statewide rent control (see the rent-control row). The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Rent-Receipt Duty in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires you to give a receipt for rent, even for cash, and no rule that a missing receipt is an eviction defense. Give a written or electronic receipt for every cash payment anyway, showing the date, amount, period covered and what the payment was applied to, because in a nonpayment eviction you must show the rent and any additional fees owed, and in a nonpayment-only case the tenant can stop removal by paying everything in the judgment by the court-ordered move-out date. Receipts also protect you if a tenant claims repair-and-deduct reimbursement, which requires the tenant to be current in rent. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Subsidy Late-Fee Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on late fees for the part of rent a housing subsidy pays, and no residential late-fee cap. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act a late fee the rental agreement requires is part of rent, so write the lease so that any late fee applies only to the tenant's own share, since the tenant does not control the agency's payment, and do not treat a late agency payment as the tenant's nonpayment for the three-day notice. Federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may limit or bar fees and are not covered here. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Late Fees: No Statutory Cap, and a Required Late Fee Is Rent
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that caps residential late fees, sets a grace period or requires notice before you charge one. A late fee exists only if the lease provides for it: under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, rent includes any late fees the rental agreement requires a defaulting tenant to pay, so an unpaid late fee is unpaid rent and can be included in the written three-day nonpayment notice and your eviction claim. In a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement, so state the amount, the day it applies and whether it is charged once or daily. Courts can refuse a fee that works as a penalty rather than a reasonable estimate of your loss, so keep it modest. The three days in the notice exclude intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays; that is a termination rule, not a grace period. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: When and Where Rent Is Due: The Lease Decides
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets no default due date, payment place or payment method for rent, so the lease must say when, where and how rent is paid. Rent under the Act means every payment the rental agreement requires, including late fees it requires of a defaulting tenant. If rent is not paid, you may deliver a written notice (or an e-mail or text, only if the tenant agreed in writing to be notified that way; deliver a paper copy too, because Mississippi's electronic-transactions law excludes eviction and default notices for a primary residence) that the rental agreement will end if the rent is not paid within three days; intermediate weekends and legal holidays do not count. In a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement. A tenancy with no definite term is week to week if rent is paid weekly and otherwise month to month.

title: No Mississippi Rule on How Rent Must Be Paid
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires you to accept, or forbids you to refuse, cash, checks, money orders, cards or electronic payment for rent, and none that bars or caps a fee for a particular payment method or a card surcharge on rent. Name the accepted methods, the payment place or portal and any method fee in the lease; once the lease requires a fee it counts as rent. If you accept checks or electronic debits, a payment issued with fraudulent intent and without sufficient funds carries Mississippi's bad-check remedies, including a $40 service charge (see the returned-payment row). The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Application Fees: No State Cap or Refund Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that caps rental application or screening fees, requires a refund of an unused fee, requires a written pre-application disclosure of rent, fees or screening criteria, or makes you process applicants in order. No state statute was found that stops a city or county from regulating application fees either, so check local ordinances. Charge a fee that reflects your actual screening cost, state it, what it covers and whether it is refundable in writing before you take it, and apply the same criteria to every applicant, because fair-housing law still governs how you screen. An application fee is not a security deposit unless you hold it to secure the tenant's performance of the lease. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Taxes on Rent: Hotels and Transient Lodging, Not Ordinary Leases
bodyText: Mississippi's sales tax list of taxable businesses includes hotels, motels, tourist courts or camps and trailer parks, at 7% of gross income, and a hotel means a business furnishing rooms for dwelling, lodging or sleeping that accommodate transient guests, including a structure held out as a place where sleeping accommodations are supplied for pay to transient guests, regardless of the number of rooms; sites that list and collect payment for those stays are treated as hotels for sales tax. Local hotel or motel taxes levied by local and private law can use the same definition. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not apply to transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings. An ordinary lease of a tenant's home is not a hotel rental under these sections, so do not add a sales tax charge to it. The statutes do not define transient by a number of days, so before renting by the night or week, or listing a unit on a short-stay platform, check with the Department of Revenue and your city or county.

title: No Statewide Rent Control; Emergency Price Limits May Reach Rent
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that controls or stabilizes residential rents, and no statute was found that either preempts or authorizes local rent control, so check your city and county. Rent is whatever the rental agreement sets. One state limit may matter: when a state of emergency or local emergency is declared under the Mississippi Emergency Management Law, the price received for goods and services sold in the designated emergency impact area may not exceed the prices ordinarily charged in the same market just before the declaration, except for costs necessarily incurred during the emergency; a knowing and willful violation is a crime and an unfair or deceptive trade practice. The statute does not say whether renting housing counts, so treat it as applying: during a declared emergency, do not raise rent or set new-lease rent above pre-emergency levels unless the increase reflects added costs. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases Need a Lease Clause
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on rent escalation clauses and no general anti-retaliation statute with a safe harbor that depends on one. During a fixed term you may raise rent only if the lease provides for it, for example a scheduled step-up or a clause allowing an increase on stated notice; without that, the agreed rent holds until the term ends. After a fixed term expires you may demand an increase, but not with the dominant purpose of retaliating against the tenant for actions the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act authorizes, where you received written notice of the conditions involved. A month-to-month rent can change for the future by ending the tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice and offering a new rent; week to week, 7 days. During a declared emergency, Mississippi's emergency pricing law may limit increases (see the rent-control row). This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Rent-Increase Notice Period; Use the Termination Notice
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that sets a notice period for a rent increase, for any type of tenancy. During a fixed term, rent can rise only as the lease allows. For a month-to-month tenancy, give written notice at least 30 days before the date the old terms end and the new rent starts; for a week-to-week tenancy, at least 7 days. These are the periods for ending the tenancy, so the notice should say the tenancy ends on that date unless the tenant stays at the new rent. After a fixed term expires you may demand an increase, but not with the dominant purpose of retaliating against the tenant for actions the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act authorizes. There is no separate duty to give notice that you will not renew a fixed term, which simply expires on its stated date. During a declared emergency, Mississippi's emergency pricing law may limit increases (see the rent-control row). This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Three Years
bodyText: Mississippi's general time limit for lawsuits reaches a landlord's claims for unpaid rent, fees and damage. A suit on an unwritten contract, or on an open account not acknowledged in a writing signed by the debtor, must be filed within three years after the claim accrues, and any action with no other prescribed limit, which includes a claim under a written lease, must also be filed within three years. If the tenant pays part of the debt, or acknowledges it or promises to pay it, before the period runs, a new period of the same length starts from that payment, acknowledgment or promise. Once the period runs, the right itself is extinguished, not just the remedy. Treat three years from each missed payment or each damage claim as your deadline; when a claim accrues is case law. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Bounced Rent Payments: $40 Service Charge and the Bad-Check Notice
bodyText: If a tenant's rent check, electronically converted check or other electronic transfer is dishonored and was issued with fraudulent intent knowing funds were insufficient, Mississippi's bad-check law lets you collect the face amount plus a $40 service charge. Send the statutory notice of dishonor by regular mail to the address on the check or the one the tenant gave; if the tenant does not pay the amount plus $40 within 15 days after receiving it, that is evidence of intent to defraud, and a notice returned undelivered is too. In a civil suit on the check you may recover a $30 service charge (check of $25 or less) or $40 (larger checks), plus reasonable attorney's fees if a licensed attorney files the suit. After the mailed notice you may also file a complaint with the district attorney. Set any returned-payment fee in the lease at no more than $40, and keep the notice and mailing proof. The unpaid rent is still unpaid rent for the three-day notice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Collection Costs: Put Them in the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that sets or bars a fee for collecting past-due rent, and its landlord-tenant statutes do not award attorney's fees or collection costs. So you may recover collection costs only as the lease provides or another statute allows. One statute does: for a rent check or electronic transfer dishonored and issued with fraudulent intent, you may collect a $40 service charge, and in a suit on it a $30 or $40 service charge plus reasonable attorney's fees if a licensed attorney files (see the returned-payment row). Any collection charge the lease requires the tenant to pay you counts as rent, and a court will look at the signed rental agreement, so state any collection fee or attorney's-fee term expressly and keep it reasonable. No Mississippi debt-collection practices statute was found; federal debt-collection law may apply to a collection agency you hire. The same rules apply to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Rent for a Defective or Destroyed Unit
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bars you from demanding rent while a unit has code violations. But a tenant is not bound to pay rent for buildings after they are destroyed by fire or otherwise, and a lease promise to keep or restore the premises in good repair does not make the tenant rebuild, unless the tenant was negligent or at fault or expressly agreed in the lease to be bound. For defects short of destruction, the tenant's statutory remedies are to terminate for your material noncompliance after a 14-day written notice, or, after 30 days' written notice of a specific material defect, to repair and be reimbursed (or offset the cost against future rent) up to one month's rent, if current in rent, not having used the remedy in the prior six months and having met the tenant's own duties. Keep up the repairs you owe under building codes and the Act, and decide in the lease how a casualty affects rent. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on reducing or prorating rent for a subsidized tenant when part of the unit becomes uninhabitable, and no general rent-abatement rule for defects. Two general rules apply to every tenant: a tenant is not bound to pay rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise unless the tenant was at fault or expressly agreed to be bound, and a tenant who gives 30 days' written notice of a material defect you fail to fix may repair it and offset the cost against future rent, within the statute's limits (up to one month's rent, current in rent, once in six months). Federal program rules, such as Housing Choice Voucher abatement, and your housing assistance contract may apply to a subsidized tenancy and are not covered here. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: Mississippi has no landlord-tenant statute on interest on unpaid rent or damages. The general rule is that the legal rate of interest on notes, accounts and contracts is 8% a year, and higher charges must be made in writing and fit Mississippi's finance-charge limits, which are written for loans and extensions of credit. A court judgment on a contract bears interest at the contract's rate; other judgments bear a rate the judge sets, from no earlier than the filing of the complaint. Whether a lease interest clause on past-due rent is a finance charge is not settled by statute, and charging more than the law allows can forfeit all interest, so if you put an interest rate in the lease, state it in writing and keep it at or below 8% a year, and do not stack it with a late fee on the same amount. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Mississippi's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Mississippi sets few money limits on residential leases. Security deposit: no cap and no interest duty, but bad-faith retention can cost you up to $200 plus the tenant's actual damages. Late fees: no cap; a late fee the lease requires is rent. Bounced checks: for a check issued with fraudulent intent (which the statutory notice helps prove), a $40 service charge, and in a suit $30 or $40 plus attorney's fees if a licensed attorney files. Holdover: after a fixed term expires and you notify the tenant to vacate, double rent from the date to vacate in the notice, unless the lease says otherwise. Tenant repair-and-deduct: limited to one month's rent and the usual and customary charge. Interest: the legal rate on contracts is 8% a year. Declared emergencies: prices for goods and services may not exceed pre-emergency levels except for added costs, which may reach rent. These rules apply to the Act's tenancies of every type; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Rental Fee-Disclosure or All-In Pricing Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires an all-in rent figure, a first-page fee disclosure, a total-price advertisement or a list of mandatory fees in a residential lease; the Code's mandatory-charge disclosure rule is for motor-vehicle rentals. Mississippi's Consumer Protection Act bars unfair or deceptive trade practices, and its definition of trade covers advertising and offering any property, including real property, so a misleading rent advertisement could be challenged; whether its private-suit section reaches a lease of a home is not settled by its text, and case law was not checked. List every fee in the lease with its amount and purpose, and advertise rent with any mandatory monthly fee shown alongside it. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Money Due at Signing: No Cap, but Know Which Payments Are Deposits
bodyText: Mississippi does not cap the security deposit or limit how much rent you collect in advance, and it does not list what may be due at signing. What matters is the label's function. Money whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance of the lease is a security deposit, whatever you call it, and must be held for the tenant, claimed only for the statute's purposes by itemized written notice and the rest returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. A payment made to secure the execution of the lease, including an advance payment of rent, is outside the deposit statute. If you end the lease for the tenant's breach, you must return all prepaid and unearned rent. State in the lease what each upfront payment is: first month's rent, a deposit and its purposes, or a nonrefundable fee for a stated service. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Move-In Condition Form: Optional but Protective
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a written inventory or a condition checklist. But the deposit statute lets you keep money for damage only if the tenant caused it, and never for ordinary wear and tear, and your duty to maintain the unit is measured against its condition at the start of the lease. Both make proof of move-in condition valuable. Walk the unit with the tenant, complete a dated condition form with photos, have both of you sign it and give the tenant a copy; repeat at move-out. Use it to support the itemized written notice of any deposit claim. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Pre-Set Deduction Schedule Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that allows or forbids a lease schedule of preset deposit charges, such as a flat carpet-cleaning or repainting fee. Whatever the lease says, you may claim from the deposit only amounts reasonably necessary to cover unpaid rent, damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning at the end of the tenancy, and other reasonable and necessary expenses from the tenant's default, and only if the deposit was made for those purposes; each claim must be itemized in a written notice. A preset charge works only as a reasonable estimate of a real cost; a flat charge taken regardless of condition risks a bad-faith finding, with damages of up to $200 plus actual damages. A lease cannot waive these limits. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit statute has no rule for a refund the tenant never collects, and it does not let you keep it. Mississippi's unclaimed property law lists security deposits and refunds as intangible property, and a holder includes any person in possession of property belonging to another. Intangible property held by a business or any other person is presumed abandoned, and subject to the State's custody, if the owner has not claimed it or written about it within five years after it was payable, where the owner's last known address is unknown and the holder is in Mississippi. So when a refund cannot be delivered: keep the 45-day itemized notice and refund, mailed to the last known or forwarding address; keep the returned envelope and a record of your search; hold the money for the tenant, not as your own; and report or deliver it to the State Treasurer as the unclaimed property law requires (its reporting sections were not reviewed here). The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or that bars you from offering it. Mississippi also has no cap on the deposit amount. If you agree to installments, write the schedule into the lease and say what happens if an installment is missed. Every installment you receive is part of the security deposit if its primary function is to secure the tenant's performance, so it is held for the tenant and returned, less itemized claims, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that restricts how you apply a last-month's-rent payment, and none that lets a tenant use the security deposit as the final month's rent. You may refuse that use: the deposit may be claimed for unpaid rent at the end, but the tenant still owes the last month's rent when due. How you label upfront money matters. A payment whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit, held for the tenant and accounted for within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. An advance payment of rent made to secure the execution of the lease is outside the deposit statute. If you end the lease for the tenant's breach, you must return all prepaid and unearned rent. Say in the lease whether a last-month payment is prepaid rent for that month or part of the deposit. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: The 45-Day Refund Clock Starts with the Tenant's Demand
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit statute makes the refund deadline depend on three events: the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession and the tenant's demand for the deposit. Any remaining deposit is due no later than 45 days after all three. So the statute itself conditions the deadline on the tenant asking; it does not require advance notice of move-out or a forwarding address, and it sets no move-out inspection notice. Ask in the lease for a written demand with a forwarding address when the tenant moves out, but do not make the refund itself depend on anything else, since a lease cannot waive the statute's rights. A notice the lease requires to end the tenancy is separate: a tenant who leaves without it may owe rent, which you may claim from the deposit by itemized written notice. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: No Special Deposit Timing After a Domestic-Abuse Move-Out
bodyText: Mississippi gives a domestic-abuse victim no statutory right to end a lease early and sets no special deposit timing when a tenancy ends because of abuse. A court's domestic abuse protection order can, however, give the victim possession of the residence and exclude the abuser, including by evicting the abuser, and can bar the parties from disposing of property they lease together. If the tenancy ends, by agreement, notice or court order, the ordinary rule applies: return any remaining deposit, less itemized claims, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. Where co-tenants share one deposit and one leaves, the statute does not say how to split it, so agree in writing with all of them. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Mississippi has no expedited deposit procedure and no statute allowing an administrative or processing fee for early handling. You may return the deposit sooner than the 45-day limit, but your claims are limited to amounts reasonably necessary to cover unpaid rent, damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear, end-of-tenancy cleaning and other reasonable and necessary expenses from the tenant's default, itemized in a written notice; a processing fee is none of those, so do not deduct one. A lease cannot waive these limits. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Deposit-Alternative Fees
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on fees charged instead of a security deposit, such as deposit-alternative, surety or deposit-waiver programs. Offer such a program only as an option, explain in writing that the fee is not refundable and does not limit the tenant's liability for damage or unpaid rent, and say who the provider is. Remember that any money whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance of the lease is a security deposit whatever you call it, held for the tenant and returned within 45 days, less itemized claims; a recurring program fee the lease requires is rent. Insurance-law treatment of surety products was not reviewed. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Furnished-Rental Rules
bodyText: Mississippi has no special rules for furnished rentals: there is no deposit cap at all, no separate furniture deposit rule, and the landlord's statutory maintenance duty names the dwelling unit, its plumbing and its heating or cooling system, not furniture. List the furniture and appliances you provide in the lease, say who repairs them, and note their condition on a signed move-in form. You may claim from the deposit, by itemized written notice, for damage the tenant caused to them beyond ordinary wear and tear. Mississippi's sales tax list includes renting or leasing personal property; whether that reaches furniture supplied with a home lease was not settled here, so ask the Department of Revenue before charging separately for furniture. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease: Outside the Deposit Statute
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit statute governs money whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance of a rental agreement, and it expressly leaves out a payment or deposit, including an advance payment of rent, made to secure the execution of a rental agreement. So a true holding deposit taken to secure the signing of a lease is not a security deposit: the 45-day return rule and the bad-faith penalty do not apply to it, and no statute sets its amount or refund. Its terms are a contract. Put a holding deposit agreement in writing: say what it holds, for how long, whether it becomes part of the security deposit or first month's rent when the lease is signed, and when it is refunded if the applicant is denied or you do not offer the lease. Once it is applied to the security deposit, the deposit statute governs it. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: Mississippi has no move-in or move-out inspection-notice duty for deposits, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct, for not offering an inspection. The penalty that applies is tied to the refund: if you keep any part of a deposit in violation of the statute and without good faith, you can owe the tenant up to $200 plus actual damages. The statute requires an itemized written notice of any claim and return of the rest within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. A joint move-out walk-through with photos is still your best evidence of good faith. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that permits nonrefundable deposits or requires a notice for them. Money whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance of the lease is a security deposit whatever you call it, so a nonrefundable deposit is still held for the tenant and returned within 45 days, less only itemized amounts for unpaid rent, tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, end-of-tenancy cleaning and other reasonable expenses from the tenant's default; a lease cannot waive that. If you want a charge you keep, make it a fee for a stated service (such as a pet or cleaning fee), call it a fee, not a deposit, and say it is not refundable. Whether a particular fee is really a disguised deposit is a question for the courts. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Mississippi has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable, because no Mississippi statute recognizes a nonrefundable security deposit. Money whose primary function is to secure the tenant's performance of the lease is governed by the deposit statute whatever its label: it is held for the tenant, may be claimed only for the statute's purposes by itemized written notice, and the rest must be returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. If you want a charge you keep, make it a separately stated, nonrefundable fee for a stated service, not part of the deposit. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Cap on Security Deposits in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not limit the amount of a security deposit, for any tenancy type, and no statute was found that lets or bars cities and counties from setting one. The deposit statute controls how you hold and return the money, not how much you take: it is held for the tenant, ahead of your creditors; it may be claimed only for unpaid rent, tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, end-of-tenancy cleaning and other reasonable expenses from the tenant's default, by itemized written notice; and the rest is due within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it, with up to $200 plus actual damages for bad-faith retention. Set a deposit you can justify, and apply the same amount rules to every applicant, because fair-housing law still applies. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Escrow or Separate-Account Rule for Deposits
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires you to keep security deposits in a separate, escrow or trust account, to tell the tenant where the deposit is held, or to post a bond. The deposit statute does say the money is held by you for the tenant and that the tenant's claim to it comes before the claims of any of your creditors. Keep deposits in a separate account anyway, with a ledger for each tenant, so the money is identifiable and you can return it on time. If you sell, the buyer who takes over the deposit is exposed to the bad-faith penalty too (see the deposit-on-sale row). A licensed property manager may be subject to trust-account rules under the real estate license law, which are not covered here. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: No Interest Owed on Deposits
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit, whatever the length of the tenancy, and it does not require the deposit to be kept in an interest-bearing account. The deposit statute requires only that the money be held for the tenant and returned, less itemized claims, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. If you promise interest in the lease, you must pay it as promised, because a promise in the rental agreement binds you. Say in the lease that no interest is paid unless the lease states otherwise. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution; local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Mishandling a Deposit in Mississippi: Up to $200 Plus Actual Damages for Bad Faith
bodyText: If you keep any part of a tenant's security deposit in violation of Mississippi's deposit statute and without good faith, you (or anyone you transfer the property and deposit to) may owe the tenant damages of up to $200 on top of the tenant's actual damages. A violation includes keeping money for something the statute does not allow (only unpaid rent, damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning at the end of the tenancy, and other reasonable and necessary expenses caused by the tenant's default), not itemizing your claim in a written notice delivered to the tenant, or missing the 45-day return deadline, which runs from the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession and the tenant's demand. The statute does not say that a late or missing notice forfeits your right to keep anything, and it does not mention attorney's fees. Good faith is what keeps you clear of the $200 penalty, so keep move-out photos, invoices and dates. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: Returning the Deposit in Mississippi: 45 Days After Move-Out and the Tenant's Demand
bodyText: Mississippi's deposit clock has three triggers, not one: you must return whatever you do not claim no later than 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession, and the tenant demands the deposit. Ask departing tenants to make the demand in writing with a forwarding address so you know when the clock started. Any amount you keep must be claimed by a written notice delivered to the tenant that itemizes each amount, and you may keep only what is reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or other reasonable and necessary expenses caused by the tenant's default. The statute sets no method of payment and does not let the lease change the deadline. The tenant's claim to the deposit comes ahead of your creditors. If the tenant never collects a refund, note that the state's unclaimed property law lists security deposits and refunds among the property it covers. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. Use the Mississippi return clause in the lease.

title: What a Mississippi Deposit May Cover, and Why the Lease Must Say So
bodyText: Mississippi lets you claim from a security deposit only amounts reasonably necessary to cover unpaid rent, repair damage the tenant caused (not ordinary wear and tear), clean the unit when the tenancy ends, or pay other reasonable and necessary expenses caused by the tenant's default, and only if the deposit was made for those purposes. So state in the lease that the deposit secures each of them. Late fees the lease requires count as rent under the Act, so unpaid late fees can come out of the deposit as unpaid rent. Each amount must be itemized in a written notice delivered to the tenant. No statute addresses pre-set cleaning or repair charges; because you may keep only what is reasonably necessary, a flat charge above your real cost is risky and could be bad-faith retention (up to $200 plus actual damages). Money paid only to secure signing of the lease, such as an advance payment of rent, is outside the deposit section. There is no statutory cap on the deposit amount. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Utility Deposits You Collect Follow the Mississippi Deposit Rules
bodyText: Mississippi has no separate rule for a utility deposit that a landlord collects from a tenant. Instead, the security deposit statute covers any payment or deposit whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance of the rental agreement or any part of it, which includes a deposit securing the tenant's payment of utilities under the lease. Treat it as part of the security deposit: hold it for the tenant, claim from it only reasonably necessary amounts for the tenant's defaults (such as unpaid utility charges the lease makes the tenant's responsibility) if the lease says the deposit is made for that purpose, itemize each claim in a written notice delivered to the tenant, and return the rest no later than 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant demands it. Bad-faith retention can cost up to $200 plus actual damages. Deposits that a utility company itself requires are between the tenant and the utility and are not governed by landlord-tenant law. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, and Mississippi sets no cap on the deposit amount. Two things still apply. First, any deposit that secures the tenant's performance of the lease is governed by the deposit statute, however you label it, so each one must be held for the tenant, claimed only for the listed purposes by an itemized written notice, and returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant demands it. Second, federal fair housing law bars setting deposits differently because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status or disability. If you vary deposits (for example by credit score or pets), write down your criteria and apply them to every applicant the same way. This applies equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on professional carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing requires it and nothing forbids a lease term requiring it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead is the deposit statute, which lets you claim amounts reasonably necessary to clean the premises when the tenancy ends, if the lease says the deposit is made for that purpose, itemized in a written notice delivered to the tenant and returned with the balance within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant demands it. During the tenancy the tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits and not deliberately or negligently damage it. If you want carpets professionally cleaned at move-out, say so in the lease and charge only the reasonable cost you actually pay when the tenant does not do it; a flat fee charged whatever the carpets look like is hard to defend as reasonably necessary. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi law does not require a tenant to warn you before leaving the unit empty in freezing weather, and the landlord-tenant statutes have no winter rule on evictions or move-outs; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: the tenant must use the plumbing, heating and other facilities in a reasonable manner, must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and must tell you about any condition the tenant actually knows of that may damage the premises. You have no duty to repair a defect the tenant caused deliberately or negligently, so freeze damage from, for example, shutting off the heat in January is the tenant's responsibility and can be claimed from the deposit as damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. If you want advance notice before an extended absence or a move-out in cold weather, a minimum thermostat setting, or dripping faucets during a freeze warning, put those duties in the lease. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Bed Bug or Pest Statute in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on bed bugs or other pests in rental housing: no disclosure duty, no inspection or treatment schedule, and no specific tenant cooperation duty; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: the tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits, dispose of garbage and other waste in a clean and safe manner, and tell you about any condition the tenant actually knows of that may damage the premises. You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so check whether your city or county code requires pest control. Mississippi's landlord-tenant act gives you no statutory right of entry, so put an entry-for-inspection-and-treatment term in the lease. If you want specific cooperation duties (prompt reporting, preparing the unit for treatment, paying for treatment the tenant caused), write them into the lease or your written rules, which bind tenants when they meet the Act's reasonableness tests. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Extended-Absence Statute in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, and none giving you a special right to enter during one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The tenant must still tell you about any condition the tenant actually knows of that may damage the premises, and must not deliberately or negligently damage them. If you want notice of absences (for example, any absence over seven days) and a right to enter to protect the unit while the tenant is away, put both in the lease; the shared extended-absence clause does this. Do not treat a long absence as abandonment on your own: to recover the unit, use the Act's breach or termination notices and the residential eviction process, which removes occupants only by a sheriff's or constable's warrant. An older general statute lets a constable return the premises to a landlord when a tenant behind on rent has deserted them, after posting a notice and a second view 5 to 15 days later. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Tenant Right to Run a Home Child Care in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving a tenant the right to run a family child care home in a rental unit, and none limiting what your lease may say about it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The default rule instead is that, unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit. So you may prohibit home child care in the lease, allow it, or allow it on conditions such as your written consent, proof of any state license the tenant's operation needs, liability insurance naming you as an additional insured, and compliance with local zoning. Any written rule you adopt about it is enforceable only if it meets the Act's tests (a legitimate purpose, reasonably related to that purpose, applied fairly to all tenants, explicit, and not a way to avoid your own duties). Child care licensing and local zoning rules were not reviewed here, so check them before you approve a request. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Home Businesses: No Mississippi Statute, and the Lease Controls
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a residential rental or limiting how a lease may restrict one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The landlord-tenant act's default is that, unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit. So decide in the lease: prohibit business use, allow quiet work-from-home use (computer and phone work with no customer traffic, signs, employees on site or inventory storage), or allow more with your written consent. A written rule about business use binds the tenant only if it serves a legitimate purpose such as safety, the welfare of other tenants or protecting your property, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies fairly to all tenants, and is explicit. Whatever the lease allows, the tenant must not disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment or engage in illegal activity on the premises, and local zoning may separately limit home occupations (not reviewed here). These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Co-Tenant Liability Statute in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute saying whether tenants who sign the same lease are each liable for the whole rent and all damage, or only for a share; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. So say it in the lease: the shared joint-and-several liability clause makes each tenant responsible for the full rent and all obligations, which is lawful in Mississippi. One statute does deal with co-signers: under the Derrick Beard Act, for leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011 (treat an earlier periodic tenancy as renewed), a cosigner may end the lease when the tenant dies (or, with several tenants, when all of them die) and is presumed to have ended it unless the cosigner notifies you within 30 days that the lease will continue; the estate and cosigner remain liable for sums owed before the death, the rest of the month or 30-day period of the death, and restoring the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear, and any waiver of this right is void. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Yard Work and Other Tenant Chores: A Good-Faith Written Agreement Is Enough in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi lets you and the tenant agree in writing that the tenant will perform some or all of your statutory maintenance duties, but only if the agreement is made in good faith. The statute does not require a separate signed writing, separate consideration, or a single-family home, so a clear term in the signed lease (such as the shared landscaping and irrigation clause) works for any dwelling unit, including apartments. Good faith means honesty and reasonable community standards of fair dealing, so keep the chores realistic for the property and the tenant, and do not use the clause to dodge major repairs. The agreement cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or relieve you of liability for your own willful misconduct. Apart from any agreement, the tenant must use facilities reasonably and not damage the premises, and you have no duty to fix damage the tenant caused deliberately or negligently. Spell out mowing, watering, irrigation-system care and who pays for equipment and water. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: A Tenant Sued for Ejectment Must Tell You at Once, and Attornment to a Stranger Is Void
bodyText: Mississippi puts a statutory duty on every tenant who is sued in a civil action seeking ejectment (a lawsuit by someone claiming the right to possession of the property): the tenant must give you notice of it immediately. A tenant who does not is liable to you for a penalty of three years' rent of the premises, which you may recover in a civil action. You may then ask the court for leave to appear and defend the case, separately or with the tenant, and a judgment binds you as if you had been named and served. Separately, a tenant's attornment to a stranger (agreeing to hold the property under, or pay rent to, someone else as landlord) is void unless you consent or a court judgment or decree requires it. The statute does not cover other papers, such as foreclosure notices or code-enforcement orders, so the shared clause asking the tenant to forward any notice of proceedings against the property is still useful. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Unpaid Garbage Fees Can Become a Lien on Your Rental Property
bodyText: In Mississippi, county and city garbage or rubbish fees are charged jointly and severally to the person who generates the garbage (usually your tenant) and to the owner of the property served, so you can be billed for a tenant's unpaid garbage fees. Unpaid fees become a lien on the real property; the county or city must mail you a notice of the lien, the property cannot be sold to satisfy it, delinquent fees can block motor vehicle tag renewals, and a county may instead put the fees on your property tax bill as a special assessment. A tenant who pays for garbage service as part of the rent is not liable if you fail to pay. So decide in the lease who pays garbage fees, require the tenant to show proof of payment, and watch for lien notices. A search of the Mississippi Code found no statute making a tenant's unpaid water, sewer, gas or electric bill a lien on your property; check your city or utility district rules. This applies equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Occupancy Limits: No Mississippi Statute, so Set a Reasonable Limit in the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi has no statewide statute setting how many people may live in a rental unit, no persons-per-bedroom or floor-area standard, and no rule letting neighbors enforce an occupancy limit; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act defines a dwelling unit as a home for one person keeping a household or two or more people keeping a common household, and you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so check your city or county code for occupancy standards. In the lease, list the people allowed to live in the unit and require your written consent for anyone else (the shared permitted-occupants clause does this). Keep any limit reasonable and tied to the unit's size and systems: federal fair housing law forbids discriminating against families with children, and an overly strict limit can be challenged on that ground. Written rules on guests and occupancy bind tenants only if they meet the Act's reasonableness tests. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Using a Rental for Prostitution or Illegal Drugs Voids the Lease Under Mississippi's Nuisance Law
bodyText: Mississippi's nuisance chapter provides that if a tenant or occupant uses the premises as a nuisance, that use annuls and voids the lease and returns the right of possession to you without any act on your part. "Nuisance" here is narrow: a place where lewdness, assignation or prostitution is conducted or permitted, or where a controlled substance is unlawfully used, possessed, sold or delivered; one single act does not count. The statute says the owner may enter without process of law, but no case law was searched on how that fits the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's eviction procedure, so do not change locks or remove anyone yourself; file a residential eviction. The Act also requires every tenant not to engage in illegal activity on the leased premises as documented by a law enforcement agency, so documented criminal use is a material breach supporting a 14-day notice or, where it materially affects health or safety, termination without a notice period (the eviction complaint still needs a written notice attached). State in the lease that illegal use of the premises is a default. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Residential Use Only: The Mississippi Default and Your Remedy
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets the default: unless you agree otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit. The shared residential-use clause repeats that rule; any exception you allow (for example, quiet home-office work) should be in writing. If the tenant materially breaches it, deliver a written notice naming the breach and stating that the rental agreement ends on a date at least 14 days after receipt unless the breach is remedied within that time (e-mail or text works only if the tenant agreed in writing, and because the electronic transactions law excludes default and eviction notices for a primary residence, also deliver paper). A cure keeps the agreement alive; a substantially similar repeat within six months, absent due care, allows termination on 14 days' notice without cure. Use of the premises for prostitution or illegal drugs falls under the separate nuisance statute. Week-to-week and month-to-month tenancies can also simply be ended with 7 or 30 days' written notice; a fixed-term tenancy needs the breach notice.

title: Disturbing Neighbors: The Mississippi Tenant's Statutory Duty and Your Remedies
bodyText: Every tenant under Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act must behave, and make everyone on the premises with the tenant's consent behave, in a way that does not disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of their premises. The shared no-disturbance clause repeats that duty. A material breach lets you deliver a written notice naming the conduct and stating that the agreement ends at least 14 days after receipt unless it is remedied within that time; a substantially similar repeat within six months, absent due care, allows termination on 14 days' notice with no cure. E-mail or text works only if the tenant agreed in writing, and the electronic transactions law excludes default and eviction notices for a primary residence, so also deliver paper. Where the violation is substantial and materially affects health or safety, no termination notice period is required (but deliver a written notice, because the eviction complaint must attach one), and the court may set a move-out date sooner than the usual seven days. Separately, using the premises for prostitution or illegal drugs voids the lease under the nuisance statute. Week-to-week and month-to-month tenancies can also be ended with 7 or 30 days' written notice.

title: What Mississippi Law Forbids Tenants to Do
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act forbids every tenant to deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so; to disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment (the tenant answers for guests too); and to engage in illegal activity on the leased premises as documented by a law enforcement agency. Unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant may also use the unit only as a dwelling. Under the separate nuisance statute, using the premises for prostitution or for unlawful use, possession, sale or delivery of controlled substances (more than a single act) voids the lease. A material breach of these duties supports the Act's 14-day breach notice, and a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety supports termination without a notice period (the eviction complaint must still attach a written notice). Your lease may add further prohibitions (smoking, hazardous materials, unapproved alterations) as lease terms or written rules; rules bind only if they meet the Act's reasonableness tests. These duties apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenants alike.

title: Subletting and Assignment: No Mississippi Statute, so the Lease Controls
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on whether a residential tenant may sublet or assign, whether you must consent, whether you must be reasonable in refusing, or how fast you must answer a request; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. So the lease controls: the shared no-sublet-or-assign clause (no subletting or assignment without your prior written consent) is lawful in Mississippi. Keep any approval process within your control; a lease term that treats your silence as consent, or a deadline you might miss, can give away the protection you meant to keep. If you do allow a sublease, the tenant who sublets becomes the subtenant's landlord under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which defines a landlord to include a sublessor, so the Act's duties and notices run between them as well. On your side, a buyer or assignee of your interest in the property can enforce the lease against the tenant as you could. Every duty under the Act carries an obligation of good faith. These rules apply equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Statute on Tenant Insurance or Insurance Claims in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring tenants to carry renters insurance, forbidding you to require it, or governing how a tenant's or landlord's insurance claim (including subrogation, where an insurer that paid a loss sues the person who caused it) works between you; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. So the lease controls. You may require renters insurance with liability coverage and ask for proof, and you may say that your property insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. Be careful with any clause that releases you from losses: Mississippi forbids a rental agreement to exculpate or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct, so word any waiver or release to exclude willful misconduct. The tenant remains liable for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes, and you may claim reasonable repair costs (beyond ordinary wear and tear) from the deposit. Rules on casualty losses (fire and destruction) are covered under the fire and casualty topics. These rules apply equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Tenant Upkeep in Mississippi, Including Septic Systems and Wells
bodyText: Every Mississippi tenant under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act must keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits, dispose of garbage and waste cleanly and safely, keep plumbing fixtures clean, use electrical, plumbing, heating, cooling and other facilities and appliances reasonably, not damage the premises, tell you about conditions that may cause damage, and, to the extent of the tenant's legal obligation, maintain the unit in substantially the same condition (wear and tear excepted) and follow health-and-safety codes. You may also agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs some of your maintenance duties. Septic systems: the state health department may order the property owner and/or lessee to repair a malfunctioning individual on-site wastewater system within 30 days of notice, with a civil penalty of up to $5 a day afterward (that section is scheduled for repeal July 1, 2028). The Code has no private-well rule for rentals. So say in the lease who maintains the septic system and well, and require the tenant to report problems promptly. These duties are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi lets you and the tenant agree in writing that the tenant will perform some or all of your statutory duties to comply with health-and-safety codes and to keep the unit, plumbing, and heating and/or cooling in substantially their move-in condition, but only if the deal is made in good faith. There is one subsection with one formality: a writing, in good faith. It needs no separate document, no separate payment and no single-family limit, so it can sit in the lease of any dwelling unit. It is subject to the anti-waiver rule: the agreement cannot strip the tenant of rights or remedies under the Act or relieve you of liability for your own willful misconduct. Good faith means honesty and reasonable fair dealing, so match the tasks to the tenant's ability and the rent, and do not shift major systems to a tenant who cannot handle them. Separately, without any agreement, a tenant may repair a material defect you leave unfixed 30 days after written notice and be reimbursed, within strict limits. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: The Mississippi Tenant's Statutory Duties
