bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lists nine duties every tenant has whether or not the lease repeats them: keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of ashes, rubbish, garbage and other waste cleanly and safely; keep plumbing fixtures clean; use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances (including elevators) reasonably; not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else; behave, and make guests behave, so as not to disturb neighbors; tell you about any known condition that may damage the premises; to the extent of the tenant's legal obligation, keep the unit in substantially the same condition (wear and tear excepted) and follow health-and-safety codes; and not engage in illegal activity on the premises as documented by law enforcement. A material breach supports the Act's 14-day breach notice, and you have no repair duty for defects the tenant causes. The Act applies to rental agreements entered into after July 1, 1991, except institutional, transient hotel or motel, condominium-owner and certain other occupancies. The duties are the same for all tenancy types.

title: Smoking Bans and Mississippi's Medical Cannabis Act
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute regulating smoking or vaping in private rental housing: no required smoking-policy disclosure, no smoke-drift nuisance rule, and no limit on adopting a smoke-free policy; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Medical Cannabis Act says a landlord may, but is not required to, allow the lawful cultivation, processing, sale or use of medical cannabis on rental property, so a lease may ban smoking or vaping cannabis, or all medical cannabis use, on the premises, including by registered patients. The Act also says a landlord may not be penalized or denied a state-law benefit for leasing to a cardholder. Put the policy in the lease (the shared smoking clause), cover tobacco, cannabis and vaping devices, and say where outdoor smoking is allowed. A smoking ban adopted mid-lease as a written rule binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if it is not a substantial modification of the rental agreement, so for current tenants add it at renewal or by signed amendment. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Who Pays Utilities in Mississippi, and the Rules When You Collect for Them
bodyText: Mississippi lets the lease decide who pays which utilities; no statute assigns them. Three statutes matter. First, if you collect money under a lease to pay utility services (water, electricity, gas, heat or sewer), it is a crime to knowingly, willfully and unlawfully fail to apply it to the bill within 60 days of receiving the bill, unless the tenant failed to pay enough or the delay came from the utility's own error; penalties scale with the amount and include restitution. Second, in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer, you may submeter water and wastewater only with written disclosure and the tenant's written acknowledgment, may charge no more than the tenant's pro rata share, and may not disconnect for unpaid submetered bills. Third, county and city garbage fees fall jointly on the tenant and you as owner and can become a lien on the property, unless the tenant pays for garbage through the rent. No statute was found letting a utility refuse a new tenant service over a former occupant's bill. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Submetered Water: No Disconnection for Unpaid Submeter Bills in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's only submetering statute covers water and wastewater in an apartment house (one or more buildings with four or more dwelling units rented monthly or longer, including a residential condominium), a condominium, or a manufactured home community. If you submeter there, you may not disconnect the tenant's water and wastewater service for nonpayment of submetered bills; collect unpaid charges as you would other sums due under the lease. Each submeter bill must show beginning and ending readings, state that it is not from the public utility, and give a phone number for tenant questions; charges may not exceed the tenant's pro rata share, submeters must meet American Water Works Association accuracy standards, and the tenant must acknowledge the submetering in writing (see the water-submetering clause). Submetering electricity or gas falls outside that statute and can make you a public utility, so get advice before doing it, and never shut off service yourself to force payment. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies; smaller properties fall outside the statute.

title: Checking a Tenant's Utility Payments in Mississippi
bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires or forbids a lease term making the tenant show proof that utilities in the tenant's name are paid; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, so the shared utility-payment-evidence clause is lawful. It is worth using here because county and city garbage fees are charged jointly to the tenant and to you as owner and can become a lien on your property if unpaid, unless the tenant pays for garbage as part of the rent. Asking for receipts lets you catch arrears before a lien notice arrives. If instead you collect money from the tenant to pay a utility bill, keep your own records too: failing knowingly, willfully and unlawfully to apply that money to the bill within 60 days of receiving it is a crime, unless the tenant did not pay enough or the utility caused the delay. A tenant's unpaid utility bill owed under the lease is a breach you can address with the Act's 14-day notice. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Keeping Utilities On in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no general statute forbidding a landlord to shut off a tenant's utilities, and no statutory lockout ban; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Two narrower rules apply. If you submeter water in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer, you may not disconnect the tenant's water and wastewater for unpaid submetered bills. And if the lease has the tenant pay you for utilities, knowingly, willfully and unlawfully failing to apply that money to the bill within 60 days of receiving it is a crime (unless the tenant underpaid or the utility caused the delay). Beyond that, you must keep the plumbing and heating and/or cooling in substantially their move-in condition and comply with health-and-safety codes, every act toward ending or removing a tenancy carries a duty of good faith, and possession is recovered through the residential eviction process. So never cut utilities to force payment or a move-out; keep landlord-paid services current and give notice of planned interruptions for repairs. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Tenant Alterations in Mississippi: The Lease Decides, Within Limits
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on tenant alterations generally, so your lease may require your written consent before any alteration (the shared no-alterations clause). By statute the tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, and you may claim the cost of repairing tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear from the deposit. Your consent has a lien consequence: under the construction lien law, a contractor hired by a tenant can claim a lien on the improvement and the tenant's leasehold, but without your written consent only detachable improvements and the tenant's estate are exposed, not your land. So give consent narrowly. Mississippi has no state law requiring you to allow disability-related modifications in private housing, but the federal Fair Housing Act does: unless an exemption applies, you must permit reasonable modifications at the disabled resident's expense and may, where reasonable, condition approval on restoring the interior at move-out. No Mississippi statute addresses tenant-installed detectors or lock changes. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Contractor Liens for Work a Tenant Orders in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's construction lien law has a section for leased property. When a tenant in possession hires someone to build or improve, and the work does not violate the lease, the contractor's lien attaches to the improvement and the unexpired lease term; the lienholder may keep the lease alive by paying you the rent, and a buyer at a lien sale may take over the rest of the term by paying rent, or remove the improvement within 60 days if it comes off without injuring the real property. You may discharge the lien before a sale by paying it, or keep the improvement after a sale by paying its value. Most important: unless the work was done with your written consent as owner, only detachable improvements and the tenant's estate are subject to the lien, not your land. So give alteration consent narrowly, say in the lease that consent does not make you responsible to pay, and require the tenant to pay its contractors and clear any lien. A lien claim must be filed within 90 days after the last work and mailed to the owner within two business days. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Move-In Condition Is the Benchmark in Mississippi, so Document It
bodyText: Mississippi has no required move-in checklist or condition report and no rule that a signed report creates a presumption; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. But the condition at the start of the lease is the yardstick on both sides. You must maintain the dwelling unit, its plumbing, and heating and/or cooling in substantially the same condition as at the inception of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded; the tenant, to the extent of the tenant's legal obligation, must keep the unit in substantially the same condition, wear and tear excepted; and you may claim from the deposit the reasonable cost of repairing damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear. When a cosigner ends a lease after the tenant's death, the estate and cosigner still owe the cost of restoring the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy. So use the shared existing-condition clause, complete a dated written inspection with photos signed by both sides at move-in, and repeat it at move-out. This matters equally for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms: No Mississippi Rental Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to install, test or maintain smoke or carbon monoxide alarms in rental housing, and none assigning that duty to tenants; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The only statutory detector rules found cover fraternity and sorority houses on state property and hotels and lodging houses (an approved fire detector on each floor), which reaches you if you rent rooms in a lodging house. The statewide Fire Prevention Code reaches only certain buildings (state buildings, buildings for public assembly where no equally strict local code exists, and buildings permitted after July 1, 1978 that are at least 75 feet tall), and counties and cities may adopt their own fire codes. You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so check your local code, which may require alarms. Good practice is to install working smoke alarms in each sleeping area and on each level, carbon monoxide alarms where there is fuel-burning equipment or an attached garage, test them at move-in, and make the tenant responsible in the lease for batteries, monthly testing and reporting failures. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Duty to Provide Alternate Housing
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to provide or pay for alternate housing when a unit becomes unlivable during repairs, after a fire or storm, or after a code closure; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: a tenant does not owe rent for buildings after they are destroyed by fire or otherwise, unless the tenant's negligence or fault caused it or the tenant expressly agreed to be bound; and if you materially fail to keep up the unit or comply with health-and-safety codes, the tenant may give a 14-day breach notice and end the tenancy, or use the limited repair-and-deduct remedy. If you want to offer substitute housing, a rent abatement, or a right for either side to end the lease after a casualty, put it in the lease so expectations are set before a loss. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, though a periodic tenancy can also simply be ended with 7 or 30 days' written notice.

title: Appliances Left at the Property: No Mississippi Presumption
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute presuming that appliances present at move-in are supplied by the landlord, and none barring you from excluding an appliance from the rental; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What matters is what the lease says. Your statutory maintenance duty covers the dwelling unit, its plumbing, and its heating and/or cooling system, kept in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, so heating and cooling equipment you supply cannot be carved out of that duty except by a good-faith written agreement for the tenant to take it over. For other appliances (refrigerator, range, washer, dryer, dishwasher), list in the lease which ones you supply and maintain and which, such as a previous tenant's leftover washer, are left "as is" for the tenant's use at the tenant's own risk and repair, without disclaiming liability for your own willful misconduct. The tenant must use all appliances reasonably whoever owns them. These rules apply equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Appliances You Supply in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's statutory repair duty names the dwelling unit, its plumbing and its heating and/or cooling system, which you must keep in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded. Other appliances are not named, but a lease that lists appliances you supply and promises to maintain them makes that promise part of the rental agreement. If you materially fail to keep it, the tenant may give a 14-day breach notice and end the tenancy, or, after 30 days' written notice of a specific and material defect, repair it and be reimbursed (only if the tenant is current in rent, has met the tenant's own duties, has not used the remedy in the past six months, and the cost does not exceed one month's rent or the usual and customary charge). You have no duty for damage the tenant causes deliberately or negligently, and the tenant must use appliances reasonably. So list each appliance supplied, say who repairs it and how to report problems (the shared appliances-included clause), and note its condition at move-in. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Common-Area Lighting: No Mississippi Landlord-Tenant Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to light hallways, stairways, entrances or parking areas, and none on billing a tenant for common-area lights wired to the tenant's meter; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's "premises" include the grounds, areas and facilities held out for tenants generally, and you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so a local code lighting requirement for shared areas binds you. Common-area lighting also bears on security and injury claims, which were not reviewed here. If a two-unit or small building has shared lights on one tenant's meter, disclose that in the lease and adjust the rent or utility terms so the arrangement is agreed in writing at the start; the Act does not allow you to change it mid-lease by a rule that substantially modifies the rental agreement. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That Mississippi Lacks
bodyText: Mississippi's habitability law is short: you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the dwelling unit, plumbing, and heating and/or cooling in substantially their move-in condition, reasonable wear and tear excluded. A search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none of these common rules from other states: a statutory list of essential services; a minimum heat or temperature standard; a tenant right to withhold rent or pay it into court; rent abatement for defects (beyond reimbursement or offset under the limited repair-and-deduct remedy); a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm duty; mold, bed bug or pest rules; a required habitability statement in the lease; a statewide rent bar for condemned units; a duty to provide alternate housing; and retaliation protection for tenants who complain (the only retaliation language bars a post-expiration rent increase made mainly to retaliate for a tenant's lawful actions). The tenant's remedies are the 14-day breach notice and termination, repair and deduct, and ordinary court remedies. Local housing codes may add standards. These points apply to all tenancy types.

title: Designated Repairers: No Mississippi Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a landlord name a designated repairer that tenants must call, or requiring tenants to use licensed contractors; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The relevant rule is the repair-and-deduct remedy: if you do not repair a specific, material defect within 30 days after the tenant's written notice, the tenant may repair it and be reimbursed within 45 days of giving you receipted bills, but only up to the usual and customary charge, only if the cost does not exceed one month's rent, and only if the tenant is current in rent, has met the tenant's own statutory duties and has not used the remedy in the previous six months. A tenant repairing shared facilities must first notify the other tenants who share them. Because rights under the Act cannot be waived, a lease may list your preferred repair contacts and require tenants to report problems to them first, but should not be written to take away the statutory remedy. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Disability Accommodations in Mississippi Rentals: Federal Law Governs
bodyText: Mississippi has no general state fair housing law requiring private landlords to make reasonable accommodations or allow reasonable modifications for tenants with disabilities, no rule on restoration deposits, and no requirement that the lease contain a restoration term; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The state's anti-discrimination housing provision reaches only Mississippi Home Corporation housing developments and loans, and the state support animal law covers public accommodations such as hotels, lodging places and businesses open to the public, not ordinary leases. The federal Fair Housing Act does apply to most rentals: unless an exemption applies, you must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies and services (for example, allowing an assistance animal despite a no-pets rule, without a pet fee) and allow reasonable modifications at the resident's expense, and where reasonable you may condition an interior modification on restoration at move-out. Handle requests in writing, promptly and consistently, and have a lawyer review any exemption you rely on. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Employee Background Checks: No Mississippi Mandate for Rental Staff
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring landlords or property managers to run criminal background checks on maintenance staff, leasing agents or other employees who may enter tenants' units; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none (the background-check statutes found cover specific licensed occupations and regulated businesses, not rental housing). Screening is still prudent, because you remain ultimately liable for duties you hand to an agent, and anyone with keys has access to tenants' homes and belongings. If you screen, follow the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act for consumer reports (written disclosure, written authorization and adverse-action notices). If you keep employees' or tenants' names together with Social Security, driver's license or financial account numbers in electronic form, Mississippi's data-breach law requires you to notify affected residents without unreasonable delay after an unauthorized acquisition of unencrypted data; the Attorney General enforces it. Limit key access, log entries and give notice before staff enter. These points apply to all tenancy types.

title: Double-Letting: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on double-letting, that is, renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and no special rent-abatement remedy for it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. General rules apply instead. Each rental agreement binds you, every duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act carries an obligation of good faith, and a tenant whose agreement you materially breach may give a 14-day breach notice and end the tenancy, recover prepaid unearned rent and the recoverable deposit, and pursue other remedies at law (case law was not searched). So avoid the problem: do not sign a second lease until the current tenant has delivered possession or the tenancy has ended under its notice, and put a possession-delay clause in the lease (the shared possession-delay clause) saying what happens if you cannot deliver the unit on the start date, such as no rent until possession and the tenant's right to cancel. These rules apply equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Which Defects Count Under Mississippi Law: Material Ones Affecting Health and Safety
bodyText: Mississippi's landlord-tenant act repeatedly limits the tenant's remedies to serious problems. Your code duty covers building and housing code requirements materially affecting health and safety. The tenant may end the tenancy only for your material noncompliance with the rental agreement or your statutory duties, after a 14-day notice you can cure. Repair and deduct applies only to a specific and material defect that breaches the rental agreement or your duties and that you leave unrepaired 30 days after written notice. Termination without notice is allowed only for a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety. The Act does not define "material" or list qualifying defects, so cosmetic or minor issues (worn paint, a dripping faucet) generally will not support these remedies, while loss of heat, plumbing failure or a code violation threatening safety likely will; case law, which decides the close cases, was not searched. Your separate duty to keep the unit, plumbing and heating and/or cooling in substantially move-in condition is not qualified by materiality. Respond to every written repair request promptly and in writing. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Can the Lease Change Mississippi's Repair Duties? Only by a Good-Faith Written Shift to the Tenant
bodyText: Mississippi forbids a landlord and tenant to agree to waive or give up any right, duty or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act except where the Act itself allows it, and forbids any lease term that exculpates or limits your liability for your own willful misconduct or that authorizes confession of judgment. The Act's one built-in exception for repairs: you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs some or all of your duties to comply with health-and-safety codes and to maintain the unit, plumbing and heating and/or cooling. So you cannot simply disclaim the duties ("landlord makes no repairs"), but you can shift specific tasks to a tenant who knowingly takes them on, for example a single-family tenant who agrees to handle yard, filter or minor plumbing upkeep. The statute has no special rule for premises without utility water or for other particular duties. Keep any shift specific, fair and written, and do not use it to avoid code compliance on systems the tenant cannot realistically maintain. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Move-In Form That Deems You in Compliance in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute under which a signed move-in defect form, inspection or certificate makes you presumed or deemed to be in compliance with your repair duties; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Instead, your maintenance duty is measured against the condition at the inception of the lease: you must keep the dwelling unit, plumbing and heating and/or cooling in substantially that condition, reasonable wear and tear excluded, and comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety whatever the form says. Because move-in condition is the benchmark, a dated move-in inspection signed by both sides, with photos, is your best evidence of what you must maintain and what damage the tenant caused later, but it is evidence, not a legal presumption, and it cannot waive your code duty. You have no duty to repair defects the tenant causes deliberately or negligently. These rules apply equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Required Fitness Statement in Mississippi Leases
bodyText: Mississippi does not require your lease to state that the unit is fit for habitation or that you will deliver it in habitable condition; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them: you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the dwelling unit, plumbing and heating and/or cooling in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, and these duties cannot be waived except by a good-faith written agreement for the tenant to take some on. You may summarize them in the lease (the shared maintenance clause does), but avoid sweeping promises beyond the statute, such as guaranteeing the unit is free of all defects, because a lease promise becomes part of the rental agreement the tenant can enforce through the breach notice and repair-and-deduct remedies. Note that some cities can declare a building unfit for human habitation and order it closed. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Health Department Rental Rules: None Statewide in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving the state or a local health department rental-housing regulations that a landlord must provide to tenants on request, and no statutory procedure for referring tenant complaints to a health department; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Health rules reach rentals in narrower ways: the state health department can order a property owner and/or lessee to repair a malfunctioning on-site wastewater (septic) system within 30 days of notice, and cities that adopt the state's unfit-building ordinances can order unfit dwellings repaired or closed. Your general duty is to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, which includes any local health or housing ordinance where your property sits. Check with your city or county code office for local rental or housing standards, and keep records of inspections and repairs. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Heating and Air Conditioning in Mississippi: Keep What Was There at Move-In
bodyText: Mississippi does not require every rental to have heat or air conditioning, and sets no minimum indoor temperature; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found no temperature standard. What the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires is that you maintain the dwelling unit's heating and/or cooling system in substantially the same condition as at the inception of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded, unless the tenant damaged it deliberately or negligently. So if the unit had working central air at move-in, you must keep it working; a material failure supports the tenant's 14-day breach notice and, after 30 days' written notice, the limited repair-and-deduct remedy. You may shift heating or cooling upkeep (such as filter changes) to the tenant only by a written, good-faith agreement. The tenant must use heating, ventilating and air conditioning equipment reasonably. If the lease has the tenant pay you for heat or other utilities, you must apply that money to the bill within 60 days of receiving the bill; knowingly failing to is a crime. Check local housing codes, which may set heat standards. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Your Repair and Maintenance Duties in Mississippi
bodyText: Under Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act you must, at all times during the tenancy, comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and maintain the dwelling unit, its plumbing, and its heating and/or cooling system in substantially the same condition as at the inception of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded. You have no duty for defects the tenant or the tenant's guests cause deliberately or negligently, or that result from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's own statutory duties. You and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs some or all of these duties, but they cannot otherwise be waived, and no lease may exculpate you for your own willful misconduct. If you materially fail, the tenant may end the tenancy after a 14-day breach notice or repair and deduct after 30 days' written notice. The Act lists no essential services and sets no repair deadline beyond those remedies. Cities may also order unfit buildings repaired or closed. Use the shared maintenance clause and answer repair requests in writing. These duties apply to all tenancy types.

title: What a Mississippi Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the rental agreement or your statutory duties, a Mississippi tenant has these remedies. Breach notice: the tenant may deliver a written notice (e-mail or text only if you agreed in writing, and a paper copy is safer) naming the breach and ending the agreement on a date at least 14 days after you receive it unless you remedy it within that time; a cure stops termination, but a substantially similar repeat within six months, absent due care, allows termination on 14 days' notice with no cure. On termination you must return prepaid unearned rent and the recoverable deposit. Repair and deduct: 30 days after written notice of a specific, material defect, the tenant may repair it and be reimbursed within 45 days of giving you receipted bills, or offset the cost against future rent, if the tenant is current in rent, met the tenant's own duties, did not use the remedy in the prior six months and spent no more than one month's rent or the usual charge. A health-or-safety violation needs no termination notice. Other legal remedies remain. The Act gives no rent withholding or escrow right.

title: Condemned Buildings: Renting a Closed Unit Can Be Fined, but No Statewide Rent Bar
bodyText: Mississippi has no statewide statute saying a landlord may not collect rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated. But cities that adopt the state's unfit-building ordinances may, after notice and a hearing, order an owner to repair a building unfit for human habitation or to vacate and close it, and if the owner does not comply, have it vacated, closed and placarded. Anyone who then rents, leases or occupies that building as a dwelling, or permits someone to, is liable for the fine the city's ordinance sets. So do not rent, renew or keep collecting rent for a closed and placarded unit. Separately, a tenant owes no rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise unless the tenant's negligence or fault caused it or the tenant expressly agreed to be bound, and a material failure to comply with health-and-safety codes lets the tenant give a 14-day breach notice and end the tenancy. Check your city's ordinance; county rules were not reviewed. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to the Tenant: Allowed in Writing and in Good Faith
bodyText: Mississippi does not list particular conditions you may hand to the tenant, and it sets no landlord precondition. Instead, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant will perform some or all of your statutory duties (complying with health-and-safety building and housing codes and keeping the unit, its plumbing and its heating and/or cooling in substantially move-in condition), but only if the deal is made in good faith. A term in the signed lease is enough; no separate document is required. The agreement cannot strip the tenant of rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or excuse your own willful misconduct. Some Mississippi forms make the tenant pay the first set dollar amount of every repair; if you use one, keep the amount modest, put it in the signed lease and do not let it limit the tenant's notice, termination or repair-and-deduct remedies. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Services and Utilities You Provide: The Lease Sets Them, Within Three Statutory Limits
bodyText: Mississippi does not list services or utilities a landlord must furnish. Your statutory duties are to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the dwelling unit, its plumbing and its heating and/or cooling system in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded, so heating or cooling equipment present at move-in must be maintained. Everything else (water, trash, internet, lawn care) is what the lease says you provide, and a promise you make becomes a term the tenant can enforce. A lease may not excuse your liability for your own willful misconduct, so limit any interruption disclaimer to causes beyond your reasonable control, as the shared services-utilities-provided clause does. If tenants pay you for utilities, apply that money to the bills on time, and follow the water-submetering rules for apartment houses or condominiums of four or more units and manufactured home communities where rent is paid monthly or longer. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Utilities You Pay: Apply Tenant Utility Money Within 60 Days of the Bill
bodyText: Mississippi lets the lease decide which utilities you pay; no statute requires you to furnish any particular utility. Two statutes matter when you do. First, if the tenant pays you money under the lease to cover utility services (water, electricity, gas, heat or sewer), it is a crime to knowingly, willfully and unlawfully fail to apply it to the bill within 60 days of receiving the bill, or to use deception about it, unless the tenant did not pay enough or the delay came from the utility company's own error; penalties rise with the amount and include restitution. Second, if you submeter water in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer, you must disclose it and get the tenant's written acknowledgment, charge no more than the tenant's pro rata share, and never disconnect water for unpaid submeter bills. Keep landlord-paid accounts current, since a shutoff can breach the lease. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Water Submetering: Written Disclosure and Acknowledgment Required in Covered Properties
bodyText: If you submeter water and wastewater in an apartment house (one or more buildings with four or more dwelling units, occupied mainly for nontransient use, with rent paid monthly or less often), a condominium, or a manufactured home community, Mississippi requires you to disclose the submetering to each tenant and get the tenant's acknowledgment in a written document; use the library's water-submetering lease clause. Charges may not exceed the tenant's pro rata share of all water and wastewater used by all tenants, submeters must meet American Water Works Association accuracy standards, each bill must show beginning and ending readings, state that it is not from the public utility and give a phone number for questions, and you may not disconnect water for unpaid submeter bills. The statute sets no type size, no separate-page rule and no late-fee cap. It does not cover electricity or gas, or smaller buildings; metered billing outside it can make you a public utility, so get advice. The rules apply to all tenancy types in covered properties.

title: No Mississippi Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to furnish a stove, range, refrigerator or other kitchen appliance; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your statutory maintenance duty names only the dwelling unit, its plumbing, and its heating and/or cooling system, kept in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, plus compliance with health-and-safety building and housing codes, so check whether a local housing code requires cooking or refrigeration equipment. If you do supply appliances, list them in the lease and say who repairs them: a promise to maintain them becomes part of the rental agreement, enforceable by the tenant's 14-day breach notice or the limited repair-and-deduct remedy. If you leave an appliance only for the tenant's convenience, say so in the lease, without disclaiming liability for your own willful misconduct. The tenant must use all appliances reasonably. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Do Not Make Repairs in Mississippi
bodyText: A Mississippi tenant has two statutory remedies when you materially fail to keep up the unit. First, the tenant may give you a written notice (or e-mail or text, if you agreed in writing to that) describing the breach and stating that the rental agreement ends on a date at least 14 days after you receive it unless you remedy it within that time; if you fix it in time, the lease continues. Second, if you fail to repair a specific and material defect within 30 days after written notice, the tenant may make the repair and be reimbursed within 45 days of giving you receipted bills, or offset the cost against future rent, but only if the tenant has met the tenant's own duties, is current in rent, has not used the remedy in the past six months, and the cost does not exceed one month's rent or the usual and customary charge. The tenant gets no lien on the property. There is no rent-escrow or rent-withholding statute. The lease cannot waive these remedies.

title: No Rent Escrow in Mississippi, So No Escrow Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states let tenants pay rent into a court or city escrow account while repairs are outstanding and require landlords who are exempt to say so in the lease. Mississippi has no rent-escrow program and no exemption notice; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, so there is nothing to disclose. The tenant's repair remedies are a 14-day breach notice that ends the lease if you do not remedy a material breach, and, after 30 days' written notice of a specific and material defect, a limited right to repair and be reimbursed or offset the cost against future rent (capped at one month's rent and usable once in six months, only if the tenant is current in rent and has met the tenant's own duties). Do not add a clause claiming an escrow exemption or telling the tenant to pay rent into court. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession in Mississippi Residential Leases
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that writes a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into residential leases; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Whether an implied covenant binds you is case law, which was not searched, so assume a court may find one. The statutes protect possession in other ways. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act makes every tenant behave so as not to disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of their premises, so you can enforce that duty with the Act's 14-day breach notice. Anyone deprived of possession of land by force, intimidation, fraud, stratagem or stealth has a summary court remedy to get it back. And every act toward ending a tenancy or removing a tenant must be in good faith, with removal done by the sheriff or a constable under a court warrant. So never lock out a tenant, remove belongings or cut services to force a move; give the statutory notice and file a residential eviction. These rules apply to every type of tenancy.

title: Repair Promises: No Mississippi Writing Rule, but a Promise Becomes a Lease Term
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date or to be made before the lease is signed; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. But a promise matters. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lets the tenant end the tenancy on 14 days' notice for your material noncompliance with the rental agreement, and lets the tenant repair and be reimbursed for a specific and material defect that breaches the rental agreement if you have not fixed it 30 days after written notice, within the Act's limits. A promised repair written into the lease, or agreed orally (the Act covers oral agreements too), can therefore be enforced like your statutory duties. Put every repair promise in the lease or a signed addendum with a clear scope and target date, and promise only what you will do. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Hiring a Manager Does Not Shift Your Repair Duties; No Rule on Assigning Rents
bodyText: Mississippi has one rule on separating rent collection from your duties: you may contract with an agent, such as a property manager, to take on all of your rights and duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, but that contract does not relieve you of ultimate liability for them, and notice to your agent counts as notice to you. The Act's "landlord" includes the owner, lessor, sublessor and their agent, and the parties cannot waive the Act's duties in the rental agreement. No statute addresses splitting rent from repair duties by an assignment of rents, deed, deed of trust or other security instrument; a search of the Code and Constitution found none. A buyer or assignee of your interest may enforce the lease against the tenant, and a transferee who keeps a deposit in bad faith faces the deposit penalty. If you hire a manager or assign rents, make the documents say who repairs and who holds deposits. This applies to all tenancy types.

title: No Statewide Rental Inspection Program, and No Lease-Authorized Inspector Entry
bodyText: Mississippi has no statewide rental registration or inspection program, and no statute lets a lease clause require the tenant to admit a housing inspector without the tenant's own consent; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Cities may adopt ordinances on buildings unfit for human habitation, under which a public officer investigates, holds a hearing and can order the owner to repair or to vacate and close the building, and the State Fire Marshal inspects only the limited classes of buildings the Fire Prevention Code covers. Check your city's ordinances for any local registration or inspection rules, which were not searched. Mississippi also has no landlord-entry statute, so your own right to enter for inspections and to bring inspectors or contractors comes from the lease; state it there, with reasonable notice, and schedule any government inspection with the tenant. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Repair Requests: The Tenant's Statutory Remedies Already Require Written Notice
bodyText: In Mississippi the tenant's repair remedies run from written notice. The repair-and-deduct remedy starts only after written notice to you of a specific and material defect and 30 days without repair, and the tenant's termination notice for your breach must be in writing (or by e-mail or text only if you agreed in writing to that). Separately, every tenant must tell you about any condition the tenant actually knows of that may damage the premises; the statute does not say how. A lease term asking the tenant to report repairs in writing, with an emergency phone line for urgent problems, therefore matches the statute and is lawful, as long as it does not take away any remedy the Act gives. Accepting a phone call does not waive written notice, but keep a written record of every request and repair. Notice to your property manager counts as notice to you. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: No Mississippi Cable, Satellite or Broadband Access Statute for Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving cable, satellite or internet providers a right of access to apartment buildings, requiring you to allow a tenant's choice of provider, or barring a rent difference for subscribers; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Federal Communications Commission rules on antennas and service in multiple-dwelling buildings were not reviewed here and may apply. Under state law the lease governs: say whether tenants may install dishes, antennas or wiring, where, who pays for installation and removal, and that installations must not damage the premises, since the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage any part of the premises. Any rule you adopt after the lease is signed must be reasonable, apply fairly to all tenants, be explicit, and not substantially modify the rental agreement. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: No Staff Work-Card or Background-Check Rule for 55+ Housing in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring work cards, fingerprinting or background checks for employees of senior (55 and older) apartment communities or other rental housing; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Licensed care settings, such as nursing homes or assisted-living facilities, fall under separate health-facility rules and are outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act when residence is incidental to medical, geriatric or similar services. For an ordinary age-restricted apartment community, screening of staff is your choice. If you run background checks, follow the federal consumer-reporting rules, which were not reviewed here, and keep screening consistent. Remember that a manager acts as your agent: hiring one does not relieve you of ultimate liability for your duties under the Act. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Code-Enforcement Receivership for Rentals; City Repair Orders Can Apply
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a city, county or tenants put a substandard rental building into receivership; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What does exist is a municipal option: a city that adopts ordinances on buildings unfit for human habitation can, after a complaint and a hearing, order the owner to repair, alter or improve the building or, at the owner's choice, vacate and close it. If the owner does not comply, the city may close and placard the building, and for a building that is dangerous because of dilapidation or defects it may have the work done or the building demolished, with the cost and a penalty of up to 20 percent becoming a lien collected as a special tax. Renting a closed, placarded building exposes you to the city's fine. Check your city's ordinance; county rules were not searched. Your own duty is to keep the unit code-compliant and in move-in condition. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Charging Tenants for Shared Utilities: Only Water Submetering Is Regulated
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute making unenforceable a lease term that has the tenant pay for utilities not separately metered to the unit, and none on ratio or allocation billing; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found only the water-submetering statute. That statute covers an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer: if you submeter water and wastewater there, the tenant's charges may not exceed the tenant's pro rata share of all water and wastewater used by all tenants, you must disclose the submetering and get a written acknowledgment, and you may not disconnect for unpaid submeter bills. For electricity, gas, or water outside that statute, the lease governs, but do not bill by meter or usage, which can make you a public utility: state the method (a flat fee is safest, since a share of the master bill by square footage or occupants may count as consumption billing), the services covered and how bills are shown to the tenant, and agree it at signing, since a later rule may not substantially modify the rental agreement. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Limit on Utility Allowances or Master-Meter Pass-Through in the Code
bodyText: The Mississippi Code has no statute limiting a landlord-set utility allowance or barring you from passing master-metered electricity or gas through to tenants other than in a fixed rent; a search of the Code and Constitution found none. But selling electricity, gas or water to tenants on a metered or consumption basis, other than water submetering under the statute below, takes you outside the tenant-service exclusion from the definition of a public utility, so get advice before billing by submeter or usage (Public Service Commission rules were not searched). The one statutory pass-through rule is for water: in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer, submetered water and wastewater charges may not exceed the tenant's pro rata share, must be disclosed and acknowledged in writing, and cannot lead to disconnection. Mississippi treats all payments due under the rental agreement as rent, so a utility charge in the lease is enforceable like rent unless the lease says otherwise; the shared allowance clause chooses not to treat it as rent, which is your concession. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Statute on Landlord Notice of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff
bodyText: No Mississippi statute lets you file an authorization with a utility to be told when a tenant's service is about to be disconnected, or lets a tenant designate you to receive copies of shutoff notices; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Public Service Commission rules and individual utility tariffs were not searched and may offer a third-party notice option, so ask your utilities. Two related points: notices cancelling or terminating utility service fall outside the Electronic Transactions Act, so expect them on paper, and if you submeter water in a covered building you may not disconnect it for unpaid submeter bills. To protect the property, require in the lease that the tenant keep tenant-paid utilities on, tell you promptly of any shutoff notice, and show proof of payment on request. A tenant's loss of service through nonpayment can be a material breach. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Transferring Utilities into the Tenant's Name
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring the tenant to transfer utilities into the tenant's name by a deadline, or letting you cut off landlord-name service the tenant failed to transfer; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. So the lease sets the rule: list which utilities the tenant must put in the tenant's name, the date by which service must be transferred, and that the tenant pays usage from the start of the term. If service stays in your name, any money the tenant pays you for it must be applied to the bill within 60 days of receiving the bill, or you risk a criminal charge. Do not shut off service to force a transfer; Mississippi has no statute authorizing that, and an interruption of heating, cooling or plumbing can breach your own duties. Treat a failure to transfer as a lease breach and bill the tenant for the usage. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Utilities in Your Name: Failing to Apply Tenant Payments Is a Crime
bodyText: When a utility account is in your name and the lease has the tenant pay you for it, Mississippi makes it a crime to knowingly, willfully and unlawfully fail to apply that money to the bill within 60 days of receiving the bill, or to use deception about it. It does not apply if the tenant did not pay enough to cover the bill or the delay came from the utility company's own administrative, clerical or technical error. Penalties rise with the amount, up to 20 years' imprisonment and a $50,000 fine at $25,000 or more, and the court must order full restitution to the tenant and others harmed. Mississippi has no statute letting tenants pay the utility and deduct, petition for a receiver, or requiring a master-meter owner to identify tenants to the utility; a search found none. Keep account records and pay promptly, since a shutoff can also breach your lease and repair duties. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Utility Shutoffs: Commission Weather and Medical Limits, and No Landlord Cutoffs
bodyText: The Mississippi Code itself sets no winter or summer moratorium on utility disconnections, but it confirms that the Public Service Commission regulates them: even electric power associations, whose rates the Commission does not set, remain subject to Commission regulations that limit disconnections during National Weather Service freeze or excessive heat warnings and in life-threatening situations certified by a medical doctor, and that set initial deposit requirements for certified domestic-violence victims. Those Commission rules were not read here; check them and your utility's tariff. For you as landlord: no statute lets you shut off a tenant's utilities, submetered water in a covered building may not be disconnected for unpaid submeter bills, and money tenants pay you for utilities must reach the utility within 60 days of the bill. Never cut services to force payment or a move-out; use the 3-day nonpayment notice and a court eviction. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Periodic Inspections in Mississippi Rest on the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving a landlord a right to inspect the unit, setting a notice period, or saying when a tenant may refuse; the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and the general landlord-tenant chapter are silent, and a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found nothing. Your inspection right therefore comes from the lease, so keep the shared inspection-rights clause, give reasonable advance notice, inspect at reasonable times, and limit frequency to what you need. A tenant who unreasonably refuses access the lease allows is in breach, which supports the Act's 14-day breach notice. Inspections help you document the tenant's statutory duties, such as keeping the unit clean and safe and reporting known conditions that may cause damage. Do not photograph or record the tenant, and keep photos to the condition of the unit. Every right you exercise under the Act carries a duty of good faith. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Entering the Unit in Mississippi: No Statute, So the Lease Sets the Rules
bodyText: Mississippi has no landlord-entry statute: no notice period, no list of permitted purposes, no emergency rule, no remedy for refused access, and no rule that a repair request is consent to entry; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your right to enter therefore comes only from the lease. State in it when you may enter (repairs, inspections, showings, emergencies), how much notice you will give (the shared landlords-access clause uses 24 hours, a figure of your choosing, not a state figure), and that you may enter without notice in an emergency. A tenant who refuses lawful access in breach of the lease can be given the Act's 14-day breach notice. In the other direction, entry in bad faith or harassment can breach the lease and your duty of good faith, and the tenant may then use the Act's remedies. Until a court-ordered move-out date, the tenant keeps the access the lease gave. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Scheduled-Service Entry: No Mississippi Rule, So Write It into the Lease
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on entering for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or HVAC maintenance, and no rule that such entry needs a conspicuous lease term; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, because the state has no entry statute at all. If you want routine service entry without a separate notice each time, put the schedule in the lease (for example, the shared scheduled-services entry clause), state the days and hours, say who will enter and how the tenant will be reminded, and set that notice no shorter than the notice your general access clause gives. Enter only for the stated service and at reasonable times, since every right you exercise under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act carries a duty of good faith. The tenant's duties to use facilities reasonably and report damaging conditions support routine service. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: Nothing Statutory to Waive in Mississippi
bodyText: Some states set an entry-notice period and allow tenants to waive it for showings only in a separate signed document. Mississippi has no entry-notice statute, so there is no statutory period to waive and no separate-document rule; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The notice for showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers is whatever the lease says. The Mississippi REALTORS lease form, for example, provides showings by appointment on 24 hours' notice, but that is a contract term, not a state figure. Set your showing notice in the lease (the shared showing-notice clause), say whether you may put up signs and when showings may start, and ask the tenant to cooperate. If you and the tenant later agree to shorter notice for a particular showing, confirm it in writing. Use showings in good faith and at reasonable times. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: No Mississippi Key-Control or Staff Background-Check Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a key-control policy, limits on who holds master keys, or background checks for maintenance staff and managers, for apartment complexes of any size; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi also has no tenant lock-change or rekeying statute, so the shared keys clause governs who may change locks and what replacement keys cost. Good practice is still to log every key and master key, keep them secured, rekey between tenants, and screen staff who hold keys, since a lost or misused key can lead to injury or theft claims (premises-liability case law was not searched). Your manager is your agent and you keep ultimate liability for your statutory duties. Using a key to enter must follow the lease's access terms, as there is no entry statute. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Mississippi Smart-Lock Statute; Breach-Notice Law Covers Some Tenant Data
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute regulating smart locks, keyless entry or app-based access systems in rentals, such as rules on tenant consent, data collection or a physical-key alternative; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. So the lease governs: say what access system is used, what entry data it records, who can see it, how long you keep it, and how the tenant gets in if the system or the tenant's phone fails. Two general laws matter. If your system or tenant files hold a tenant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code, and that data is breached, Mississippi's breach-notice law requires you to notify affected residents without unreasonable delay, unless an investigation reasonably shows the breach will not likely harm them. And using access to film a tenant with lewd intent in the home is a felony. Remember there is no entry statute; access logs do not expand your right to enter. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Locks and Security Devices: Only Pool-Yard Doors and Windows Are Regulated in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no general statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or rekeying between tenants. The one lock rule is in the pool-safety chapter, which applies only to a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership or management on the same or adjacent lots) or a condominium, cooperative or townhome project with a pool, and not to a complex that does not allow residents under 12. There, no door may open directly into the pool yard where the building or pool first received electrical service on or after July 1, 2012; for older buildings, a hinged door into the pool yard needs a self-engaging latch, an automatic closer and a keyless bolting device 36 to 48 inches above the floor, with set rules for French and sliding doors, and walls used as the enclosure need latched windows. You must keep the enclosure, gates and self-closing and self-latching devices in good working order, keep window latches and sliding-door locks working once the tenant reports a problem, and inspect pool gates at least every 31 days. Elsewhere, follow local codes and the lease. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi List of Other Facilities You Must Supply
bodyText: Beyond your two general duties (comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the dwelling unit, its plumbing and its heating and/or cooling system in substantially move-in condition), Mississippi has no statute requiring you to supply particular facilities such as hot water, door locks, window screens, garbage receptacles, extermination, smoke alarms or appliances; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Two narrow rules exist: pool-yard doors and windows in multiunit complexes with pools must have specified latches and bolting devices, and the State Fire Prevention Code reaches only listed buildings, such as state buildings, public-assembly buildings and buildings 75 feet or taller permitted after July 1, 1978. Local housing and fire codes may require more, and your code duty makes them binding, so check your city or county code. Anything else you promise in the lease (screens, trash service, pest control) becomes a term the tenant can enforce through the Act's remedies. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Domestic Violence and Lock Changes: No Mississippi Tenant Right, but Court Orders Control
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence require you to change the locks, or letting the tenant change them, and none setting who pays; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Courts can act, though. In a domestic abuse protection order, a municipal or justice court (temporarily, for up to 30 days, or up to a year where the parties have no minor children in common) or a chancery or county court (in a final order) may give the petitioner possession of the residence to the exclusion of the abuser by evicting the abuser. If a tenant shows you such an order, follow it: rekey promptly at the tenant's request so the excluded person cannot enter, and do not give that person keys. Without an order, do not lock out a person who is a tenant or occupant under the lease; possession disputes go through the court. Put a lock-change procedure in the lease. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Bar on Evicting a Domestic-Violence Victim
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute barring you from evicting or refusing to renew a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because of police calls about the abuse; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Federal law can apply, including the Violence Against Women Act in federally assisted housing and the federal Fair Housing Act, which were not reviewed here. Under state law, act carefully: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lets you end a tenancy for a material breach caused by the tenant, but a party may not terminate for a condition caused by that party's own act, and every termination or nonrenewal must be in good faith. If a court protection order gives your tenant possession and evicts the abuser, the abuser's removal comes from that order. Consider a lease term that does not hold a victim responsible for the abuser's acts. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Early-Termination Right for Domestic-Violence Victims in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking or trafficking end a lease early, and so no rule on whether that ends the lease for co-tenants, which abusers count, or a landlord's right to terminate against an abuser left as sole tenant; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The tenant is bound by the lease unless you agree otherwise or another rule applies, such as a periodic tenancy ended on 7 or 30 days' written notice, or federal protections in assisted housing (not reviewed here). A protection order may give the victim possession and evict the abuser, but it does not end the lease. You may offer a victim early termination in the lease or by agreement; the shared early-termination clause leaves room for that. Courts list protection orders in a statewide registry, and the Attorney General runs an Address Confidentiality Program for victims. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Proof of Domestic Violence: No Mississippi Housing Rule to Apply
bodyText: Because Mississippi gives domestic-violence victims no statutory lease-termination, lock-change or eviction protection, there is no state list of documents a tenant must show you to qualify; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Two state documents may still come up. A domestic abuse protection order must state its reasons and specific findings of fact, describe the prohibited acts, and is entered in the Mississippi Protection Order Registry; a temporary order may give the victim possession of the residence and evict the abuser, so read any order you receive and follow it. The Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program certifies victims of domestic violence, stalking or sexual assault and issues an authorization card; a participant may use a substitute address and has designated the Attorney General's office as agent for service of process and mail. If you offer victims lease relief voluntarily, state in the lease which documents you will accept. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: A Tenant's Belongings Left Behind in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's property rules depend on how the tenancy ended. After a court eviction, if the tenant moves out by the court-ordered date and leaves property, you may dispose of it without further notice. If law enforcement executes a warrant of removal, you must give the tenant reasonable access for 72 hours to remove belongings, including a manufactured home; property left after that may go to the curb, a garbage area or a place you both agree on, and you need not preserve it. The eviction summons must tell the tenant these rules. After a voluntary move-out, no statute applies, so use the optional abandoned-property-ms lease clause (written notice and a claim period). If a tenant behind on rent deserts the premises, a constable can post notice, view the premises again 5 to 15 days later, and the court can restore you to possession and void the lease. Never remove property or change locks during a tenancy without a court order. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Tenant Abandonment, Re-Renting and Rent Acceleration in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has a procedure for deserted premises: if a tenant behind on rent deserts the unit, a constable, on your affidavit, posts notice of a second view 5 to 15 days later, and if the rent and late fees are not paid the court puts you back in possession and the lease becomes void. The statutes say nothing about a duty to mitigate by re-renting, how unpaid future rent is measured, or rent acceleration; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, and case law, which governs mitigation, was not searched. Be careful: when a rental agreement terminates, the Act requires you to return all prepaid and unearned rent, and every step to end a tenancy must be in good faith. So the library does not offer rent acceleration for Mississippi; it offers an optional re-renting clause instead (rent until the unit is re-rented, less the new rent, plus reasonable costs, with reasonable efforts to re-rent). If you want acceleration anyway, add your own clause and take legal advice first. The re-renting clause is for fixed-term leases; periodic tenancies end on 7 or 30 days' notice. The deserted-premises procedure applies to all tenancies.

title: Attorney's Fees in Mississippi Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: No Mississippi statute awards attorney's fees to the winner of a residential eviction or rent case, requires a lease fee clause to be reciprocal, caps fees or bars a lease from shifting them; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, and the courts' treatment of lease fee clauses (case law) was not searched. So fees depend mainly on the lease. Mississippi forms commonly make the tenant pay your reasonable attorney's fees for collecting rent and recovering possession; if you use one, keep it to reasonable fees actually incurred, and consider making it mutual. Four statutes award fees: the pool-safety act lets a tenant recover fees for the owner's intentional, malicious or grossly negligent noncompliance, and lets the court award fees to the prevailing party in a civil-penalty action after written notice; a court of record must award reasonable fees against a party who brings or defends a claim without substantial justification or for delay or harassment; a suit by a licensed attorney on a bad check issued with fraudulent intent carries reasonable attorney's fees plus the statutory service charge; and in a squatter hearing the prevailing party gets fees. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: The Federal 30-Day Notice Compared with Mississippi Notices
bodyText: For a covered property (one with a federally backed mortgage or in certain federal housing programs), federal law requires 30 days' notice to vacate; the shared federal education row explains it and is tagged for Mississippi. Mississippi's own notices are shorter: a 3-day notice for nonpayment of rent, a 14-day breach notice for other material noncompliance, a 3-day holdover notice after a fixed term expires, and 7 or 30 days' written notice to end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy. Periods under seven days skip intermediate weekends and legal holidays, and a last day falling on one moves to the next business day. No Mississippi statute or court rule addresses the federal notice, so for a covered property give at least 30 days' notice to vacate before filing even when the state period is shorter, and say so in your notice. The eviction complaint must attach the written notice you delivered. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Fire and Casualty Damage in Mississippi: No Rent for Destroyed Buildings
bodyText: Mississippi has one casualty statute: a tenant is not bound to pay rent for buildings after they are destroyed by fire or otherwise, and a lease promise to leave or restore the premises in good repair does not make the tenant rebuild or pay for destroyed buildings, unless the tenant's negligence or fault caused the loss or the tenant expressly agreed to be bound. No statute gives you or the tenant a right to end the lease after a casualty, sets a rent reduction for partial damage, or requires you to let the tenant retrieve belongings by a set date; a search found none. So put a casualty clause in the lease (the library's casualty clause works in Mississippi): who may terminate, on what notice, how rent abates, and access to retrieve property. A material failure to keep the unit fit lets the tenant use the Act's 14-day breach notice. Every termination must be in good faith. A lease could lawfully make the tenant expressly agree to keep paying rent or rebuild; the library does not offer that, because it shifts an owner's insurable risk to the tenant. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Condominium Conversion Notice or Tenant Purchase Right
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring notice to tenants before you convert a rental building to condominiums or cooperatives, giving tenants a right of first refusal to buy their units, or requiring a conversion statement at the top of the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The condominium statute lets a project's restrictions regulate sales and leases of units and says the management body need not be given a first right to buy or lease. Local ordinances were not searched. If you plan a conversion, your existing leases still bind you and any buyer: a fixed-term lease runs to its stated end date, and a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy ends only on 7 or 30 days' written notice. Every termination or nonrenewal must be in good faith, and possession is recovered only through the court. Give tenants as much notice of a conversion as you can and disclose it in new leases. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Criminal Activity by Tenants: Mississippi Duties and Eviction Routes
bodyText: Every Mississippi tenant must not engage in illegal activity on the leased premises as documented by a law enforcement agency. A violation is a material breach: give the 14-day breach notice, or, where the violation is substantial and materially affects health or safety, end the tenancy without a notice period (still deliver a written termination notice, because the eviction complaint must attach one), and the court can set a move-out date shorter than seven days if the tenant poses an immediate and significant risk to people or property. Separately, under the nuisance law, using the premises for lewdness, prostitution or unlawful controlled-substance use or sale (more than one single act) voids the lease and returns the right of possession to you; an owner or lessee of a nuisance can also be enjoined. A court may order an owner to evict persons from premises used by a criminal street gang for illegal activity, after 30 days' notice to the owner. There is no expedited criminal-eviction procedure, so file a residential eviction rather than locking out. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Lease Addenda: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute authorizing, requiring or limiting a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and none letting a city require crime-free program participation; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. You may still use an addendum, because the lease can make illegal conduct a default, and state law already supports it: every tenant must not engage in illegal activity on the premises as documented by law enforcement, and using the premises for lewdness, prostitution or unlawful drug use or sale (more than a single act) voids the lease under the nuisance law. Keep the addendum consistent with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: enforce it with the 14-day breach notice or, for a substantial health-or-safety violation, termination without a notice period (still deliver a written notice, which the complaint must attach), followed by a court eviction, and apply it to all tenants fairly. Avoid terms that waive notice or court process. Federally assisted housing has its own rules, not reviewed here. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Grounds for Eviction and Cure Periods in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi allows a residential eviction on two grounds: a breach of the rental agreement or the Act, after the proper notice, or failing to move out after the tenancy ends. Cure works on two tracks. For nonpayment, a notice that the agreement will terminate unless rent is paid within 3 days; that period skips intermediate weekends and legal holidays. For other material breaches, a notice stating the breach and that the agreement ends on a date at least 14 days after receipt unless remedied within a reasonable time of no more than 14 days; a timely cure saves the lease. A substantially similar breach within six months after such a notice, absent due care, allows termination on 14 days' notice with no cure, and a substantial violation materially affecting health or safety needs no notice period, though the eviction complaint must still attach a written notice. After a fixed term expires, a 3-day holdover notice; periodic tenancies end on 7 or 30 days' notice. Deliver paper notice; e-mail or text needs the tenant's written agreement (for the holdover notice, the tenant's agreement). These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Tenant Default in Mississippi: How the Shared Clause Fits the Statute
bodyText: The shared default-by-tenant clause is tagged for Mississippi and works with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Mississippi gives you a 3-day pay-or-terminate notice for nonpayment of rent and a 14-day notice-and-cure for other material breaches, with no cure for a repeat within six months and no notice period for a substantial violation materially affecting health or safety (the eviction complaint must still attach a written notice); the clause's statement that no cure is needed where the law permits keeps those routes.
