In a nonpayment case the judge must follow the signed rental agreement. Mississippi counts late fees required by the lease as rent, so a clause that excludes unpaid late fees from nonpayment is your concession. No statute requires reciprocal attorney-fee language or sets a mitigation duty (case law not searched). Remedies must not waive the tenant's rights under the Act, and every step must be in good faith. On termination, return prepaid unearned rent and any recoverable deposit. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: After a Hurricane or Other Declared Disaster in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute ending a tenancy automatically after a declared disaster or suspending rent while the unit is inaccessible; a search found none. Three rules apply. A tenant owes no rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise, unless the tenant's negligence or fault caused the loss or the tenant expressly agreed to keep paying. When a state or local emergency is declared under the Emergency Management Law, the price for goods and services sold in the emergency impact area may not exceed the prices ordinarily charged in the same market just before the declaration, apart from added costs actually incurred; whether that reaches rent was not determined, so avoid raising rent or fees for displaced people during an emergency. And your repair and code duties continue, so a unit left unfit lets the tenant use the 14-day breach notice. Put casualty, abatement and access terms in the lease and act in good faith. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: When a Mississippi Tenant May End a Lease Early
bodyText: Apart from a tenant ending the tenancy for your material noncompliance after a 14-day notice (see the statutory early-termination row), Mississippi has one statutory early-termination rule: under the Derrick Beard Act, when the lessee dies (or all lessees die), a cosigner of a residential lease may end the lease and is presumed to have done so unless the cosigner notifies you within 30 days of the death of a choice not to terminate. The estate and cosigner still owe rent and sums due before the death, rent for the rest of the month or other 30-day period in which the death occurred, and the cost of restoring the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear. Any waiver of this right is void. It applies to leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011; treat a periodic tenancy that began earlier as renewed and covered. There is no state military, domestic-violence or medical termination right (federal servicemember protections may apply), and no statute sets or bars an early-termination fee; a tenant who deserts while behind on rent can be handled under the deserted-premises procedure. Otherwise the tenant is bound unless the lease allows early exit, as the library's Mississippi early-termination clause does for a flat one-month fee.

title: Condemnation of Rental Property: No Mississippi Lease Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute saying what happens to a residential lease, or to the tenant's rent, when the property is taken by eminent domain, and none letting the condemnation court cancel the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Constitution requires due compensation, paid first, to the owner or owners of private property taken or damaged for public use, and makes the question whether a use is public a judicial one; how compensation is split between you and a tenant is case law, which was not searched. Because the statutes are silent, put a condemnation clause in the lease: say the lease ends (in whole or for the part taken) on the date possession is taken, rent abates from then, any award belongs to you except a separate claim the tenant may make for its own moving costs or property, and neither side owes damages for the early end. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Who Can File for an LLC or Corporate Landlord in Mississippi
bodyText: No Mississippi statute or court rule says expressly whether a manager, officer or other non-lawyer may file or appear in an eviction for a landlord that is a company; the Rules of Justice Court are silent, and they and the court system's sample eviction forms contemplate either a party or its attorney signing, with the warrant application signable by the landlord's duly authorized agent. Mississippi's unauthorized-practice statute makes it a misdemeanor for an unlicensed person to practice law, and treats as practicing law anyone who, for a fee or reward, writes papers to be filed in court for another or gives counsel in a case. Whether a company may appear through a non-lawyer is decided by case law, which was not searched. A landlord may contract with an agent to take on its rights and duties, but that does not settle who may appear in court. The safe course for an LLC or corporation is to use a licensed Mississippi attorney. This applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Environmental-Event Termination Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a landlord or tenant end a residential lease because of an environmental event, such as a chemical spill, contamination, mold, flooding or a boil-water order, and no mold, radon or flood disclosure or remediation statute for rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What applies: your duty to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the plumbing and heating and/or cooling in move-in condition; the tenant's 14-day breach notice and limited repair-and-deduct remedy if you fall short; no notice period needed to end a tenancy for a substantial violation materially affecting health or safety (though an eviction complaint must attach a written notice); and no rent owed for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise. If you want a termination right for environmental events, write it into the lease, with notice, rent abatement and a good-faith standard, since every termination must be in good faith. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Delays and Stays of a Mississippi Eviction
bodyText: Mississippi has no hardship-stay statute, but several rules can delay an eviction. The judge orders the tenant out in seven days from the judgment unless a shorter or longer period is justified by an emergency or other compelling circumstances. The court may adjourn the hearing at either party's request, but no single adjournment may exceed ten days without both sides' consent, and adjournments may not carry the hearing beyond 30 days from filing. In a case based only on nonpayment, no warrant of removal issues if the tenant pays all unpaid rent and judgment sums by the move-out date, and you must accept a full tender made by then in good faith. A tenant may ask the justice court to set aside a default judgment, and the judge may stay execution pending that hearing. An appeal does not by itself stop the eviction; the circuit court may grant a discretionary supersedeas, with a bond, applying preliminary-injunction standards. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: How Residential Evictions Work in Mississippi
bodyText: A Mississippi residential eviction may be filed in justice, county or circuit court. You file a sworn affidavit or complaint stating the facts, the unit address and any rent and fees owed, with a copy of the written breach or termination notice you delivered. A summons issues for the person in possession, commanding the tenant to vacate or show cause at a hearing, and must include the statutory eviction notice; the constable serves it personally, on a family member over 16 with mailing, or by posting and mailing. The court grants a default judgment if the tenant does not appear and you have complied, and judgments are signed the same business day. The tenant gets seven days to move out unless the court sets a shorter or longer period. Afterward you may request a warrant of removal; the sheriff or a constable must physically remove occupants, since posting is not execution. For 72 hours after removal you must allow the tenant to retrieve belongings. Never use self-help. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Eviction-Record Sealing or Expungement Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute sealing, expunging or removing eviction case records from public indexes, whether the case was dismissed, settled or won by the tenant, and so no procedure for a landlord to object; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The state's expunction statutes concern criminal arrests and convictions, not civil eviction cases. Justice court dockets are kept by the court clerk, and court rules on records were read without finding any sealing rule for evictions. So eviction filings generally remain part of the court record. If you screen applicants using eviction records, check whether a case was dismissed or ended in the tenant's favor before relying on it, and follow federal consumer-reporting rules when you use a screening company (not reviewed here). Do not promise a tenant in a settlement that the court record will be sealed, since no statute provides for it. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Who May Be Served with Eviction Papers in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi eviction papers are served under the court rules, not the lease. In justice court the constable delivers the summons and complaint to the tenant personally or to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive process; if that fails with reasonable diligence, to the tenant's spouse or a family member over 16 at the home, followed by first-class mail; and failing that, by posting on a door of the home and mailing. Each named tenant must be served separately. No statute lets a lease name someone, such as the property manager or a co-tenant, to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and whether a lease appointment counts as an agent appointed to receive process is untested, so do not rely on one; a search found none. One special case: a tenant enrolled in the Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program has designated the Attorney General's office as agent for service of process. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: Drug, Prostitution and Gang Activity: No Separate Fast Track, but Faster Rules Apply
bodyText: Mississippi has no separate fast-track eviction for drug or other criminal activity; you use the ordinary court eviction, but several rules speed it up. A tenant must not engage in illegal activity on the premises as documented by a law enforcement agency, and breaking that duty is a material breach. If a tenant's violation of the lease or the Act is substantial and materially affects health or safety, no notice period is required (the complaint must still attach a written notice), and the judge may set a move-out date shorter than the usual seven days; the same is true when the tenant poses an immediate and significant risk of damage or harm. Separately, using the unit for prostitution or lewdness, or for unlawful use, possession, sale or delivery of a controlled substance (more than one single act), voids the lease by law and returns possession to you; the statute lets the owner enter without court process, but if anyone still lives there a court eviction is the safe course. If a criminal street gang uses the property, anyone may sue to make you evict them, after 30 days' notice to you, so act as soon as you learn of it.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Mississippi, with a Few Situational Limits
bodyText: Mississippi has no just-cause or good-cause eviction law, and no subset of tenancies (such as manufactured home lots) needs a reason to end; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. A fixed-term lease expires on the date it states; if the tenant stays, you may give written notice that the tenant is holding over and file an eviction no earlier than three days later, not counting intermediate weekends and legal holidays. A week-to-week tenancy ends on at least 7 days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days', and no reason is needed. Some limits apply whatever the lease says: ending or not renewing a tenancy and removing a tenant must be done in good faith; you may not demand a rent increase after the lease expires with the dominant purpose of retaliating against the tenant for actions the Act authorizes; and after a judgment based only on unpaid rent, a tenant who pays everything awarded by the move-out date keeps the home. Federal fair-housing and subsidized-housing rules may require more (not reviewed).

title: Foreclosure of a Rental: No Mississippi Tenant-Protection Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute of its own protecting tenants when a rental property is foreclosed, requiring you to tell tenants or applicants about a foreclosure, or saying whether a lease survives the sale; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, not reviewed here) generally lets a bona fide tenant stay to the end of the lease, or for at least 90 days after notice, when a buyer at foreclosure takes over; check it before anyone tries to remove a tenant. A few Mississippi rules do follow the property: a mortgagee in possession counts as an owner and so as a landlord under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; a later owner can face the deposit penalty for keeping a deposit in bad faith; and a tenant who paid rent to you before learning of a transfer is not harmed by it. Notices of foreclosure or eviction for a primary residence cannot rely on the electronic-transactions law. If you are behind on the mortgage, telling tenants early is good practice.

title: Paying to Stay: Cure Periods and Payment by the Move-Out Date
bodyText: Mississippi gives tenants several chances to save a tenancy by paying or fixing a breach. For unpaid rent, your written notice must say the rental agreement will end if the rent is not paid within three days, so payment within that period keeps the tenancy (count the three days without intermediate weekends and holidays). For other breaches that can be remedied by repairs, paying damages or otherwise, the tenancy does not end if the tenant remedies before the date in your 14-day notice, unless substantially the same breach recurs within six months. After a court judgment based only on unpaid rent, the judge may not issue the warrant for removal if the tenant has paid all unpaid rent and other sums in the judgment by the court-ordered move-out date, or if you accept those amounts later; you must accept full payment tendered by the move-out date in good faith. The court's summons tells the tenant this. Judgments for other breaches or for holding over carry no payment cure. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies under the Act.

title: Lease Guarantors and Cosigners: Writing, Renewals and the Derrick Beard Act
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute limiting a guarantor to the original lease term or setting the form or limits of a lease guaranty; a search of the Mississippi Code found none, so whether a guarantor stays liable after a renewal, a month-to-month holdover or a rent increase depends on the guaranty's wording (case law not searched). Two statutes do apply. A promise to answer for another person's debt cannot be enforced unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor. And under the Derrick Beard Act, a cosigner of a residential lease may end the lease, and is presumed to have ended it, when the lessee dies (or all lessees die), unless the cosigner tells you within 30 days that the lease will continue; the estate and cosigner still owe rent and sums owed before the death, the rest of that month or 30-day period, and restoration costs, and no waiver is valid. It covers leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011; treat an earlier periodic tenancy as renewed. Have the guarantor sign a written guaranty that says whether it covers renewals, extensions, holdover periods and rent changes.

title: Tenant Holds Over: Three-Day Notice and Double Rent in Mississippi
bodyText: When a fixed-term lease expires and the tenant stays, you may give the tenant written notice that the tenant is holding over and that you will begin eviction no earlier than three days after the notice, not counting intermediate weekends and holidays; keep a copy, because it must be filed with the eviction complaint. If the definite term has expired and the tenant fails or refuses to vacate after you notify the tenant to do so, you may charge double the rent for the time the tenant stays after the move-out date in your notice, unless the lease says otherwise. An older general statute also gives double rent to a landlord whose tenant stays after lawful notice; whether it reaches tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is not settled by statute. A week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy must first be ended with 7 or 30 days' written notice; a tenant who stays after that date can then be evicted. You may send the holdover notice by e-mail or text only if the tenant has agreed to it; deliver a paper copy too. The library's holdover clause builds these rules into the lease.

title: Holdover Rate: Double Rent by Statute, and Why the Library Sets No Other Rate
bodyText: Mississippi law sets its own holdover rate: after a fixed-term lease expires and you notify the tenant to vacate, you may charge double the rent for the time the tenant stays after the date to vacate in your notice, unless the rental agreement says otherwise. No statute caps or forbids a different holdover rate written into the lease, and a search of the Mississippi Code found none, so a stipulated rate is lawful. The library does not offer one for Mississippi, because the double-rent rule applies only if the lease does not contradict it: a lease that names its own rate would likely replace the statutory double rent rather than add to it, and the statutory measure is already as high as most stipulated rates. The library's holdover clause instead keeps double rent for fixed-term holdovers after your notice and reasonable rental value for other days. A rate far above the rent could be attacked as a penalty (case law not searched). If you want your own rate anyway, add your own clause and take legal advice first. Week-to-week and month-to-month holdovers fall outside the double-rent statute, which speaks of a definite term.

title: Tenants' Exemptions from Seizure: No Lease Waiver Rule, and Your Lien Is Not Affected
bodyText: Mississippi protects some of a debtor's property from seizure under execution or attachment, including when you collect a judgment for unpaid rent. A tenant may select tangible personal property up to $10,000 in total value from listed kinds, such as household goods, clothing, a motor vehicle, tools of the trade, cash on hand and health aids, and residents aged 70 or older get an additional $50,000 exemption; the homestead exemption protects a home the debtor owns, so it rarely matters to a renter. At a levy the officer asks the tenant to select the exempt property. No Mississippi statute lets a lease waive these exemptions or expressly forbids it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, so leave waivers out of the lease. The exemption statute also says it does not affect the rights of the holder of a statutory lien, which includes your landlord's lien on the tenant's property on the premises; how far that reaches exempt household goods is case law (not searched). Enforce any claim through the court, never by taking belongings yourself.

title: No Early Termination for Illness or a Move to Care
bodyText: Mississippi gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of illness, disability, old age or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A month-to-month tenant can always leave on 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week), so the question matters mainly for fixed-term leases, where the tenant stays liable under the lease unless you agree otherwise. The statutory exits Mississippi does have are narrow: a tenant may end the lease after a written 14-day notice for your material breach of the lease or your repair duties that you do not remedy; no rent is owed for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault; and a cosigner may end the lease when the lessee dies. You may agree in the lease or later to let a tenant leave early for a move to care, and federal fair-housing law may require you to consider a disabled tenant's request for a reasonable accommodation (not reviewed).

title: Mississippi Landlord's Lien and Attachment for Rent
bodyText: Mississippi gives every lessor a lien on all personal property the lessee owns that is on the leased premises (except a stock of merchandise sold in the ordinary course), to secure rent contracted to be paid, whether due or not. The lien yields to earlier perfected liens and security interests, and the Uniform Commercial Code's secured-transactions article does not apply to it. While rent is unpaid the tenant may not remove that property from the premises without your written consent, and removing lien property from the county, or hiding or selling it to defraud you, is a crime. You enforce the lien only through the court, by an attachment (distress) for rent: a sworn complaint before a justice court judge and a bond of double the sum claimed, then seizure and notice by an officer and a public sale after three months unless the tenant replevies with bond or swears the rent is not owed. Distress must be reasonable, may be made within six months after the lease ends while your interest and the tenant's possession continue, does not reach other people's property, and a wrongful distress can cost you double the property's value. Never seize belongings yourself.

title: Your Remedies When the Tenant Breaches: Possession, Rent and Damages
bodyText: When a tenant materially fails to comply with the lease or the tenant's statutory duties, you may end the tenancy under the Act's notice rules or use any other remedy at law or in equity the Act does not prohibit. Your sworn eviction complaint states the rent and other fees owed, and the court can award a money judgment with the possession judgment. You may also sue for rent in arrear, recover a reasonable sum for use and occupation where there is no written contract, charge double rent after a fixed-term holdover notice, and use the landlord's lien and attachment for rent. When the rental agreement ends you must return any prepaid, unearned rent and the refundable part of the deposit. No Mississippi statute governs rent acceleration, a duty to re-rent to reduce damages, or lease-set liquidated damages; a search of the Mississippi Code found none, so those turn on case law (not searched). The safe course is to claim rent only for the time the unit is actually lost, make and record reasonable re-renting efforts, and apply the deposit only to the purposes the deposit statute allows.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting you enter, fix a tenant's breach and bill the tenant; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Your statutory route is the written breach notice: if the breach can be remedied by repairs, paying damages or otherwise and the tenant does so before the date in the notice (at least 14 days after receipt), the tenancy continues; if not, it ends. You owe no repair duty for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests caused deliberately or negligently, you may sue for damages, and at move-out you may claim from the deposit what is reasonably necessary to repair tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, with an itemized written notice. A lease clause letting you repair tenant-caused damage and charge the reasonable cost is a lawful contract term; because Mississippi treats every payment the lease requires as rent, an unpaid charge of that kind can support a nonpayment notice, so itemize it and keep receipts. The library offers no separate self-cure clause, since the breach notice already reaches this; you may add one. Mississippi has no entry statute, so state your access rights in the lease.

title: Liquidated Damages in a Lease: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: No Mississippi statute governs liquidated-damages amounts that a residential lease sets for a tenant's breach, such as a fixed early-termination charge or a flat fee for breaking the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Mississippi's own fixed measures are few: double rent when a tenant holds over after a fixed term and your notice to vacate, and up to $200 plus actual damages against a landlord who keeps a deposit in bad faith. Whether a lease-set amount is enforceable or an unenforceable penalty is case law (not searched). The safe course is an amount that is a reasonable estimate of your likely loss when the lease is signed, stated plainly, and not added to actual damages for the same loss. Do not take a flat liquidated amount out of the security deposit as such: the deposit statute lets you keep only amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning at the end of the tenancy and other reasonable and necessary expenses caused by the tenant's default, itemized in writing.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in Mississippi
bodyText: No Mississippi statute lets a residential landlord change the locks, padlock the door or otherwise lock a tenant out for unpaid rent, even with notice or a lease clause; a search of the Mississippi Code found none (the only lockout-type rule is for self-storage units). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets the route instead: a three-day written nonpayment notice, an eviction filed in court, a judgment with a move-out date (usually seven days), and removal by the sheriff or a constable under a warrant, which posting on the door does not complete. Even after a judgment for unpaid rent only, the tenant can stop the warrant by paying all the sums awarded by the move-out date, and you must accept a full tender in good faith. A tenant put out by force or stealth may sue to recover possession, and the Act bars waiving its rights in the lease, so a lockout clause will not protect you. The narrow exception is a nuisance use (prostitution or drug activity), which voids the lease by law; even then, use the court.

title: Young Tenants and Minors: Who Can Sign a Lease and Whom to Name in an Eviction
bodyText: In Mississippi a "minor" is generally anyone under 21, but where a statute concerns contracts affecting real or personal property, a minor is anyone under 18. Anyone 18 or older can make binding contracts affecting real property, and an 18-, 19- or 20-year-old can sign a binding lease for the home he or she will live in and contract for the utilities it needs; a person who signed at 18 or older can sue and be sued as an adult on that contract. No statute lets someone under 18 sign a binding lease, and none bars naming a minor in an eviction; whether a lease signed by a minor binds the minor is case law (not searched), though a chancery court can remove the disability of minority as to real estate. If you rent to someone under 18, get an adult co-signer. The eviction summons goes to the person in possession or claiming possession, so name the adults who signed the lease or are entitled to occupy under it; children ordinarily leave with the named parent and need not be named.

title: The Three-Day Notice Before a Nonpayment Eviction in Mississippi
bodyText: Before you file an eviction for unpaid rent, deliver the tenant a written notice specifying that the rental agreement will terminate if the rent is not paid within three days. You may send it by e-mail or text message only if the tenant has agreed in writing to be notified that way; deliver a paper copy as well, because Mississippi's electronic-transactions law does not cover eviction or default notices for a primary residence. Count the three days without the day of delivery and without intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, and if the last day falls on one, the period runs to the next business day. Rent includes every payment the lease requires, including a late fee the lease makes payable. No statute prescribes the notice's wording, lets the lease serve as the notice, or lets the lease waive it. If the rent is not paid, file a sworn complaint with a copy of the notice; the judge in a nonpayment eviction must follow the rental agreement you and the tenant signed, and the tenant can still stop removal by paying everything owed by the court's move-out date.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Fees for Preparing or Serving Notices
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that allows, caps or bans a fee for preparing or serving a notice to a tenant, such as a three-day nonpayment notice or a 14-day breach notice; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Charge such a fee only if the lease provides it, and keep it to a reasonable amount close to your actual cost. Be aware that Mississippi counts every payment the lease requires as rent, so an unpaid notice fee written into the lease is rent; because every right and remedy under the Act carries a duty of good faith, do not use an unpaid notice fee by itself as the basis for a nonpayment eviction. Your costs of an eviction itself come through the court as court costs, and attorney's fees depend on the lease (see the attorney-fees row). The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: A Lease Cannot Waive or Shorten Mississippi's Termination Notices
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says that in any agreement, oral or written, for renting a home, a landlord and tenant may not agree to waive or give up any right, duty or remedy under the Act unless the Act itself allows it. The Act allows no waiver of its notices, so a lease cannot shorten or waive the three-day nonpayment notice, the 14-day breach notice, the three-day holdover notice after a fixed term, or the 7-day and 30-day notices that end week-to-week and month-to-month tenancies. The Act itself dispenses with notice only where the landlord or tenant has committed a substantial violation of the rental agreement or the Act that materially affects health or safety, and even then an eviction complaint must attach a written notice. Mississippi's older general notice-to-quit statute does not apply to agreements under the Act. Give the required notice every time; a written agreement to receive notices by e-mail or text changes only how a notice may be delivered, not whether it is required.

title: Nuisance Abatement Suits That Reach Rental Owners
bodyText: Mississippi's nuisance chapter treats a place used for lewdness, assignation or prostitution, or for unlawful use, possession, sale or delivery of a controlled substance (more than one single act), as a nuisance, and makes the user and the owner, agent or lessee guilty of maintaining it. The Attorney General, district or county attorney, or any citizen of the county may sue in chancery court. If you as owner had five days' notice of the hearing and cannot show the nuisance was abated, the court can close the place until trial; you can get it released by paying the costs, posting a bond for its full value and abating the nuisance, if the court is satisfied of your good faith. After trial the court enters a permanent injunction and an order closing the place for one year unless released, and violating it is contempt (a $200 to $1,000 fine, jail, or both). A tenant's nuisance use voids the lease by law. Gambling places and gang-used buildings have similar suits, so act promptly on reports of such activity.

title: Ending a Lease to Move In: Mississippi Has No Owner Move-In Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving you, or limiting, a right to end a tenancy so that you or a relative can move in; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy can be ended for any lawful reason on at least 7 or 30 days' written notice before the termination date. During a fixed term you may end the lease early to move in only if the lease reserves that right; a silent lease gives you none, and the tenant may stay until the term expires. If you want the option, use the library's optional owner-occupancy clause, give the notice it sets, and act in good faith, because the Act attaches a duty of good faith to every termination. If the tenant does not leave by the termination date, recover possession through a court eviction, not by self-help.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond, and No Confessed Judgments
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting you require a tenant to sign a bond, with or without a confessed judgment, promising to give up possession at the end of the term; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act goes further: no rental agreement may authorize any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of it, so leave confession-of-judgment and possession-bond clauses out of the lease. The bonds Mississippi does have are set in court proceedings: a landlord who sues out an attachment for rent must post a bond of double the sum claimed, and a tenant whose goods are distrained can get them back by giving a replevy bond. Appeals of eviction judgments follow the Mississippi Rules of Court (not reviewed here). To protect yourself, use the security deposit, which has no statutory cap, and the court eviction process. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Delay in Delivering Possession: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on what happens if you cannot deliver possession on the lease start date (for example because a prior tenant holds over), and no statutory tenant remedy for it; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The lease controls: the library's possession-delay clause, under which rent abates until possession and the tenant may cancel with a full refund if possession is not delivered within the stated time, is lawful in Mississippi. Your repair duty is measured against the unit's condition at the start of the lease, so document the condition on the day the tenant actually takes possession. If a holdover tenant is the cause, give that tenant the three-day holdover notice and evict; for a fixed-term holdover after your notice to vacate you may also charge double rent. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: The Tenant's Belongings After a Mississippi Eviction: 72 Hours, Then the Curb
bodyText: Until the court-ordered move-out date the tenant keeps the access the lease allowed. If the tenant moves out by that date and leaves belongings, you may dispose of them without further notice. After the date you may ask for a warrant for removal; it is not executed by posting it on the door, and law enforcement must remove the occupants and put you in physical possession. For the 72 hours after the warrant is executed you must give the tenant reasonable access to remove personal property, including a manufactured home. If the tenant moves out within those 72 hours leaving property, you may dispose of it without further notice; after 72 hours you may move anything left to the curb, an area for garbage or another place you and the tenant agree on. The tenant may still retrieve it there, but you need not preserve it. The court's sample summons form predates 2025 changes, so follow the statute. Property left after a voluntary move-out, and squatters' belongings, follow different rules.

title: Redemption After a Nonpayment Judgment: Payment by the Move-Out Date
bodyText: In Mississippi a tenant who loses an eviction based only on unpaid rent can still keep the home. The judge may not issue a warrant for removal if, by the court-ordered move-out date, the tenant has paid in full all unpaid rent and other sums awarded to you in the judgment, or if you accept those amounts after that date. You must, in good faith, accept full payment of everything owed under the money judgment if it is tendered on or before the move-out date. The eviction summons tells the tenant that paying all sums owed, before the hearing or afterwards by the move-out date, avoids having to move out. The right does not apply to judgments based on other breaches or on holding over. No statute requires special wording when you take a partial payment, sets a limit on how often a tenant may redeem, or addresses payments from charities or agencies; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. If you take partial money and still want removal, say in writing that you accept it without waiving the judgment.

title: Counterclaims in a Mississippi Eviction, and No Rent-into-Court Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a tenant to pay rent into court to defend an eviction or to raise counterclaims, and none making a tenant's counterclaims mandatory; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A tenant may defend and counterclaim: the court grants you a possession judgment after a hearing only if it finds the tenant failed to present a valid defense or counterclaim and you are otherwise entitled to it, and the court's sample judgment form nets a tenant's counterclaim or set-off (within justice court limits) against your money claim. A tenant who properly used the repair-and-deduct remedy may offset those repair costs against future rent. Hearings move quickly: a single adjournment may not exceed ten days without both sides' consent, and adjournments may not carry the hearing past 30 days from filing. Rent keeps coming due while the case is pending, so keep accurate records, and ask the court about any payment you receive during the case.

title: False Rental Applications: No Special Mississippi Remedy, and Expunged Records
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving you a special right to end a lease because the tenant's rental application was false; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The library's application-accuracy clause (the Louisiana-derived version tagged for Mississippi) makes the truth of the application a lease term, so a material misstatement is a material breach you enforce like any other: written notice describing it and stating that the agreement will end not less than 14 days after the tenant receives it if not remedied. Mississippi's expunction law says a person whose record has been expunged is not to be held to have given a false statement by failing to recite or acknowledge the expunged arrest, indictment or conviction in answer to any inquiry, so do not treat that silence as a lie. Federal fair-housing law limits what you may ask and how you may use the answers (not reviewed).

title: No Right to End the Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute letting a landlord end a lease because a repair would be uneconomical, and none giving a tenant that right; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Your duty is to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the unit, its plumbing and heating or cooling in substantially the condition they were in at the start of the lease, apart from reasonable wear and tear and tenant-caused damage. If you materially fail, the tenant may end the tenancy by a written notice giving you up to 14 days to remedy, or may repair and deduct within the statute's limits. When buildings are destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault, the tenant owes no rent for them. If you want a right to end the lease when the property is badly damaged, put a casualty clause in the lease (the library's tagged casualty clause works in Mississippi). A week-to-week tenancy can be ended on 7 days' and a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice.

title: Retaliation: One Narrow Mississippi Rule and a General Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Mississippi has no general statute barring a landlord from evicting, refusing to renew or raising rent because a tenant complained about conditions, called an inspector or joined a tenants' group; a search of the Mississippi Code found no such rule and no presumption of retaliation. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has one narrow limit: after the lease expires you may demand a rent increase only if it does not have the dominant purpose of retaliating against the tenant for actions the Act authorizes (such as a repair notice or repair-and-deduct), and the statute ties this to your having received written notice of each condition. More broadly, the Act requires good faith in every termination, nonrenewal and removal of a tenant. Federal fair-housing law separately bars retaliation for asserting fair-housing rights (not reviewed). Even where no statute applies, avoid acting soon after a complaint without a documented, independent reason. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no special rules for seasonal or vacation rentals of homes; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings is outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a short vacation stay offered as lodging is generally not a tenancy under the Act (see the rent-tax row for when lodging taxes apply). A seasonal rental that is a tenancy is an ordinary fixed-term lease: it expires on the date the lease states, and if the tenant stays you may give the three-day holdover notice, evict, and, after notifying the tenant to vacate, charge double rent unless the lease says otherwise. If you instead let the tenant stay on without a new fixed term, treat the tenancy as week-to-week (weekly rent) or month-to-month and end it with 7 or 30 days' written notice. City or county short-term-rental ordinances may also apply (not searched).

title: Self-Help Evictions: No Statute Allows Them, so Use the Court
bodyText: No Mississippi statute lets a residential landlord remove a tenant without a court, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lays out the route instead: notice, a sworn eviction complaint, a hearing, a judgment with a move-out date, and removal by the sheriff or a constable under a warrant, which is not executed by posting it on the door. Every removal of a tenant carries a duty of good faith, and the Act bars waiving its rights in the lease, so a lease clause allowing self-help does not protect you. A person deprived of possession of land by force, intimidation, fraud, stratagem or stealth can sue within one year to recover possession. Whether Mississippi courts allow any peaceable self-help against a residential tenant is case law (not searched). Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out. Two statutes are different: a tenant's prostitution or drug nuisance voids the lease and lets the owner enter, and squatters (who are not tenants) are removed by law enforcement on your affidavit.

title: Military Tenants: Federal Protections, No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute of its own letting a servicemember or National Guard member end a residential lease, shortening notice periods for military tenants, or staying evictions of military families; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Federal law governs: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act lets servicemembers end residential leases in qualifying circumstances (such as entering active duty or receiving orders for a change of station or a deployment) and limits evictions of servicemembers and their dependents during military service (federal law, not reviewed here). Follow it whenever a tenant or a tenant's spouse is in the armed forces, and check military status before seeking a default judgment. The library's tagged early-termination clause keeps the tenant's federal rights. Mississippi's own rules otherwise apply as usual: 7 or 30 days' written notice to end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, the three-day nonpayment notice and the 14-day breach notice.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a continuance, stay or reinstatement when a tenant's Social Security, other public benefit or housing-voucher payment arrives late; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The ordinary rules apply: a written notice that the rental agreement will terminate if rent is not paid within three days (not counting intermediate weekends and legal holidays), then an eviction. A delayed benefit can still save the tenancy in two ordinary ways: the tenant may pay within the three-day notice period, and after a judgment based only on unpaid rent the tenant may pay everything awarded by the court's move-out date, which you must accept in good faith. The court may adjourn the hearing at a party's request, but each adjournment is limited to ten days without both sides' consent and the hearing must end within 30 days of filing. Federal rules for subsidized housing and vouchers may require more (not searched). If a tenant shows that a benefit payment is simply delayed, a short written payment agreement is often cheaper than an eviction.

title: A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End a Mississippi Lease Early
bodyText: Mississippi gives tenants few statutory ways out of a fixed-term lease. (1) Your breach: if you materially fail to comply with the lease or your duty to meet health-and-safety codes and keep the unit, plumbing and heating or cooling in their move-in condition, the tenant may give written notice that the agreement will end not less than 14 days after you receive it unless you remedy the breach within that time; a repeat within six months needs no cure period, and no notice is needed for a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety. A tenant cannot end the lease over a condition the tenant's own household or guests caused. (2) Destruction: a tenant owes no rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise unless the tenant was at fault or agreed to pay. (3) Death: under the Derrick Beard Act a cosigner may end the lease when the lessee dies. Mississippi has no statutory early-exit right for domestic violence, military service (federal law applies), illness or a move to care. A periodic tenant may always leave on 7 or 30 days' notice.

title: End of the Lease in Mississippi: Surrender, Belongings and the Deposit Clock
bodyText: In Mississippi a fixed-term lease expires on the date it states; there is no good-cause renewal right, so the library's surrender clause works as written. If the tenant stays, give the three-day holdover notice and, after notifying the tenant to vacate, you may charge double rent unless the lease says otherwise. No statute governs belongings a tenant leaves after moving out voluntarily (the statutory disposal rules apply only within a court eviction), so use the library's optional property-left-behind clause. If rent is still owed at move-out, your landlord's lien technically bars removing the tenant's goods without your written consent, but you may enforce it only through the court; never block a move-out yourself. The 45-day deadline to return the deposit, with an itemized written notice of what you keep, runs only after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant demands the deposit, so record the date the keys come back and any demand. Wear and tear is judged by the ordinary standard, not by your own discretion.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term in Mississippi
bodyText: Under Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a rental agreement that does not fix a definite term creates a week-to-week tenancy if the tenant pays weekly rent and a month-to-month tenancy in every other case. Either side ends it by written notice given at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month) before the termination date, and no notice is needed where the other side has committed a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety (a landlord who then evicts must still attach a written notice to the complaint). The Act does not use the term "tenancy at will"; that phrase survives only in the nonresidential eviction statute, and the older general notice-to-quit statute does not apply to agreements under the Act. Separately, Mississippi's statute of frauds bars suing on a lease for a longer term than one year unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged; what an unwritten long lease becomes is case law (not searched). Treat any unwritten or open-ended home rental as month-to-month (or week-to-week for weekly rent), give full written notice, and put leases longer than a year in writing.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no landlord-tenant rule of its own for a tenant's bankruptcy; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Federal bankruptcy law governs: once a tenant files, the automatic stay generally stops you from starting or continuing an eviction or collecting past-due rent without the bankruptcy court's permission, with some exceptions (federal law, not reviewed here). A lease clause making the tenant's bankruptcy itself a default is generally not enforceable under federal law. Stop collection, attachment for rent and eviction steps when you learn of a filing, and get advice before going further. Mississippi law matters mainly for the property a tenant may protect from creditors, which the state's exemption statute sets (see the exemptions row). The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes in Mississippi
bodyText: A Mississippi tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so, and must tell you of conditions the tenant knows of that may cause damage. You owe no repair duty for a defect the tenant, or someone on the premises with the tenant's permission, caused deliberately or negligently, and a tenant may not end the lease over a condition the tenant's own household or guests caused. A tenant whose fault destroys a building, or who expressly agreed to be bound, can still owe rent for it and, under a repair promise in the lease, its rebuilding. Your remedies are a written notice to remedy the damage (repair or payment of damages) within up to 14 days or the agreement ends, no notice period where the violation is substantial and materially affects health or safety (the eviction complaint must still attach a written notice), a damages claim, and at move-out a claim against the deposit for repairs beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in writing within 45 days after termination, move-out and the tenant's demand. The library's optional tenant-damage clause is tagged for Mississippi.

title: When a Tenant Dies: Mississippi's Cosigner Rule and Little Else
bodyText: Mississippi's only tenant-death statute is the Derrick Beard Act: a cosigner of a residential lease may end it, and is presumed to have ended it, when the lessee dies (or all lessees die), unless the cosigner tells you within 30 days that the lease will continue; the estate and cosigner still owe rent and sums owed before the death, the rest of that month or 30-day period, and restoration costs beyond ordinary wear and tear, and no waiver is valid. It covers leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011; treat an earlier periodic tenancy as renewed and covered. No statute ends a lease at a tenant's death where there is no cosigner, or governs the tenant's belongings or deposit; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Deal with the estate's personal representative, agree in writing on a move-out date, an inventory and the deposit, and remember that a surviving co-tenant on the lease may stay. Do not treat belongings as abandoned while the lease runs. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy can be ended with 30 or 7 days' written notice. The library's optional emergency and death contact clause is tagged for Mississippi.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy in Mississippi
bodyText: A week-to-week tenancy ends on written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy on written notice given at least 30 days before it; either you or the tenant may give it, and no reason is needed. A fixed-term lease expires on the date it states without any notice, but before filing an eviction against a tenant who stays you must give the three-day holdover notice. Breach notices are separate: three days to pay rent, and not less than 14 days for other material breaches the tenant can remedy. No notice period applies to a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety, but an eviction complaint must still attach a written notice. In counting, the day of delivery is excluded, and if the last day falls on a weekend or legal holiday the period runs to the next business day; for periods under seven days, intermediate weekends and holidays are also excluded. Give periodic-tenancy notices on paper: the Act allows e-mail or text only for breach notices (by written agreement) and holdover notices (by the tenant's agreement). The lease cannot shorten any of these periods.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants: The Real Property Owners Protection Act
bodyText: Since July 1, 2025 Mississippi has a fast removal process for squatters, who are not tenants: a trespasser who remains on the premises, or a person a tenant invited who stays after the tenant's rental agreement has ended (heirs excluded). Remaining after the owner's, agent's or police's written notice to leave is the crime of squatting. The owner or agent files a sworn affidavit with the local law enforcement agency, which must cite the occupant within 24 hours; the occupant must leave or tell the municipal or justice court within three days that he or she will contest. Without a contest, police remove the occupant without a writ; with one, a hearing follows within seven days, and a squatter must leave within 24 hours of judgment. A certified deed copy proves the owner's case, the prevailing party gets attorney's fees, and false statements are a misdemeanor. Presenting a fake lease, renting property you do not own, or intentionally damaging a home by more than $1,000 while unlawfully occupying it are felonies. Since July 1, 2026, only the owner or a person the owner designates may manage or collect payments for the property. Evict tenants and former tenants the ordinary way.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice or Judgment in Mississippi
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, a tenant who pays all sums owed before the hearing need not move out; after a judgment based only on unpaid rent, the judge may not issue the warrant for removal if, after the move-out date, you have accepted the sums in the judgment, and you must accept full payment tendered by that date in good faith. Mississippi has no statute on accepting rent at other points, for example after a three-day or 14-day notice, after a termination date has passed, or after a judgment for a breach other than nonpayment; a search of the Mississippi Code found none, so whether acceptance then waives the breach or creates a new tenancy is case law (not searched). If you want to keep an eviction alive, decide before you take money; if you take a partial payment, give the tenant a written statement that you accept it without waiving the notice, the termination or the judgment. A lease clause saying acceptance is not a waiver helps but is not a guarantee. The rules are the same for every kind of tenancy under the Act.

title: When a Notice Counts as Given in Mississippi: No Definition, so Prove Delivery
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not define when a notice is given or received, or say when mailing or posting counts; a search of the Mississippi Code found no such rule. Its periods run from events you must be able to prove: the 14-day breach notice runs from the tenant's receipt, and the periodic-tenancy notices must be given at least 7 or 30 days before the termination date. The only alternative method the Act recognizes is e-mail or text message for breach, nonpayment and holdover notices, and only if the tenant has agreed to it (in writing, for breach and nonpayment notices); the electronic-transactions law does not cover eviction, default or cure notices for a primary residence, so deliver a paper copy too. Notice to your agent counts as notice to you. Hand-deliver notices when you can, or use a method that gives proof of receipt, and keep a dated copy, because the eviction complaint must attach the notice. Serving the eviction summons is governed separately by the court rules.

title: Addenda and the Lease: No Mississippi Precedence Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a separate addendum that controls over the lease, or saying which controls when a lease and an addendum conflict; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act treats all written or oral agreements for the unit as the rental agreement, so an addendum is part of the lease and the library's precedence clause decides conflicts. Rules you adopt after signing bind the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if they do not substantially modify the agreement, so use a signed addendum, not a new rule, for a real change in terms. Two Mississippi items work best as signed text: the written disclosure and acknowledgment of water submetering in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units rented monthly or longer, or a manufactured home community, and the tenant's written agreement to receive notices by e-mail or text, which carries its own sentence about controlling. Federal disclosures, such as lead-based paint, keep their own rules.

title: Claims Against the Property: The Tenant Must Tell You of an Ejectment Suit
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that the property is in foreclosure or subject to another claim; a search of the Mississippi Code found none (see the foreclosure row for federal protections). It does put a duty on the tenant: every tenant sued in a civil action seeking ejectment must give you notice at once, on penalty of three years' rent, which you may recover in a civil action, and you may be admitted to defend the suit. Separately, an attornment by a tenant to a stranger is void unless you consent or a court orders it. Watch for papers posted on the property: in a nuisance-abatement suit a restraining order may be served by posting it on a principal door, and a petition against a building used by a criminal street gang may be filed only 30 days after notice to the owner by return-receipt mail or personal service. The library's tagged clause asking the tenant to forward legal papers about the property matches these rules.

title: Automatic Renewal of a Lease: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute governing automatic renewal of a residential lease, such as a required reminder notice, special type size or opt-in; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none (the automatic-renewal statutes it has concern corporate charters, insurance, securities and similar contracts). An automatic-renewal clause is therefore an ordinary lease term: state the renewal period, the rent for it and how either side may give notice of nonrenewal, and remember that every nonrenewal must be in good faith. Without a renewal clause, a lease with a definite term simply expires on its stated date; a rental agreement that fixes no definite term is week-to-week (weekly rent) or month-to-month and ends on 7 or 30 days' written notice. Each renewal counts as a renewal for the Derrick Beard Act, which covers leases entered into or renewed after July 1, 2011. A courtesy reminder before an automatic renewal is good practice even though Mississippi does not require it.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Mississippi Leases
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute specific to arbitration of landlord-tenant disputes; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Its general arbitration statutes are narrow: one lets persons other than minors and persons of unsound mind submit an existing controversy to arbitration by a signed writing, and the statute making clauses for future disputes valid and enforceable applies only to construction, design and related agreements, not leases. So no Mississippi statute makes a pre-dispute arbitration clause in a home lease enforceable (Mississippi case law was not searched); whether the Federal Arbitration Act would enforce one was not reviewed. Eviction is a court proceeding in justice, county or circuit court under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the Act bars waiving its remedies in the lease, and the Constitution keeps the right of trial by jury inviolate. Some Mississippi lease forms offer a mandatory arbitration addendum; if you use one, keep eviction and possession actions and small claims in court, make it mutual, and have a lawyer review it. Federal law also matters here: the Federal Arbitration Act overrides state rules that block arbitration directly or indirectly (for example, a rule against giving up a jury), and the U.S. Supreme Court has held that renting out real estate is activity it reaches. On that basis the library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you. Because state law points the other way, a court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: Other Rules Mississippi Does Not Have
bodyText: Many rules found in other states are not in Mississippi's statutes; each item below has its own row. (1) No just-cause eviction rule and no owner move-in statute. (2) No state servicemember lease statute (federal law governs), no early exit for illness or a move to care, and no late-benefit eviction defense. (3) No tenant protection or disclosure duty at foreclosure. (4) No permission to lock out a tenant, and no self-help eviction statute apart from the nuisance entry below. (5) No end-of-term possession bond, and no rental agreement may authorize a confessed judgment. (6) No rule on delivering possession at the start, on false rental applications, or on ending a lease because a repair is too costly. (7) No landlord self-cure statute, no liquidated-damages rule and no notice-fee rule. (8) No seasonal-rental, tenant-bankruptcy, automatic-renewal, emergency-contact or energy-data rule, and no landlord-tenant arbitration statute. Two rules Mississippi does have that many states lack: a tenant's prostitution or drug nuisance voids the lease by law and lets the owner enter (still file an eviction), and squatters can be removed by law enforcement on your affidavit. This search covered the Mississippi Code and Constitution, not case law or local ordinances.

title: Checked Across the Whole Mississippi Code
bodyText: The whole Mississippi Code and Constitution, not only the landlord-tenant chapters, were searched for three things landlords ask about. (1) Squatters: Mississippi does have a rule, the Real Property Owners Protection Act (2025), outside the landlord-tenant chapters: a squatter is not a tenant, remaining after written notice to leave is a crime, and law enforcement cites and removes squatters on the owner's sworn affidavit, with a court hearing within seven days if the occupant contests (see the unauthorized-occupant row). (2) Rent receipts: no statute requires a receipt for rent, even cash rent; give receipts anyway, because you must prove the rent owed in a nonpayment eviction (see the rent-receipts row). (3) Landlord registration: Mississippi has no statewide rental registration, license or inspection program as a condition of renting or of winning an eviction, except that an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here must register with the Secretary of State and may not maintain an eviction or other court action until it has registered (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 79-29-1003, 79-29-1013, 79-4-15.01, 79-4-15.02); check your city's ordinances, which were not searched (see the rental-inspection row). Separately, Mississippi's general data-breach notice law applies when you hold tenants' Social Security, driver's license or account numbers.

title: Domestic Abuse Protection Orders: Citations Unchanged in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's domestic abuse protection orders remain in Title 93, Chapter 21 of the Code; the section on temporary and final orders (Section 93-21-15) has not moved, and no Mississippi landlord-tenant statute cites that chapter, so no lease or notice needs a citation update. Because Mississippi gives victims no statutory lease-termination, lock-change or eviction protection, these orders matter to you mainly through what they direct. A municipal or justice court's temporary order, and a chancery or county court's final order, may give the victim possession of the home to the exclusion of the abuser by evicting the abuser, may bar the abuser from coming near the residence, and may forbid transferring or disposing of property the parties own or lease. A temporary order lasts up to 30 days, or up to one year if the parties have no minor children in common. Orders are entered in the Mississippi Protection Order Registry and are effective in every state. If you receive an order, read it and follow it.

title: Electronic Signatures and Records in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, which can be shown by the circumstances and conduct. Between them, a lease or signature may not be denied effect just because it is electronic, an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature. Limits remain: either party may refuse to continue electronically for later transactions, and that right cannot be waived; an electronic record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing is not enforceable against the recipient; and where a law requires a specific delivery method, that method must still be used. Unlike some states' versions, Mississippi's excludes notices of default, eviction or right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, and notices ending utility service. The landlord-tenant statutes separately let breach, nonpayment and holdover notices go by e-mail or text if the tenant agreed (in writing, for breach and nonpayment notices), so for those notices use both the agreed electronic method and paper. The library's electronic-signature clause works in Mississippi.

title: No Mississippi Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour phone number, or regulating an emergency contact a tenant names for you; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Giving tenants a way to reach you for urgent repairs is still good practice: a tenant's repair-and-deduct right starts 30 days after written notice of a specific and material defect, and a tenant must tell you of conditions the tenant knows may cause damage, which works only if the tenant can reach you. Asking a tenant to name an emergency contact, with the contact's consent, is a lawful lease term; it does not let that person act for the tenant's estate if the tenant dies or occupy the unit. The library's optional emergency and death contact clause is tagged for Mississippi. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Releasing Tenants' Energy Data
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy or utility usage data to the owner, for building benchmarking or any other purpose, and no statute that requires, permits or forbids a lease clause authorizing that release; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. If you want a tenant's usage data from a utility, get the tenant's written authorization in the lease or a separate signed form, limit it to usage data and the stated purpose, and use the utility's own release process. Water submetering is different: if you submeter water in an apartment house of four or more units, a condominium or a manufactured home community, your bills to tenants must show the beginning and ending meter reads, so you hold that data already. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. Public Service Commission rules, utility tariffs, local ordinances, federal law and case law were not searched.

title: Entire-Agreement Clause: Works in Mississippi, but Oral Side Deals Can Count
bodyText: The library's entire-agreement clause works in Mississippi as written. Two Mississippi points matter. First, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act defines the rental agreement as all written or oral agreements for the unit, so a promise made outside the written lease can become part of the deal; the clause's signed-writing rule helps, but put every side promise in the lease or a signed addendum. Second, no Mississippi statute lets you change an existing lease by notice to comply with a new law. The only change-by-notice rule is for written rules: a rule adopted or amended after signing binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice and it does not substantially modify the lease. During a fixed term, change other terms only by signed amendment; in a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, end it with 7 or 30 days' written notice and offer new terms. A lease longer than one year must be in a writing signed by the party to be charged. No lease term can waive the Act's rights.

title: Mississippi Law Governs Every Mississippi Rental
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs any rental agreement entered into after July 1, 1991, wherever it was signed, for a dwelling unit located in Mississippi, so a lease cannot pick another state's law to avoid it. The library's governing-law clause, naming Mississippi law plus applicable city and county law, matches that. The Act covers the parties' rights to possession after the lease ends, and other rights and remedies at law or in equity stay available unless the Act prohibits them. Residential evictions are heard by a justice, county or circuit court. The Act does not reach the arrangements it excludes, such as transient hotel or motel stays, occupancy under a contract to buy the home, condominium owners, fraternal housing, institutions and agricultural rentals (see the scope row). Check your city or county ordinances, which this review did not search. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Informal Dispute Resolution
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires, regulates or limits a lease clause asking you and the tenant to try to settle a dispute informally (by written notice and a meeting, or by mediation) before going to court; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Such a clause is a lawful contract term if it stays optional or short and does not delay anything the law sets on a clock: the 3-day notice for unpaid rent, the 14-day notice to remedy a breach, the 7- or 30-day notice ending a periodic tenancy, the 3-day holdover notice, or an eviction. Keep possession actions, nonpayment, emergencies and health-and-safety breaches out of it, and do not let it condition the tenant's statutory rights such as repair-and-deduct, because a lease cannot waive the Act's rights or remedies. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing requirement, and no statute making registration a condition of renting or letting a tenant end the lease because you are unregistered; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Three state rules touch the subject. First, a person who, for a fee or commission, rents, leases or manages real estate for others is a real estate broker and needs a Mississippi license; an owner managing its own property, and its salaried regular employees, are exempt. Second, only the owner or an agent the owner designates may manage, control or receive payments for the use of real property, so put any manager's authority in writing. Third, an out-of-state limited liability company must register with the Secretary of State before transacting business here; until it registers it may not maintain an eviction or other court action, though its leases stay valid, and by transacting business unregistered it appoints the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process on claims arising from that business (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 79-29-1003(1), 79-29-1013). Owning real property, without more, is not transacting business (Miss. Code Ann. § 79-29-1015(1)(i)), so whether renting it out is depends on the facts. An out-of-state corporation must likewise get a certificate of authority before transacting business and may not maintain an eviction or other court case until it does (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 79-4-15.01, 79-4-15.02). Cities and counties may have their own registration or inspection ordinances, which this review did not search. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Blank-Space Rule for Leases
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, and no rule that an incomplete lease is a breach or unenforceable; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Fill in every blank anyway, or strike it with "N/A". The rental agreement includes oral as well as written agreements, so a blank rent, due date, term or deposit invites a dispute over what was said. The written terms also matter in court: your eviction complaint must be based on the terms of the rental agreement and state the rent and fees owed, and in a nonpayment case the judge must follow the rental agreement the parties signed. If the lease fixes no definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week when rent is paid weekly and otherwise month-to-month. Whether a court reads an unclear term against you as drafter is case law (not searched).

title: What a Mississippi Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute listing what a residential lease must contain and no required lease form; a lease may even be oral. Several rules, though, work only if the lease says so in writing: e-mail or text notice of a breach or nonpayment requires the tenant's written agreement to be notified that way; a tenant may take over repair or maintenance duties only by written good-faith agreement; double rent after a holdover notice applies only if not contradicted by the lease; the deposit may be applied to rent, damage, cleaning and default costs only if it was made for those purposes; and the tenant uses the unit only as a dwelling unless otherwise agreed. If you have four or more units in an apartment house, a condominium or a manufactured home community and submeter water, you must disclose it and get the tenant's written acknowledgment. The federal lead-based paint disclosure also applies to pre-1978 housing.

title: No Mississippi Duty to Deliver a Lease Copy
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and none making a missing copy a defense to enforcing it; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Give each tenant a fully signed copy anyway and keep your own, together with copies of every written notice you deliver: to file an eviction you must attach a copy of the written breach notice or termination notice, and in a nonpayment case the judge follows the signed rental agreement. If the lease is signed electronically, let the tenant download, save and print it, because under Mississippi's electronic transactions law an electronic record the sender keeps the recipient from storing or printing is not enforceable against the recipient. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Mississippi Initials Requirement for Lease Terms
bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires a residential tenant to initial any lease term, or sets a special format for a term that departs from the statute, for the term to bind the tenant; the signatures are enough as far as the statutes go. The one initials rule the search found is for rent-to-own contracts under the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, not home leases. Two Mississippi rules do turn on a written agreement: e-mail or text notice of a breach or nonpayment needs the tenant's written agreement to be notified that way, and a tenant may take over your repair or maintenance duties only by written good-faith agreement. Put each in a clearly labeled, signed section or addendum. Initials beside unusual terms (fees, chores, electronic notice) are still good evidence the tenant saw them. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Limit on Residential Lease Length
bodyText: Mississippi sets no minimum or maximum length for a private residential lease; a search of the Mississippi Code found term limits only for leases of public land and public facilities. A lease of land for a longer term than one year must be in a writing signed by the party to be charged (see the statute-of-frauds row), so put any lease or renewal running past a year in a lease signed by you and every tenant. If the lease fixes no definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week when rent is paid weekly and otherwise month-to-month, ended by written notice at least 7 or 30 days before the termination date. A fixed-term lease expires on the date it states. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to rental agreements entered into after July 1, 1991, and the cosigner-death rule to leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011.

title: No Mississippi Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute setting a minimum type size or print format for a residential lease, and no evidentiary penalty for small print; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The bold-type rules the search found are for other contracts: a self-storage rental agreement must state the storage lien in bold type (and a self-storage unit may not be used as a residence), and rent-to-own contracts have their own disclosure rules. Use readable type (10-point or larger) throughout anyway, and set fees, waivers, electronic-notice consent and tenant repair agreements where the tenant will see them. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Out-of-State Owners: LLC Registration and a Licensed Manager
