bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires an individual owner who lives outside Mississippi to name an in-state agent in the lease or for service of process, bars a suit until an agent is named, or requires tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. An out-of-state limited liability company is different: it must register with the Secretary of State before transacting business here, it may not maintain an eviction or other court action until it has registered (its leases stay valid), and by transacting business here unregistered it appoints the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process on claims arising from that business (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 79-29-1003(1), 79-29-1013). Owning real property, without more, is not transacting business (Miss. Code Ann. § 79-29-1015(1)(i)), so whether renting it out is depends on the facts; register before you need to file. An out-of-state corporation is under the same rule: it needs a certificate of authority before transacting business, may not maintain a court case until it has one (its contracts, deeds and liens stay valid), and owes a civil penalty of $10 a day, up to $1,000 a year; owning real property without more is not transacting business (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 79-4-15.01, 79-4-15.02). Registering a name you rent under is voluntary in Mississippi and is for public notice only (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 75-93-3, 75-93-13). Three rules still matter. Anyone who, for a fee or commission, rents, leases or manages your property for you must hold a Mississippi real estate license (an owner managing its own property, and its salaried regular employees, are exempt). Only you or an agent you designate may manage, control or collect payments for the property, so give your manager written authority. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, notice to your agent counts as notice to you, and hiring an agent does not relieve you of ultimate liability. Give tenants a written address for notices and rent. Cities may have their own rules (not searched).

title: How Notices Are Delivered in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires your key notices to be in writing and does not define how a written notice is delivered: it has no mailing rule, no deemed-receipt rule and no list of methods. The 14-day breach notice runs from the tenant's receipt, so use a method you can prove (hand delivery with a witness or signed receipt, or certified mail), keep a copy, and attach it to any eviction complaint. You may send the breach, repeat-breach or 3-day nonpayment notice by e-mail or text only if the tenant has agreed in writing to be notified that way; the holdover notice may go by e-mail or text if the tenant has agreed. Mississippi's electronic transactions law does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, so deliver a paper copy too. Notice to your agent counts as notice to you. Short periods skip weekends and holidays.

title: No Mississippi Rule on Move-Out Notice Forms
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on the content of a tenant's notice to vacate or of a move-out form you ask the tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Keep the form to what the notice needs: the move-out date and a forwarding address, because the deposit refund clock runs only after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant demands the deposit, so ask the tenant to make that demand in writing on the form. A tenant ending a periodic tenancy must give written notice at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month) before the termination date; a fixed-term lease expires on the date it states. Do not use a move-out form to add new charges or waivers: the lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Act, and every duty carries an obligation of good faith.

title: The Notices Clause in Mississippi
bodyText: The library's notices clause works in Mississippi as written: it sends notices to the addresses in the lease and lets any statutory method, form or timing control. Mississippi's Act requires the breach, nonpayment, holdover, periodic-termination and deposit notices to be written (or, for some, e-mail or text if the tenant agreed) but has no general delivery or mailing rule, so the addresses in the lease and your proof of delivery do the work. Fill in both notice addresses, update them in writing, and keep a copy of every notice: you must attach the written breach or termination notice to an eviction complaint. Notice to your agent counts as notice to you. For e-mail or text delivery, use the electronic-notice consent and see the notice-delivery row. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Where Mississippi Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Many Mississippi rules apply only if the lease says so, or until it says otherwise. The lease decides: the length of the tenancy (otherwise week-to-week for weekly rent, else month-to-month); whether the tenant may use the unit for anything but a dwelling ("unless otherwise agreed"); whether you may send breach and nonpayment notices by e-mail or text (only with the tenant's written agreement); whether the tenant takes on repair or maintenance duties (only by written good-faith agreement); what the deposit secures (rent, damage, cleaning, default costs, only if made for those purposes); whether double rent applies after a holdover notice ("if not contradicted" by the lease); and late fees, which become rent when the lease requires them. In a nonpayment eviction the judge follows the signed rental agreement. Written rules bind if reasonable and fairly applied. What the lease cannot do: waive the Act's rights, authorize confession of judgment, or excuse your willful misconduct.

title: No Mississippi Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no plain-language statute for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers, and no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Mississippi's Consumer Protection Act bars unfair or deceptive trade practices and defines trade to include offering real property, but whether its private-suit section reaches a lease of a home is not settled by its text, and case law was not checked, so treat it as possibly applying (see the fee-transparency row). Write the lease in plain words anyway and set fees, chores the tenant takes on, electronic-notice consent and other unusual terms where the tenant will see them. Terms the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act forbids, such as a waiver of its rights, a confession of judgment or a release of your willful misconduct, are unenforceable however plainly written. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on requiring renter's insurance: none lets the tenant choose the carrier by law, limits a force-placed policy or its fee, requires an advisory that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, or requires a flood or insurance notice before signing; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. You may require renter's insurance by lease, as the library's clause does. Let the tenant choose any licensed insurer, state the minimum liability coverage, and ask for proof at move-in and on request. Requiring insurance does not shift your own duties: you must keep the unit, plumbing and heating or cooling in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease unless the tenant agrees in writing, in good faith, to take some on, and no lease may limit your liability for your own willful misconduct. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers in Mississippi
bodyText: When you sell, the buyer steps into your rights under existing leases and is bound by their covenants to the tenants, and a tenant who paid rent to you before learning of the sale is protected; the buyer, as transferee, is also exposed to the deposit penalty if it keeps a deposit in bad faith (see the deposit-on-sale row). No Mississippi statute requires a written notice to tenants of a sale or a new manager, releases you on notice, or protects tenants when a lender forecloses (see the foreclosure row); a search found none. Send each tenant a written notice anyway naming the new owner or manager, the rent payment address and who holds the deposit, because rent paid to the old owner before notice protects the tenant. A manager who rents or manages for a fee needs a real estate license (your own salaried employees are exempt), only the owner or a designated agent may collect payments, and hiring a manager does not relieve the owner of ultimate liability.

title: What Mississippi Landlord-Tenant Law Covers
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs rental agreements entered into after July 1, 1991 for a dwelling unit in Mississippi, including possession after the lease ends. It does not govern: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious services; occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale of the unit; fraternal or social organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; and agricultural rentals. A trespasser or squatter is not a tenant; a separate squatter law gives owners a law-enforcement removal process. Recreational vehicle parks have their own statute: the park may refuse service to, and have officers remove, a person who fails to pay rent when agreed or misbehaves, with 48 hours to retrieve property. Mississippi has no manufactured-home park landlord-tenant act; lot rentals fall under the general rules, and a tenant's manufactured home is personal property in eviction. Some statutes reach only certain properties: pool safety (complexes of two or more units that allow residents under 12) and water submetering (four or more units, or a manufactured home community, rented monthly or longer).

title: Written Leases and Long Terms in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act treats oral as well as written agreements as rental agreements, so a week-to-week, month-to-month or other short tenancy can be made orally. But Mississippi's statute of frauds bars a suit on a lease of land for a longer term than one year, and on any agreement not to be performed within fifteen months, unless the agreement or a note of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged (or by someone that party authorized in writing). Put every lease of more than a year, and every renewal or extension that runs past a year, in a writing signed by you and every tenant; an electronic signature works if both sides agreed to deal electronically. A cosigner's promise to answer for the tenant's debt also must be in a signed writing. The deposit, notice and eviction rules apply the same way to written and oral rental agreements.

title: State-Prescribed Forms in Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi prescribes no lease form and no verbatim wording for your ordinary notices (the 14-day breach notice, the 3-day nonpayment notice, the 3-day holdover notice, periodic termination notices or the deposit itemization); you write those yourself, meeting each statute's content and timing rules. The verbatim text Mississippi does prescribe is for court papers: the residential eviction summons must contain statutory paragraphs on the hearing, the move-out period of at least seven days, paying to stay in a nonpayment case, abandoned property and the 72-hour access period after removal. The squatter law prescribes a citation text, and the old attachment-for-rent procedure in the general landlord-tenant chapter has its own forms. The Administrative Office of Courts publishes sample eviction forms, but its sample summons predates the 2025 amendments and omits some required sentences, so make sure the summons used in your case tracks the current statute. These rules apply to all tenancy types.

title: No Mississippi Tenant Portal Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no law on tenant portals; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. No statute sets where or how rent must be paid, so the lease may make an online portal the agreed way to pay, and leases, renewals and routine notices may be handled electronically if you and the tenant both agreed to do business electronically. Three limits come from Mississippi's electronic transactions law and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A tenant who agreed to electronic dealings may refuse to handle later transactions electronically, and the lease cannot take that right away, so keep a paper option. A document the tenant cannot save or print is not enforceable against the tenant. And notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence fall outside the electronic transactions law, while breach and nonpayment notices go by e-mail or text only with the tenant's written agreement, so deliver those on paper too.

title: Rent Records and Tenant Data in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to keep a rent ledger, give the tenant a payment history on request, attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice, or give rent receipts; a search of the Mississippi Code found none (see the rent-receipts row). Keep a complete ledger anyway: your eviction complaint must state the rent and fees owed, and your deposit claim must be itemized. For applicant and tenant data, Mississippi's breach-notice law applies to anyone doing business in the state who owns or maintains residents' personal information, meaning a name with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code. If unencrypted data of that kind is acquired without authorization, you must notify the affected people without unreasonable delay unless an investigation shows harm is unlikely; the Attorney General enforces it, and it creates no private lawsuit. Encrypt or lock up applications and payment data.

title: Tenant's Property Insurance: Do Not Disclaim Your Willful Misconduct
bodyText: No Mississippi statute regulates a lease term saying your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings or requiring renter's insurance, so the library's tenant's-property clause that states those two points (and sets a liability minimum, with a disclaimer that excepts your gross negligence and willful misconduct) works in Mississippi. One Mississippi rule limits the wording: no rental agreement may exculpate or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct. An unqualified sentence that you are "not liable" for loss of the tenant's property reaches willful misconduct too, so do not use it as written; a disclaimer limited to causes outside your control, or one that expressly excepts your willful misconduct, is acceptable. Requiring insurance does not move your repair duties to the tenant's policy: you must keep the unit, plumbing and heating or cooling in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, unless the tenant agrees in writing, in good faith, to take some duties on. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute setting a notice period for changing a term of an existing tenancy, other than its rule for written house rules; a search found none (rent increases have no notice rule either; see the rent-increase row). A written rule adopted or amended after the tenant signs binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice and the rule does not substantially modify the rental agreement, and every rule must be reasonable, explicit, fairly applied and not a way to evade your duties. Anything bigger is a lease change. During a fixed term, change terms only by a signed amendment or as the lease itself provides. In a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, end the tenancy by written notice at least 7 or 30 days before the termination date and offer a new tenancy on the new terms, saying plainly the tenant may stay on those terms. After a fixed term expires you may demand a rent increase, but not to retaliate for the tenant's lawful actions.

title: No Sunset on Mississippi Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Mississippi's core landlord-tenant statutes is on a repeal or expiration date: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (including the 2022 eviction procedure and its 2025 amendments), the general landlord-tenant chapter, the 2025 squatter law and the recreational vehicle park section carry no sunset clause. The Act's timing rules look backward instead: it applies to rental agreements entered into after July 1, 1991, and the cosigner-death rule applies to leases entered into or renewed from July 1, 2011. Several sections of the general chapter were repealed outright in 2022 when residential evictions moved into the Act. Watch each legislative session for amendments, which Mississippi often makes effective on passage. This finding covers the Mississippi Code and Constitution.

title: No Mississippi Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a residential lease, or any landlord notice, to be translated or provided in a language other than English, including when you advertise or negotiate in another language; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. If you negotiate with a tenant in another language, consider giving a translated copy for reference while stating which version controls, and make sure the tenant understands the key terms (rent, term, fees, deposit, notices, any electronic-notice consent and any repair duties the tenant takes on). Federal fair housing rules on national origin may bear on language practices (not reviewed here). The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in Mississippi
bodyText: Several Mississippi notices must be in writing, and your lease should not suggest a spoken notice will do. In writing (or by e-mail or text only if the tenant agreed in writing): your notice of a breach giving up to 14 days to remedy, the 14-day notice for a repeat breach within six months, and the 3-day nonpayment notice. In writing (or e-mail or text if the tenant agreed): the 3-day holdover notice after a fixed term expires. In writing only: a notice ending a week-to-week (7 days) or month-to-month (30 days) tenancy, from either side; your itemized notice claiming deposit money; and the tenant's 30-day notice of a defect before repair-and-deduct. If you submeter water in a covered property, the tenant's acknowledgment must be in a written document. You must attach the written breach or termination notice to an eviction complaint. Notices with no writing rule (a new house rule, a double-rent holdover notice) are still best given in writing.

title: Animals Left in a Mississippi Rental
bodyText: Mississippi gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of a pet left after an eviction or a move-out; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Mississippi has no landlord-entry statute, so your access during the tenancy comes from the lease. After an eviction, the statute lets you dispose of abandoned personal property, but it does not address living animals, so do not treat a pet like furniture. The cruelty law makes it a misdemeanor to deprive a dog or cat of adequate shelter, food or water intentionally or with criminal negligence, protects good-faith emergency care for an abandoned dog or cat, and lets a court have law enforcement seize an abandoned animal and name animal control or a shelter as custodian. So try the tenant and any emergency contact first, then call local animal control or law enforcement rather than keeping, rehoming or disposing of the animal yourself.

title: Service and Assistance Animals in Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi's own animal-access laws do not reach ordinary rental housing. The Mississippi Support Animal Act gives blind, mobility-impaired and hearing-impaired people and veterans with PTSD who use a trained support animal (limited to a dog or miniature horse) equal access to public conveyances, hotels, lodging places, businesses open to the public and other public accommodations, with no fee for the animal; the older guide-dog statute is similar and makes the handler liable for damage. A lease of a home is not on either list. It is a crime to willfully and maliciously harass, injure or interfere with a guide, hearing, service or support dog. In housing, the federal Fair Housing Act governs: an assistance animal is not a pet, no pet fee or deposit may be charged for it, documentation may be requested only when the need is not apparent, and the tenant pays for damage. The library's assistance-animal clause follows those rules and works in Mississippi.

title: No Mississippi Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Mississippi has no requirement to give a tenant a state fact sheet or other notice about pets and eviction, at signing or when you learn the tenant has a dog or cat; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The required eviction summons speaks only of personal property left behind, not animals. If an eviction or move-out may leave animals behind, tell the tenant in writing to take every animal, and call animal control or law enforcement rather than disposing of an animal yourself (see the animal-care row). The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no pet-fee statute, so the general rules decide. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit: any deposit whose main function is to secure the tenant's performance is governed by the deposit statute, so you may keep only amounts reasonably needed for unpaid rent, tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning at the end, and other reasonable costs of the tenant's default, if the deposit was made for those purposes, itemized in a written notice; return the rest within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. Mississippi has no deposit cap, so a pet deposit adds no cap problem. Monthly pet rent is rent, because rent includes all payments the lease requires, so unpaid pet rent supports a 3-day nonpayment notice. No statute addresses a nonrefundable pet fee; label it clearly. Never charge any pet fee, rent or deposit for an assistance animal (federal fair housing law).

title: No Mississippi Rule on Pet Liability Insurance
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on requiring a tenant with a pet to carry liability insurance, naming you as an interested party, or limiting breed or insurance rules; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The library's pet-insurance clause works as written, and it rightly does not apply to an assistance animal: under federal fair housing law an assistance animal is not a pet, and an insurance or fee condition on one is risky. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. Insurance Department rules were not searched.

title: Pet Rules Are Set by Your Lease in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on pets in rentals: you may ban pets, limit their number, kind or size, require approval, and charge pet rent or a pet deposit (see the pet-fees row). No Mississippi statute gives seniors or anyone else a right to keep a pet. The limits come from other law. An assistance animal is not a pet under federal fair housing law. The tenant must not damage the premises or disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, so a damaging or nuisance animal supports a 14-day notice to remedy, and a written pet rule must be reasonable, explicit and fairly applied. Two drafting points: a tenant indemnity for pet claims must not reach your own willful misconduct, which no Mississippi lease may excuse, and Mississippi has no entry statute or pet-removal procedure, so say in the lease when you may enter and call animal control instead of removing a pet yourself.

title: No Mississippi Penalty for Refusing an Assistance Animal in Housing
bodyText: Mississippi has no state penalty aimed at a landlord who refuses a tenant's or applicant's service or assistance animal; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The state access laws reach public conveyances, hotels, lodging places, businesses open to the public and other public accommodations, not leases of homes, and they carry no stated penalty. The one related crime is willfully and maliciously assaulting, harassing, injuring or interfering with the duties of a guide, hearing, service or support dog, a misdemeanor of up to 90 days or a $500 fine; do not confront or obstruct an animal while a dispute is pending. Refusing a needed assistance animal can violate the federal Fair Housing Act, with federal remedies (not reviewed here), so handle every request as a reasonable-accommodation request. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Penalty for Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute penalizing a person who falsely claims a pet is a service, support or emotional support animal, whether to a landlord or to a business; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The state Support Animal Act defines a support animal as a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability and says a pet is not one, but that Act governs public accommodations, not housing. For a housing request, follow federal fair housing guidance: if the disability or the need for the animal is not apparent, you may ask for reliable documentation, but do not demand certificates, registrations or vests, and decide each request individually. Keep records of what you asked and received. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Assigned Parking Spaces in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on assigned parking spaces in rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A space you promise the tenant is part of the leased premises under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so change or take it away only as the lease allows; the library's assigned-space clause, letting you reassign a comparable space on reasonable notice, is lawful in Mississippi. A parking rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if it does not substantially modify the lease, so reassignment rights belong in the lease itself. If someone parks in a tenant's assigned space, Mississippi lets a vehicle on private property be towed at the request of the property owner or the owner's designee (see the towing row). The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving a tenant the right to install or use an electric vehicle charger, and none requiring you to approve a request, provide charging or follow a procedure; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Whether to allow charging is your choice under the lease. If you allow a tenant-installed charger, treat it as an alteration needing your written consent (the tenant must not damage or remove any part of the premises), and put in writing who installs it (a licensed electrician), who pays for installation and electricity, insurance, and what happens at move-out. If you plan to bill tenants for charging, note Mississippi's public-utility law: it excludes a person who resells utility electricity to the public exclusively for vehicle charging, but separately says utility service furnished to tenants is outside regulation only if not resold on a metered basis; ask the Public Service Commission before metering charging to tenants. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: EV Chargers When a Mississippi Lease Ends
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends: no rule on removal, restoration or reimbursement; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Settle it in your written approval: whether the charger stays (and whether you pay anything for it) or the tenant removes it through a licensed electrician and restores the wall and circuit, and that restoration costs may be claimed from the deposit as tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in your written notice. Property left after a court eviction may be disposed of under the eviction statute, but a charger wired into the building is better handled by agreement than by treating it as abandoned. After a voluntary move-out no statute applies (see the abandoned-property row). The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi EV Charger Installation Rules for Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute setting installation, insurance, metering or approval requirements for electric vehicle chargers in rental housing, and no deadline for answering a tenant's request; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Set your own conditions in a written approval: a licensed electrician, any permits your local building code requires, a separate meter or a stated way to bill electricity, insurance, and responsibility for damage. Before billing tenants for metered charging, check with the Public Service Commission, because Mississippi's public-utility definition treats resale to tenants on a metered basis differently from resale to the public for vehicle charging (see the EV charging row). The same applies to every tenancy type. Local building and electrical codes were not searched.

title: No Mississippi Rules on EV Charging in Shared Areas
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on electric vehicle charging in shared parking areas of rental property: no tenant right to a shared charger, no rule on assigning or reserving charging spaces, and no cost-sharing formula; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. If you provide shared chargers, adopt written rules on use, time limits, fees and removal of vehicles that block them. Rules must serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or a fair distribution of facilities, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit; a rule added mid-lease binds only with reasonable notice and if it is not a substantial change. Towing a blocking vehicle must follow Mississippi's private-property towing rules (see the towing row). The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Parking Areas and Vehicle Damage in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on residential parking areas; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A parking area you hold out for tenants or promise to a tenant is part of the leased premises, so reduce or move it only as the lease allows. The library's parking clause, which limits tenants to designated areas, says you do not provide security and disclaims liability except for your gross negligence and willful misconduct, works in Mississippi. Do not add an unqualified sentence that you are "not liable" for damage to or theft of vehicles: no Mississippi rental agreement may exculpate or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct, and a blanket disclaimer reaches that too; a disclaimer limited to causes outside your control, or excepting willful misconduct, is acceptable. Parking rules adopted mid-lease bind only with reasonable notice and if not a substantial change. For towing, see the towing row. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Mississippi Parking Rules Notice Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring parking or towing rules to be delivered before the lease is signed, given a prescribed heading, limited in mid-term changes, or limited in the vehicle information you may ask for; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Your parking rules are written rules under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: they bind tenants only if reasonable, explicit and fairly applied, and a rule adopted or changed after signing binds only with reasonable notice and if it does not substantially modify the lease. So give tenants the parking rules in writing with the lease and change them during a fixed term only as the lease allows. The only towing-sign rule found is for nonconsensual towing of commercial motor vehicles, which requires a posted sign with the international towing symbol at each entrance; for ordinary cars, post clear signs anyway. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Vehicle Rules and Towing a Tenant's Car in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi lets the lease set vehicle rules (operable, registered passenger vehicles only; no trailers, boats or RVs without consent; no repairs on site), and no statute limits what vehicle information you may ask for or bars towing for expired registration. Towing is governed separately: a vehicle on private property may be towed only at the request of its owner or lienholder, at a law enforcement officer's direction, or at the request of the property owner or the owner's designee or assignee, or as other law allows. The tow company must record who asked for the tow and report it to local law enforcement within 24 hours. Whether a tenant's own car parked in breach of your rules on premises the tenant leases can be towed as your request alone is not settled by the statutes, so give written notice first, tow only under a clear lease term, and use a licensed tow company. The library's vehicle-rules clause, which tows only in accordance with applicable law, works in Mississippi.

title: Storage Space Leased With a Mississippi Home
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute aimed at storage space leased with a home; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. A storage locker or room you promise the tenant is part of the leased premises. Do not rely on Mississippi's self-storage lien law against a tenant's locker: it covers facilities renting individual storage space on a self-service basis under a storage rental agreement with a bold-type lien notice, and says that space may not be used for residential purposes. Your remedies are the residential ones: the general landlord's lien on a tenant's personal property on the leased premises for contracted rent, enforced only through the court attachment-for-rent process, and, after a court eviction, the statutory property rules. Do not lock a tenant out of storage or sell its contents yourself. The library's storage clause, whose disclaimer excepts your gross negligence and willful misconduct, works as written; an unqualified "not liable" sentence would reach your willful misconduct, which no Mississippi lease may excuse. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Towing From Your Mississippi Rental Property
bodyText: Mississippi lets a vehicle on private property be towed only at the request of its owner or lienholder, at a law enforcement officer's direction, or at the request of the real property owner or the owner's designee or assignee (such as your manager), or as other law allows. From July 1, 2026, the tow company must record the name, phone number or e-mail of whoever requested the tow and in what capacity; if it fails to, it loses all towing and storage fees unless the vehicle owner asked for the tow. The company must report the tow to local law enforcement within 24 hours, notify the owner and lienholders by certified mail, and may sell an unredeemed vehicle after the statutory notices. For commercial motor vehicles, you must give the tow company written permission and post a sign with the international towing symbol at each entrance. The abandoned-vehicle chapter does not cover a car simply left in your lot. Never tow a tenant's car in a dispute without a clear lease term and written notice.

title: No Mississippi Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no unbundled-parking law: you may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately, as you and the tenant agree; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. If parking is separate, put the space, the charge (as a fixed amount) and what happens to the parking when the lease ends in writing. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act every payment the lease requires is rent, so an unpaid parking charge supports a 3-day nonpayment notice. Mississippi's sales tax list of taxable businesses includes parking garages and lots; whether a parking charge billed with a home lease is taxable was not settled here, so ask the Department of Revenue before charging it separately. A promised space is part of the leased premises (see the assigned-parking row). The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Mississippi Rules That Depend on Property Size
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no small-landlord exemption: its deposit, repair, notice and eviction rules apply whatever the size of your portfolio; a search of the Mississippi Code found no portfolio-size exemption. A few other rules turn on the size or type of the property, and each applies only within its own definition. Water submetering rules apply to an apartment house of four or more dwelling units rented monthly or longer, a condominium, or a manufactured home community. The pool-safety chapter applies to a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership or management on the same or adjacent lots, including condominium, cooperative and townhome projects, but not single-family homes outside such a project) with a pool, and not to a complex that bars residents under 12. Affordable rental housing of any size gets a special property-tax appraisal, with an annual income statement due to the assessor.

title: Medical Cannabis in Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi allows only medical cannabis, under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act; the Code has no adult-use (recreational) law. Under the Act you may, but need not, allow the lawful cultivation, processing, sale or use of medical cannabis on rental property, so your lease may ban growing, smoking, vaping or any use of medical cannabis on the premises, including by registered patients. The Act also says no landlord may be penalized or denied a state-law benefit for leasing to a cardholder, but it contains no rule barring you from refusing one. Cannabis possessed or used outside the Act is not protected and can fall under the tenant's duty not to engage in illegal activity on the premises as documented by a law enforcement agency. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules (not reviewed). The initiative that put a medical marijuana article in the Constitution was voided by the Mississippi Supreme Court, according to the Secretary of State's edition. Put your cannabis policy in the lease (see the smoking row).

title: Use of the Property and Common Areas in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi lets the lease restrict how tenants use the unit and common areas (no holes or fixtures without consent, balcony limits, no candles, no water-filled furniture, no exterior signs), and a search of the Mississippi Code found no statute protecting a renter's flag, waterbed, clothesline, satellite dish or solar device. Common areas held out for tenants are part of the premises. Written rules for them are enforceable only if they serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect your property or fairly share facilities, are reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants, are explicit, and do not evade your own duties; a rule added after signing binds only with reasonable notice and if it is not a substantial change. In a condominium or cooperative, the tenant must also follow the association's bylaws. The library's common-area clause works as written. Federal rules on antennas and similar devices were not reviewed. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no law letting a tenant take in people displaced by a hurricane, flood, fire or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting such stays or deciding when a displaced guest becomes a tenant; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to federal fair housing law and local codes, and the tenant answers for guests' conduct toward neighbors. After a disaster, consider giving written, time-limited consent to displaced guests rather than treating the stay as a default. Note one Mississippi rule: a person a tenant invited who stays after the tenant's rental agreement has ended is a squatter under the 2025 squatter law, not a tenant. During a declared emergency, Mississippi's emergency pricing law caps prices for goods and services in the emergency area (see the rent-control row). The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Statute on Grills or Open Flames at Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that limits, or requires, lease rules on grills, barbecues, charcoal or other open-flame devices at a rental, or that sets a distance from the building; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. The library's grilling clause is a lease rule you may use as written. The state fire prevention code applies only to listed buildings, such as state buildings, public-assembly buildings and buildings at least 75 feet high permitted after July 1, 1978, and yields where a city or county has adopted a code at least as stringent; local fire codes, which this review did not search, may limit open-flame cooking near multifamily buildings, so check them and make your lease rule at least as strict. The tenant must already keep the premises as safe as their condition permits and not damage them, so a fire-safety breach supports a 14-day notice to remedy. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Firearms: Private Leases May Set Rules; Public Housing Authorities and Parking Lots Are Limited
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bars, or protects tenants against, a firearm rule in a private residential lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Two statutes limit you. A public housing authority may not adopt a rule restricting a tenant of a dwelling it owns and operates from lawfully possessing firearms or ammunition inside the unit, or carrying them to and from it. And a public or private employer may not keep or enforce a policy or rule that has the effect of prohibiting a person from transporting or storing a firearm in a locked vehicle in any parking lot, garage or designated parking area, except a private employer's access-restricted employee lot. That statute speaks of employers, but its words are not limited to employees, so if your business has employees, do not ban firearms locked in vehicles in your parking areas (case law was not searched). The Mississippi Constitution protects the right to keep and bear arms in defense of home, person or property. The cautious lease rule bans only unlawful possession, unsafe discharge and unsafe storage, and applies to every tenant alike. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Guest Rules in Mississippi: A Lease Matter, with the Tenant Answerable for Guests
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on how long a tenant's guests may stay, on guest fees, or on when a guest becomes an occupant; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Guest limits are lease terms, and the library's guest clause works as written; if you put them in separate written rules, they must serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or protect your property, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit. The Act already makes the tenant answer for guests: the tenant must not knowingly let anyone damage the premises and must require people there with the tenant's consent not to disturb neighbors, and you owe no repair duty for defects they cause. A guest who stays after the tenant's rental agreement ends is a squatter under the 2025 owner-protection law, not a tenant. Enforce a guest rule with the 14-day breach notice, in writing, or by e-mail or text only if the tenant agreed to that in writing. Apply guest limits evenly; federal fair housing law bars rules that single out families with children. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Statutory Guest-Day Limit in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi sets no number of days after which a guest becomes an occupant or a tenant, and no rule on how a lease may count guest days; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The 14-consecutive-day and 14-days-in-six-months limits in the library's guest clause are your choice and are lawful in Mississippi. Under the Act a tenant is a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy the unit, so a guest who overstays does not become your tenant unless you agree to rent to the person; and someone a tenant invited who stays after the tenant's rental agreement has ended is a squatter, removable under the 2025 owner-protection law. Enforce the limit promptly with the 14-day written breach notice; see the guest policy row for the rest. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Statutory Rights for Tenants' Guests or Visitors
bodyText: Mississippi gives a tenant's guests, visitors, caregivers or delivery people no statutory right of access to a rental, and bars no guest fee; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Guest access is governed by the lease and any written rules that meet the Act's tests (a purpose of tenant convenience, safety or welfare or protecting your property, reasonably related, applied fairly to all tenants, explicit). Two statutes touch guests: the tenant answers for damage and disturbance by people on the premises with the tenant's consent, and a person a tenant invited who stays after the tenant's rental agreement has ended is a squatter, not a tenant. Whether you owe a duty of care to a tenant's guest is case law, which was not searched. Apply any guest rule evenly under federal fair housing law. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Keys and Locks in Mississippi: The Lease Decides
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on how many keys you must give, key deposits or fees for lost keys, rekeying between tenants, or a tenant's right to change the locks, and no domestic-violence lock-change rule; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The library's keys clause, including charging the tenant the cost of rekeying when keys are not returned, is a lawful lease term, and a key charge the lease requires the tenant to pay you counts as rent under the Act. The only lock statute is in the pool-safety chapter, which covers doors and windows opening into the pool yard of a multiunit rental complex with a pool that allows residents under 12 (see the security devices row). Rekeying between tenants is still good practice. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Police Calls and Crime-Free Leases in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no crime-free lease statute, no law requiring you to join a crime-free housing program, and no statute requiring you to give police tenant information or access to a unit without legal process; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. No statute found bars a lease term about calls for police help either. The Act ties criminal conduct to police records: every tenant must not engage in any illegal activity on the leased premises as documented by a law enforcement agency (see the criminal activity row). Separately, it is a misdemeanor for anyone to verbally or physically obstruct, prevent or hinder another person from seeking or receiving emergency medical, police or other emergency help with the intent to cause or allow physical harm to that person. That crime turns on intent to harm, not on lease wording, but a lease term that discourages calls for help invites trouble. So do not limit, penalize or count against a tenant calls for police, fire or medical help; enforce criminal-activity terms against conduct, not calls. Three reporting duties bind you as they bind anyone. Any person having reasonable cause to suspect that a child is neglected or abused, or a victim of commercial sexual exploitation or human trafficking, must immediately make an oral report, by telephone or otherwise, to the Department of Child Protection Services, followed as soon as possible by a written report, and anyone who willfully violates that section faces a fine of up to $5,000, up to one year in jail, or both (Miss. Code Ann. § 43-21-353(1), (7)). Any person who knows or suspects that a vulnerable person has been or is being abused, neglected or exploited must immediately report it to the Department of Human Services or the county department of human services, and failing to report as required is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $5,000, up to six months in jail, or both (Miss. Code Ann. § 43-47-7(1)). And a death affecting the public interest, which includes a violent, accidental or suicidal death, an unexpected or unexplained death, a suspected drug overdose, a death with no physician in attendance in the prior 36 hours, and the death of anyone under 18, must be reported promptly to the medical examiner by any person present or any person who knows or suspects it, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit; no one may disturb the body until the medical examiner authorizes it, and willfully moving or concealing a body in violation is a misdemeanor (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 41-61-59(1), (2), 41-61-61(1), (3)). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Access Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building, gated community or other multi-unit property, and no statute on political or campaign signs at rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Whether outsiders may enter common areas is up to you and your lease rules. If you adopt a written rule on solicitation or signs, it must serve a purpose the Act allows, be reasonably related to it, be explicit and apply fairly to all tenants, so treat all causes and candidates alike. A tenant's displays are covered in the display-rights row. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Tenant Right to Install a Window or Portable Air Conditioner
bodyText: Mississippi gives tenants no statutory right to install a window, portable or other cooling unit, and no statute requires a lease to say whether such units are allowed; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your lease decides, and the library's consent-before-alterations and fastening terms cover window units. What the Act does say: you must keep the unit's heating and/or cooling system in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded, and the tenant must use the heating, ventilating and air conditioning facilities reasonably. So a cooling system the unit had at move-in is your duty; a unit the tenant adds is not, unless the lease says otherwise. If you allow window units, set conditions on installation, electrical load and removal. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In or Balcony Solar in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, portable or balcony solar device, or other solar equipment, at a rental, and has no statute voiding lease, covenant or association restrictions on solar equipment; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your lease decides: the library's consent-before-alterations and fastening terms cover solar devices, and you may allow them on conditions (placement, safe wiring, no fastening to exterior surfaces, removal and repair at move-out). In a condominium the tenant must also follow the association's bylaws. Utility interconnection and net-metering rules of the Public Service Commission were not reviewed. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to provide recycling containers or service, or to put recycling information in the lease, whatever the building's size; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Act's waste rule is on the tenant: each tenant must remove ashes, rubbish, garbage and other waste from the unit in a clean and safe manner that complies with community standards, so say in the lease where trash and any recycling go. Your city or county may have its own collection rules and fees (see the garbage-fee row); check local ordinances. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, a cross or holiday decorations, against your lease rules, and none barring you from limiting them; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi also has no general state fair housing law for private rentals, but the federal Fair Housing Act bars different terms or treatment because of religion, and a written rule must apply fairly to all tenants. So apply any display rule evenly, without singling out one faith, and consider allowing small door-frame items. The Mississippi Constitution's freedom-of-religion section was not reviewed for private leases (no case law was searched). The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: House Rules in Mississippi: Five Tests, and Notice for Later Rules
bodyText: Mississippi's Act lets you adopt written rules about the tenant's use and occupancy, but a rule binds the tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property from abuse, or fairly distributes services and facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies fairly to all tenants; is explicit enough to tell tenants what to do; and is not meant to evade your own duties. A rule adopted or changed after the tenant signs binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if it does not substantially modify the lease; a bigger change needs a signed amendment, or for a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, 7 or 30 days' written notice ending the tenancy and new terms. Valid rules are part of the rental agreement. In a condominium or cooperative, the tenant must also follow the bylaws. The library's rules clause tracks these tests.

title: No Smoke-Drift Waiver Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on tobacco or marijuana smoke drifting between units, and none authorizing a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims over drifting smoke, so the library does not offer a smoke-drift waiver for Mississippi; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Two Act rules frame the risk: a lease may not waive the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act, including your duties to comply with housing codes affecting health and safety and to maintain the unit, and it may not excuse or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct. Whether a waiver of ordinary claims would hold up is case law, which was not searched. Use a no-smoking rule instead (see the smoking policy row); you may, but need not, allow medical cannabis on rental property. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Snow and Ice Removal: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute saying whether the landlord or the tenant must clear snow and ice at a rental; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The library's snow-removal clause, which puts the duty on the tenant for the areas the tenant uses unless you provide the service, is a lawful lease term: the Act lets you and the tenant agree in writing that the tenant performs some of your duties, but only if the agreement is made in good faith, and it needs no separate writing. Keep shared walks, stairs and parking areas safe yourself, since you remain responsible for code compliance, and whether you owe a duty of care for icy common areas is case law, which was not searched. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays: No Mississippi Tenant Display Right
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving tenants a right to display a United States or other flag, a political sign or a religious item at a rental, and none limiting lease rules or association covenants on displays; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Displays are a lease matter: the library's common-area clause allows you to bar exterior signs and fixtures without consent, and its last sentence preserves any display the law protects. Written display rules must serve a purpose the Act allows, be reasonably related to it, be explicit and apply fairly to all tenants, so treat all flags, causes and faiths alike. Federal laws on flags, antennas and religion were not reviewed here. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving a tenant a right to install security cameras or a video doorbell, and none limiting your lease rules on them; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your lease controls: the library's terms requiring your written consent before the tenant fastens anything to the property or makes alterations cover cameras and doorbells, and you may allow them on conditions (placement, no recording into other units or private areas, removal and repair at move-out). Mississippi criminal law makes it a felony for anyone, tenant or landlord, with lewd, licentious or indecent intent to photograph or film another person without permission where the person would be undressed and expects privacy, including private dwellings, bathrooms and bedrooms; never place a camera, yours or the tenant's, where it can capture such areas. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi gives you two trespass tools. It is a misdemeanor to go into or stay on any building, premises or land of another, or any part or area of it, after being forbidden to do so orally or in writing (including by a posted sign) by the owner, lessee, custodian or other authorized person; the fine is up to $500, jail up to six months, or both. A separate misdemeanor covers knowingly entering another's lands without the permission of the landowner, the lessee or their agent, but it does not apply to the landowner's or lessee's family, guests or agents or to people there on lawful business. Your tenant is a lessee, so a tenant's guests are protected under the second law, and the first law lets a lessee as well as an owner forbid entry; only for public housing does it say a tenant's invitation does not override a ban. So to keep a non-tenant out of parking lots and common areas, give a dated written no-entry notice, keep a copy, tell police; limit a tenant's own guests through the lease. A guest who stays after the lease ends is a squatter; a tenant leaves only by eviction.

title: Waterbeds: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: nothing requires you to allow them, bars you from banning them, or sets insurance or installation rules; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your lease decides. The library's shared common-area and fastenings terms require your written consent before a tenant keeps a waterbed or other water-filled furniture, and you may condition consent on proof of insurance, a liner and frame, or a ground-floor location. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and you may apply the security deposit to tenant damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, if the deposit was made for that purpose, with an itemized written notice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Duty to Disclose Association Obligations to a Tenant
bodyText: Mississippi does not require a lease of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' or property owners' association to disclose the association's obligations, or require you to give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. But if the unit is an apartment in a horizontal property regime or a cooperative housing corporation, your tenant must comply with the association's or corporation's bylaws, and a condominium's recorded restrictions may regulate leasing of units. Condominium assessments are your debt as owner, not the tenant's, and an unpaid assessment can become a recorded lien that the association may enforce by selling the unit. So give your tenant the bylaws and rules before signing, make compliance a lease term (the library's association-compliance clause), check the covenants for leasing limits or approval steps first, and keep assessments paid. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to disclose a unit's bed bug history to an applicant or tenant, to give a bed bug information sheet, or to follow a treatment timeline; the words do not appear in the Mississippi Code, and a search of the Code and Constitution found no pest disclosure rule for rentals. See the bed bug and pest row for the tenant's cleanliness and reporting duties. You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so check whether your city or county code addresses pests. Whether keeping quiet about an infestation you know of is misrepresentation is case law, which was not searched; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing about any known current infestation and recent treatment. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell a tenant whether the rental has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to state it in the lease, and no statute makes a lease of a unit without one unenforceable or bars collecting rent for it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Certificates of occupancy come from local building-code enforcement, and you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so check your city or county rules before you rent. Separately, a city that has closed and placarded a building as unfit for human habitation can fine anyone who rents it (see the condemned-premises row). The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Defective Drywall Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall in rentals: no disclosure duty, no remediation standard and no tenant remedy specific to drywall; the word does not appear in the Mississippi Code, and a search of the Code and Constitution found none. Your general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the plumbing and heating and cooling systems in their move-in condition, which corrosive drywall can damage. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is misrepresentation is case law, which was not searched; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing about any known problem drywall and its repair. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Billing Tenants for Electricity by Meter Can Raise a Utility-Law Question
bodyText: Mississippi has no electric or gas submetering disclosure statute; its only submetering law covers water and wastewater (see the water submetering row). But the utility law matters. A "public utility" includes anyone furnishing electricity to the public for compensation, and the exclusion for someone who furnishes service only to tenants as part of the tenancy applies only if the service is not sold or resold to the tenants on a metered or consumption basis, other than the water submetering the law authorizes. So including electricity or gas in the rent fits that exclusion, and tenants on their own utility accounts raise no issue, while billing tenants by submeter for electricity or gas falls outside it and may draw Public Service Commission regulation. Get advice before submetering electricity or gas, and state any utility arrangement in the lease. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone or floodplain, whether it has flooded before, or whether you carry flood insurance, and has no flood disclosure form or flood-based termination right for tenants; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi's old casualty rule still applies: a tenant owes no rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise unless the tenant was at fault or expressly agreed to be bound, so put a casualty clause in the lease (see the casualty row). Telling applicants in writing about known flood history and that your insurance does not cover their belongings is good practice. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Duty in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell an applicant or tenant that the rental is in foreclosure, before signing or during the tenancy, and has no state statute protecting tenants when the property is foreclosed; a search of the Mississippi Code found none. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, not reviewed here) may let a bona fide tenant stay for the lease term or a notice period after a foreclosure sale; see the foreclosure row, which also covers who answers for the deposit. Telling tenants early is good practice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers the unit, and nothing to put in the lease about one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. A fixed-term lease expires on the date it states; a week-to-week tenancy ends on at least 7 days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days', and no reason is needed. Every termination and nonrenewal must still be done in good faith. See the for-cause eviction row for the limits that do apply. Public and federally assisted housing may have federal good-cause rules, which this library does not cover.

title: Contamination Disclosure: No General Rule; Brownfield Property Statement
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell a tenant that a rental is or was contaminated with hazardous substances, and a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found no statute requiring contamination or former drug-lab disclosures in residential leases. Brownfield property is the exception. If a Notice of Brownfield Agreement Site covering your property is recorded and not canceled, any instrument conveying an interest in the property must state that it is brownfield property subject to a brownfield agreement; treat your lease as such an instrument and use the library's brownfield clause. Anyone who owns or leases property in the site must abide by its recorded land-use restrictions and engineering controls (for example no groundwater use or digging), and owners, the state environmental commission, the local government and neighbors may enforce them. Whether keeping quiet about other known contamination is misrepresentation is case law, which was not searched; disclosing what you know is the cautious course. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Renting a Condominium or HOA Home in Mississippi
bodyText: If your rental is a condominium unit, read the condominium's recorded restrictions and covenants first: Mississippi lets them regulate sales and leases of units, and those restrictions are valid, though the management body need not be given a first right to lease. If the unit is an apartment in a horizontal property regime or a cooperative, your tenant must comply with the association's or corporation's bylaws. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern an owner living in his or her own condominium unit, but it does govern your lease to a tenant. Assessments are your debt as owner; unpaid, they can become a recorded lien that the association may enforce by selling the unit, and the association may then hold or lease it. No Mississippi statute found caps association lease-approval fees or deposits, or lets an association collect rent directly from your tenant. For a homeowners' association that is not a condominium, the recorded covenants govern. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Making the Tenant Follow Association Rules in Mississippi
bodyText: The library's association-compliance clause, which makes the tenant follow the association's rules and pay fines the tenant's violations cause, is a lawful lease term in Mississippi. For a condominium apartment the Act itself requires the tenant to comply with the association's bylaws; for other associations the duty comes from the lease. Mississippi caps no association fines you may pass to a tenant and requires no separate notice. Because the Act counts every payment the lease requires the tenant to make to you as rent, a passed-through fine the tenant owes you is rent, so the 3-day nonpayment notice can apply (see the fees-as-rent row). Give the tenant the association's rules before signing. Satellite dishes and antennas: Mississippi has no statute, and the federal rule on them was not reviewed. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to give applicants or tenants copies of outstanding code-violation notices, inspection orders or condemnation orders, or to disclose them before signing; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. But a city that has adopted the state's unfit-building ordinance may, after notice and hearing, order you to repair a building unfit for human habitation or to vacate and close it, and if you do not comply, have it vacated, closed and placarded; anyone who then rents or lets someone occupy it as a dwelling is liable for the city's fine (see the condemned-premises row). So do not rent a closed unit, and tell applicants about any pending order that could affect their occupancy. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Landlord Liability Insurance Mandate in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to carry liability insurance on a rental, to file proof of insurance with a city or county, or to tell tenants whether you are insured; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Insurance is still wise: a lease cannot excuse or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct, and the Act's duties to comply with housing codes and maintain the unit cannot be waived. Some local rental programs may require insurance; check local ordinances. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure in Mississippi: Federal Rule Only
bodyText: For housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule applies: before the lease is signed, give the tenant the federal lead warning, disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and any records or reports, give the federal pamphlet, and keep the signed acknowledgment (the library's lead disclosure clause does this). Mississippi adds no state lead disclosure, notice or certificate at lease signing; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi's lead law is a certification program for lead-based paint professionals and firms, so hire certified people for lead inspection, risk assessment or abatement work. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, including renewals.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no lead-safe or lead-free certification for rental housing, and no certificate that must be obtained for a unit or attached to a lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi's lead law certifies people and firms who do lead-based paint work (inspectors, risk assessors, renovators, abatement workers and others), not dwellings. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet still apply (see the lead-based paint row). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No State Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, Mississippi requires no state lead notice, inspection certificate or information packet at lease signing or during the tenancy, and no repeat notice at renewal; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi's lead statutes certify lead-based paint professionals and firms and do not address leases. Give the federal disclosure before each new lease and keep the signed acknowledgment (see the lead-based paint row). The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on a meter conservation or energy-efficiency charge attached to a rental's utility meter, and no landlord notice or rent deduction for one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Utility rates and any on-bill programs are set by the Public Service Commission and local utilities, whose rules this search did not cover. If a utility bill the tenant will pay carries a special charge, say so in the lease. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Former Meth Lab Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a rental was once used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, no cleanup standard before re-renting, and no owner reporting duty for a found lab; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. You must still comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. Separately, a tenant's use of the premises for unlawful controlled-substance activity (more than a single act) is a nuisance that voids the lease (see the nuisance row). Whether keeping quiet about known contamination is misrepresentation is case law, which was not searched; have a known former lab professionally cleaned and tell applicants in writing. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Military Base or Air Zone Disclosure in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require a lease disclosure for a rental near a military base or airfield, or in an aircraft noise or accident potential zone, and gives tenants no right to end a lease because of such a location; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi has no state servicemember lease-termination statute either (see the servicemember row; federal law applies). Local zoning and federal airport rules were not reviewed. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to disclose mold to an applicant or tenant, to give a mold information sheet, or to follow a mold remediation standard; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mold often follows a leak, so your general duties matter: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the plumbing and heating and cooling systems in their move-in condition; the tenant must keep the unit clean and tell you about conditions that may damage the premises. Whether keeping quiet about mold you know of is misrepresentation is case law, which was not searched; disclosing known mold and its repair is the cautious course. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi requires none of the three pre-signing disclosures some states group together; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Ordnance: no duty to disclose a former military ordnance or munitions site near the rental. Demolition: no duty to tell applicants or tenants that you plan to demolish the unit or have applied for a demolition permit. Shared meters: no statute requires you to disclose that a tenant's meter serves other areas; the only metering disclosure is the written water-submetering disclosure in covered properties, and metered resale of electricity or gas raises a utility-law question (see the electric submetering row). If you plan to demolish, a fixed-term lease still runs to its end date, and a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy ends only on 7 or 30 days' written notice, given in good faith.

title: No Owner or Manager Identity Disclosure Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to give a tenant, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the owner, a property manager or an agent for notices and legal papers, and no statute bars or delays an eviction because you did not; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The disclosure statement for public improvement districts applies to sale contracts and deeds, not leases. Name the owner and any manager and their notice addresses in the lease anyway: under the Act, notice to your agent counts as notice to you, you keep ultimate liability when an agent acts for you, and only you or an agent you designate may manage the property or collect rent. See the nonresident-owner and sale-or-management-change rows. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Pest Control or Pesticide Notice Rule for Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell tenants about a pest control contract, to give notice before pesticide is applied in a unit or common area, or to post pesticide notices in a rental building; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Pesticides and pest control businesses are regulated by the state; those licensing statutes and rules were not reviewed here.
