Mississippi has no landlord entry statute, so set entry for treatment and the tenant's preparation duties in the lease, give reasonable advance notice, and tell tenants what product will be used if they ask (see the bed bug and pest row). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Private Wells: No Testing or Disclosure Duty in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to test a private well serving a rental or to give tenants well test results; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your general duties still reach the water system: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the unit's plumbing in substantially its move-in condition. Testing the well before each tenancy, sharing the results, and saying in the lease who maintains the well, pump and any septic system are the cautious course (see the tenant maintenance row, which covers the septic repair duty). The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no law like California's Proposition 65: no duty to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property, and no warning-sign requirement for rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Specific hazards are covered elsewhere in the library: lead paint (the federal disclosure), mold, radon and former drug labs (no Mississippi rule). You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Property-Tax Share-of-Rent Statement in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether annually, when the rent changes or otherwise, and gives renters no property-tax credit that depends on such a statement; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The one rental statement in the property-tax law goes to the county, not the tenant: if you own affordable rental housing whose rents and occupancy are restricted by tenant income under a federal or state program (such as the low-income housing tax credit or HOME), it is appraised on actual net operating income, and you must give the county tax assessor an accurate statement of that income for the prior year by April 1 each year. If your lease passes tax increases to the tenant, see the tax-escalation row.

title: No Radon Law for Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no radon law for rentals: no duty to test for radon, to disclose radon test results or a radon hazard to tenants, or to give a radon information sheet, whatever the floor level of the unit, and no radon-resistant construction mandate in its statutes; the word "radon" does not appear in the Mississippi Code, and a search of the Code and Constitution found nothing. You must still comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. Testing ground-floor and basement units and sharing results is good practice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Disclosures for a Mississippi Lease: The Short List
bodyText: Mississippi has no single list of required lease disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a just-cause or rent-increase law covers the unit (Mississippi has neither). What applies, each in its own library entry: (1) for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet; (2) water or wastewater submetering in an apartment house or condominium of four or more units, or a manufactured home community, where rent is paid monthly or longer, needs a written disclosure and the tenant's acknowledgment; (3) e-mail or text breach and nonpayment notices work only if the tenant agrees in writing; (4) federal rules, such as the CARES Act 30-day notice, for covered properties. If the lease gives the tenant an option to buy, Mississippi's seller property-condition disclosure statement must be delivered before the lease is signed if the property is subject to that law, so check its scope. The public improvement district statement applies to sales, not leases.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Guide in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to give tenants a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Attorney General's office has published a consumer guide that reprints the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act as it stood after the 2018 session, but it is not law, nothing requires you to hand it out, and it predates later amendments (such as the 2022 and 2025 changes to notices and evictions), so do not rely on it for current rules. A plain-language summary in your welcome materials is good practice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Code Variance Notice in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to give tenants a copy of a variance from a housing, health, building or sanitary code, or to attach one to the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, and no statewide sanitary code for rental housing was found. You must comply with the building and housing codes that apply to your property and materially affect health and safety; any variance under a local code is governed by the ordinance or agency rule that grants it, which this search did not cover. Follow any conditions a variance imposes, and tell the tenant about any that affect the tenant's use. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Sex Offender Information: No Duty to Volunteer, but Answer If Asked
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to volunteer to applicants or tenants that a registered sex offender lives nearby or in the building, or to put a registry notice in the lease. A failure to disclose registry information in a real estate transaction gives no cause of action against an owner, and is not grounds to end or rescind a transaction in which property is leased. But the same statute says that, if known to the owner, those factors shall be disclosed if a consumer asks, so answer a direct question truthfully and never misstate what you know. Registry information is public: the sheriff and the Department of Public Safety release it on request, and the Department keeps a searchable public website, so you may point tenants there. Do not misuse it: willfully misusing or altering public registry information about an offender, or about a person living or working at an address an offender reported, is a misdemeanor, and selling it for profit is banned. Public housing agencies are sent registration information for offenders living in their area. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No First-Page Occupancy Notice or Font Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no rule requiring a notice at the top of the first page of a lease, or in a larger type size, about a tenant's lawful occupancy, and no presumption that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized or states particular facts; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi sets no general type-size rule for residential leases (see the lease type-size row). Removing people with no right to be there works through the 2025 owner-protection law: at the hearing the owner or agent must show its right to possess, and a certified deed or documentation that the occupant is not a tenant or other person with a right to remain decides the case. A written lease signed by both parties is your best proof of who is a tenant. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a lease to disclose public access to a shoreline, beach or waterfront, or the tenant's rights to use one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. If the property is on the Gulf Coast, a lake, reservoir or river, describe in the lease only the access you actually control (a private pier, boat ramp or shared waterfront, and any rules for it), and do not promise rights to land or water you do not own. Tidelands and submerged lands, and reservoir lands leased from water districts, have their own statutes, which this search found but did not review. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi law does not protect a tenant's source of income: no statute requires you to accept a housing choice voucher (Section 8) or other rental assistance, or bars refusing an applicant because the rent would be paid by a program, and a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi has no general state fair housing law for private rentals; its only housing anti-discrimination section covers Mississippi Home Corporation developments and loans. The federal Fair Housing Act does apply to most rentals, and it does not list income source, but a no-vouchers policy applied selectively, or as a cover for race, disability or familial status, can violate it. So decide whether to take part in a voucher program and apply the decision the same way to every applicant. If you accept a voucher, the program's lease addendum and rules bind you.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty for Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a lease or notice to tell tenants whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, or to describe it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The only statutory sprinkler requirement found is for fraternity and sorority houses on state property built after April 20, 2005, which must have an approved automatic sprinkler system; that housing is outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act anyway. If your building has sprinklers, say so in the lease or rules and tell tenants not to hang things from, paint, cover or tamper with sprinkler heads and to report leaks or damage at once; if it has none, do not suggest that it does. Local fire and building codes were not searched. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Disease at a Property: Not Material Facts in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi law says that the fact or suspicion that a property was the site of a natural death, suicide, homicide or felony crime, was the site of an event that had no effect on its physical condition, or was owned or occupied by someone affected by or exposed to a disease not known to spread through common occupancy (such as HIV or AIDS) is not a material fact that must be disclosed in a real estate transaction. Failing to disclose it gives no criminal, civil or administrative action against the owner, and is not grounds to end or rescind a transaction in which property is leased. So you need not volunteer such events to an applicant or tenant. Two limits: illegal drug activity that affects the property's physical condition or environment is not covered, so disclose that; and never answer a direct question falsely. If you grant an option to purchase on a home of one to four units through a licensed real estate agent, a separate seller's disclosure statement applies. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement Required
bodyText: Mississippi does not require you to give tenants a state-prepared statement or summary of their rights, to attach one to the lease or renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one, and no eviction or lawsuit depends on having done so; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The documents the law does require are specific: an itemized written notice for any deposit deduction, a written disclosure and acknowledgment if you submeter water in a covered apartment house or manufactured home community, and the written notices that start a termination or eviction. Telling tenants in plain words how repairs, notices and deposits work is still good practice. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants that a property is exempt from a statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction law or tenant purchase right. Mississippi has none of those laws, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice belongs in your lease. Rent is set by the lease, a fixed term ends on its stated date, and a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy ends on 7 or 30 days' written notice without a stated cause, always subject to the Act's duty of good faith. The Mississippi rules that do turn on the kind of property, such as the pool-safety chapter for multiunit rental complexes and the water-submetering rules for apartment houses of four or more units, are explained in their own rows.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice in Mississippi
bodyText: Some states require a lease notice about a statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction protections or a tenant's right to buy the building. Mississippi has none of these laws, so no such notice is required and none should go in your lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Rent is what the lease says. A fixed-term lease ends on the date it states; after that you may give written notice that the tenant is holding over and file for eviction no earlier than three days later, not counting intermediate weekends and legal holidays. A week-to-week tenancy ends on 7 days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice, without a stated cause, but every termination and nonrenewal carries the Act's duty of good faith, and the narrow retaliation limit on post-expiration rent increases still applies.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law, but Void Terms Stay Void
bodyText: Mississippi has no truth-in-renting statute: no law requires a lease to carry a state notice that some terms may be unenforceable, and no law sets a penalty for offering or using a lease that contains a prohibited term; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The forbidden terms are still unenforceable: a lease may not waive any right, duty or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act except where the Act allows it, may not authorize a confession of judgment, and may not excuse or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct (see the prohibited lease terms row). Leave such terms out rather than relying on a severability clause. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Mississippi)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest. The only place the word appears in the Mississippi Code is a sentence of the Foreign Land Ownership Act saying that a forfeiture under that Act does not affect leases, servitudes, usufructs and other real rights, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise for an ordinary Mississippi home lease. The nearest Mississippi interest is a life estate. One statute covers rent when a tenant for life who has leased out land dies: if death comes on or after a rent day, the life tenant's executor or administrator may recover the whole rent then due from the under-tenant; if before, the share of rent that accrued before death. No statute found says whether a residential lease signed by a life tenant survives the end of the life estate; that is case law (not searched). If you lease as a life tenant, say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign or agree in writing that the lease will continue.

title: Utility Disclosure: Only Water Submetering Needs a Signed Acknowledgment
bodyText: Mississippi requires a separate written utility disclosure in one situation: if you submeter water in an apartment house (one or more buildings with four or more dwelling units occupied primarily for nontransient use, including a residential condominium) or a manufactured home community, where rent is paid monthly or longer, you must disclose the submetering to each tenant and get the tenant's written acknowledgment; the library's water-submetering disclosure clause does this. Submetered charges may not exceed the tenant's pro rata share, each bill must show beginning and ending reads, state that it is not from the utility and give an inquiry phone number, and water may not be cut off for unpaid submeter bills. For any other utility billing, no statute requires an attachment, so write the terms into the lease: who pays which utility, how you bill, the due date and any fee. These rules apply to every tenancy type.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units: No Mississippi State Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires cities or counties to allow accessory dwelling units (a garage apartment, backyard cottage or in-law suite), bars owner-occupancy requirements for them, or sets special rules for renting one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Whether you may build and rent an accessory unit depends on local zoning and building rules and on any subdivision covenants or association rules, so check them first (local ordinances were not searched). Once rented as a home, the unit is a dwelling unit like any other: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, and you must keep it in compliance with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that allows, sets or caps a fee for a tenant who removes, disconnects or disables a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and no rental alarm statute at all (see the alarm duties row); a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. You may make tampering with an alarm you provided a lease breach and require the tenant to pay the actual cost of repair or replacement. Because rent in Mississippi includes every payment the lease requires, a charge the lease requires is rent, but keep it to your real cost: a flat penalty beyond that is untested (case law not searched) and every remedy carries a duty of good faith. You may also enforce the breach with a 14-day notice, or deduct the damage on the itemized deposit notice. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Asbestos: No Mississippi Rental Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose asbestos to tenants, inspect a rental for it, or put an asbestos notice in the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code for asbestos near tenancy, dwelling or rental words found nothing, and the Constitution has no such provision. Your general duty still applies: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. Before renovating or demolishing an older building, assume federal and state environmental rules on asbestos inspection, notification and licensed abatement apply (not searched here), keep tenants away from the work, and tell them in writing about work that may disturb asbestos. Do not describe a unit as asbestos-free unless it has been tested. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairs or railings of rental buildings, or a report to tenants; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The only balcony statutes found are old fire-escape rules for certain hotels and lodging houses over two stories. Your general duties still cover balconies that are part of the premises: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the dwelling unit in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease, reasonable wear and tear excluded. So inspect balconies and railings yourself, repair hazards promptly, and close off any you know are unsafe; local codes may impose more (not searched). The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Changing the Casualty and Re-Renting Rules by Lease
bodyText: Mississippi's one casualty statute can be changed by agreement: a tenant owes no rent for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise, and a promise to keep the premises in repair does not make the tenant rebuild, unless the tenant's negligence or fault caused the loss or the tenant has expressly stipulated to be bound. So a lease could lawfully make the tenant agree to keep paying rent or to rebuild after a casualty; the library does not offer that, because it shifts your insurable risk to the tenant (see the casualty row). There is no statute requiring you to re-rent (mitigate) after a tenant leaves early, so nothing statutory to waive; whether a lease can excuse mitigation is case law (not searched). What a lease cannot change is the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act itself, such as the tenant's 14-day notice remedy for your material noncompliance. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Children in the Household: Federal Law Governs Most Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no general state fair housing law protecting families with children in private rentals, and no state occupancy limit; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. One state rule applies only to housing projects assisted by the Mississippi Home Corporation: no family may be discriminated against because of children in admission to or continued occupancy of those projects, except housing restricted to people 62 or older. For other rentals the federal Fair Housing Act protects familial status (households with children under 18 and pregnant persons), so do not refuse to rent, set different terms or advertise a preference against children, such as adults-only rules, unless a federal exemption applies. A neutral occupancy limit applied to people of all ages is allowed if reasonable; put it in your written criteria and lease. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Confession of Judgment Clauses Are Banned in Mississippi Leases
bodyText: No Mississippi rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement. So do not use a cognovit or warrant-of-attorney clause, or any clause letting you take a judgment for rent or possession without notice and a hearing. The ban appears in the same section that forbids waiving the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's rights and remedies. Collect unpaid rent and recover possession through the Act's eviction process instead: written notice, a sworn complaint, a hearing, and a judgment. Mississippi's general office-confession procedure in its civil practice title does not change this, because the lease clause itself is prohibited. Court rules on supersedeas in eviction appeals were not reviewed. The ban applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Mississippi Consumer Protection Act and Home Leases
bodyText: Mississippi's Consumer Protection Act prohibits unfair or deceptive trade practices, and it defines trade to include advertising and offering any property, real or personal, so misleading rental advertising can fall under it. Its list of specific banned practices does not include leaving blanks in a lease or failing to give the tenant a copy at signing. Enforcement of the general ban runs through a separate section the Act names (not read here; the Attorney General enforces the related data-breach rule). A tenant's own lawsuit is narrower: it belongs to a person who purchases or leases goods or services for personal, family or household purposes and loses money or property, after first trying an Attorney General-approved informal dispute program, with no class actions. Whether a home lease is goods or services is not settled by the text, and court decisions were not checked. Treat the Act as possibly applying: advertise accurately and disclose all fees. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Victim Information: No Landlord Confidentiality Statute in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to keep confidential what a tenant or applicant tells you about domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, such as a protection order, police report or new address; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program gives certified victims a substitute address that public bodies must generally accept, and its confidentiality rules bind public bodies and the Attorney General, not private landlords. But a fraudulent attempt to get a program participant's confidential address is a felony, so never try to obtain it by deception and do not help anyone else do so. Protect the information anyway: keep orders and reports in a restricted file, share them only with staff who need them, and never give a victim's address or unit number to anyone without the victim's written consent. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Help: No Mississippi Statute Either Way
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute protecting a tenant's right to call police or other emergency help, and none barring lease terms that penalize such calls; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Do not put anything in a lease, rule or addendum that fines a tenant or counts as a breach a call to police, fire or medical help: written rules bind a tenant only if they promote safety or welfare and apply fairly, and every remedy carries a duty of good faith, so such a rule is hard to defend. Act on the underlying conduct instead. The tenant must not engage in illegal activity on the premises as documented by a law enforcement agency and must not disturb neighbors, and a material breach can be enforced with a 14-day notice. Federal rules may protect domestic violence victims in assisted housing (not reviewed). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Eviction Fees and Penalties: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute aimed at lease clauses that charge a fee or penalty because you served a notice or filed an eviction, and none that expressly allows or bans passing your filing costs to the tenant; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Because rent in Mississippi includes every payment the lease requires, a fee the lease requires becomes rent, which is why a large flat eviction or notice fee is risky: it can turn a cured breach into a new nonpayment, every remedy must be pursued in good faith, and a charge unrelated to your actual loss may be refused as a penalty (case law not searched). Leave such fees out. Recover unpaid rent, actual damages and court costs through the eviction case, and attorney's fees only as your lease or a statute allows (see the attorney's fees row). The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Liability Waivers and Indemnity in Mississippi Leases
bodyText: Mississippi bars one kind of liability waiver by statute: no rental agreement may exculpate or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct, or the costs connected with it. So an unqualified sentence that you are "not liable" for injury or loss is not lawful as written, because it reaches willful misconduct; a disclaimer limited to causes outside your control, or one that expressly excepts your willful misconduct, is. The statute does not address ordinary negligence, but a lease also cannot waive the tenant's rights and remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and whether Mississippi courts enforce a waiver of your own negligence is case law (not searched). Keep any waiver narrow: losses you do not cause, such as theft by third parties, weather, or the tenant's uninsured belongings, pair it with a renters insurance requirement, and limit any tenant indemnity to claims caused by the tenant, occupants and guests. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Fair Housing in Mississippi: Federal Law Governs Private Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi has no general state fair housing act for private rentals: no state list of protected classes, no state exemptions, no state advertising rule, no election-of-forum right and no source-of-income protection; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The one state housing discrimination rule covers Mississippi Home Corporation housing developments and loans: no discrimination because of race, religious principles, color, sex, national origin, ancestry or handicap, and in assisted projects none because of age or children (except housing for people 62 and older). For every other rental the federal Fair Housing Act applies, with its own exemptions and its advertising ban (federal law not reviewed here). Use written screening criteria applied the same way to everyone, advertise without preferences, and handle accommodation requests promptly. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Farmland in Mississippi
bodyText: No Mississippi statute says whether a tenant who rents a home together with farmland gets the right to hunt or fish on that land, or keeps that right with the owner. The hunting-trespass law makes it a crime to knowingly enter another's land to hunt, fish, shoot or trap without the permission of, or being accompanied by, the landowner, the lessee of the land, or an agent of either; fines start at $500. Because a lessee can give that permission, a tenant whose lease covers the land may be able to let others hunt there unless the lease says otherwise. The Constitution protects a right to hunt and fish, but not as a change to trespass or property law. Land leased for hunting or fishing can still be valued as agricultural land for property tax. So settle it in the lease: say whether the tenant may hunt or fish or allow others to, where and when, and whether you or others will keep hunting there and crossing the land. The rule is the same for every tenancy type and does not arise for a home rented without land.

title: Which Fire and Building Codes Apply to Mississippi Rentals
bodyText: Mississippi's statewide fire code, the Mississippi Fire Prevention Code, applies only to listed buildings: state buildings; buildings used for public assembly or permitted after July 1, 1978 and at least 75 feet tall, unless the local fire code is at least as strict; and a few others. Hotels and lodging houses need an approved fire detector on each floor. Construction codes are local: counties and cities must adopt, as the State Uniform Construction Code, one of the last three editions of the International Building Code and International Residential Code as adopted by the Mississippi Building Codes Council, unless they opted out by resolution in 2014; manufactured homes and some other structures are exempt. Cities may also adopt unfit-dwelling ordinances, and renting a building posted as unfit can bring a fine. You must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, which covers any law, ordinance or regulation on fitness for habitation, construction, maintenance or occupancy. Ask your city or county which codes it has adopted. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Fire Sprinklers: No Mississippi Retrofit Duty for Rentals
bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires a landlord to install fire sprinklers in an existing rental home or apartment building, or sets a sprinkler duty specific to rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. State law goes the other way for houses: the Mississippi Building Codes Council may not adopt any code or rule requiring a sprinkler system in a new or existing one- or two-family dwelling, and the State Uniform Construction Code leaves out the residential code's sprinkler provisions for those dwellings. But a county or city may adopt codes requiring sprinklers in any structure, so a local code can require them, especially in new apartment buildings. The only statewide sprinkler requirement found is for fraternity and sorority houses on state property built after April 20, 2005. Ask your local fire or building official before building, renovating or changing a building's use. If a building has a sprinkler system, keep it maintained and tell tenants not to cover or hang things from the heads. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Foreign Ownership Limits: Mississippi Rules for Forest and Agricultural Land
bodyText: Mississippi's Foreign Land Ownership Act reaches "nonresident aliens": people domiciled in, entities domiciled in or majority-owned from, and governments of countries the U.S. Secretary of Commerce designates as foreign adversaries. It covers possessory interests in forest or agricultural land, defined as any direct interest held for a term of one year or longer, so on its words a lease of a year or more can count; week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed terms under a year fall outside. Majority holdings by such a party are prohibited outside inheritance and debt-collection exceptions, and the Secretary of State and Attorney General enforce with large fines and forfeiture. As lessor you have no duty to investigate whether a party is a foreign adversary and no liability for failing to identify one. So before renting farmland or forest land, including a farm with a house, for a year or more to a foreign entity or a person domiciled in a designated country, get legal advice. An older law lets resident aliens hold land as citizens do and lets nonresident aliens hold up to five acres for residential purposes; an ordinary home lease is not restricted by these statutes.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in Mississippi
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not freeze any code edition: you must comply with the applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, meaning whatever law, ordinance or regulation applies to the premises now. Mississippi's construction-code statutes mostly roll forward too: the Mississippi Building Codes Council adopts one of the last three editions of the International Building and Residential Codes, and counties and cities adopt one of the last three adopted editions as their minimum code. One rule is fixed: in Jackson, Harrison, Hancock, Stone and Pearl River Counties and their cities, the wind and flood mitigation requirements of the 2003 International Residential and Building Codes stay in force until the local government adopts the latest editions, unless it opted out in 2006. Fraternity and sorority houses on state property follow the national fire alarm and sprinkler standards as revised. Construction codes govern building and improvement work, so ask your local building official which edition applies to your building and to any renovation. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Waiving Repair Duties: Only a Good-Faith Written Shift of Tasks
bodyText: A Mississippi lease cannot remove your duties to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the unit, plumbing and heating or cooling in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease. Neither side may agree to waive any right, duty or remedy of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act except where the Act allows, and no lease may excuse your willful misconduct. The Act's one allowance is a reassignment, not a removal: you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs some or all of those duties. No statute lets a tenant accept a listed defect in exchange for lower rent, and none requires a separate document for heating terms, so do not offer a defect-for-discount waiver. Details are in the row on whether the lease can change the repair duties. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Immigration Status: No Mississippi Rental Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that requires, forbids or limits asking rental applicants about immigration or citizenship status, and none that bars renting to a person unlawfully present or makes it a crime; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. National origin is protected for private rentals by the federal Fair Housing Act (Mississippi's own housing discrimination rule reaches only Mississippi Home Corporation developments and loans). The safe practice: do not ask about immigration status or citizenship; verify identity and ability to pay with documents any applicant can supply, such as a passport, consular ID or taxpayer identification number as well as a Social Security number; and apply the same criteria to everyone. The foreign land ownership rules for forest and agricultural land are covered in the foreign ownership row. Federal immigration law was not reviewed. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Jury Waivers in Mississippi Leases
bodyText: Mississippi's Constitution says the right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate. No Mississippi statute addresses a jury waiver in a residential lease, makes one presumptively unconscionable, or requires a special signed writing for it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Whether a court would enforce a jury waiver signed in a lease before any dispute is a case-law question that was not searched. In practice a jury is rarely available in an eviction: the Act's eviction sections provide for a hearing before a judge and never mention a jury, and the older statute on rent claimed in an unlawful entry and detainer case says such cases are tried by the judge without a jury. The library offers no jury-waiver clause for Mississippi; if a jury matters to you, address it in the case under the court rules. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Penalty for Including a Void Lease Term
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that penalizes you simply for putting a prohibited term in a lease or for knowingly using a lease that contains one; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The term itself is unenforceable: a lease may not waive the rights, duties or remedies of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act except where the Act allows, authorize a confession of judgment, or excuse your willful misconduct, and a waiver of a cosigner's right to end the lease when the tenant dies is void. Money exposure comes when you act on a void term or break the underlying rule, for example retaining a deposit in bad faith, which can cost up to $200 in addition to actual damages. Leave prohibited terms out. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Mississippi Landlord-Tenant Act Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: In any oral or written agreement to rent a home, Mississippi says a landlord or tenant may not agree to waive or give up any right, duty or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, except where the Act itself allows it. That covers the whole Act: notice and cure periods, termination notices, deposit return, repair remedies and the eviction process. The Act's own exceptions are where it lets the lease decide: the tenancy term, use other than as a dwelling (unless otherwise agreed), e-mail or text notices (with written consent), a good-faith written shift of repair tasks, and double rent after a holdover notice unless the lease says otherwise. Two other statutes add non-waivable rules: a cosigner's right to end the lease when the tenant dies, and the pool-safety inspection and repair duties. A waiver clause is unenforceable even if signed. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Mississippi has no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability standard, no requirement that a lease be divided into captioned sections or printed in a minimum type size, and no consumer-contract statute that reaches leases below a dollar ceiling; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi's Consumer Protection Act bars unfair or deceptive trade practices and covers offering real property, but whether a tenant can sue under it over a home lease is unsettled (see the consumer protection act row). Write the lease in plain words with headings anyway, and put fees, chores the tenant takes on, electronic-notice consent and other unusual terms where the tenant will see them. The details are in the plain-language and consumer statement row. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Pools at Mississippi Rental Complexes: Enclosure, Door and Inspection Rules
bodyText: Mississippi's pool-safety chapter applies only to pools owned, controlled or maintained by the owner of a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership or management on the same or adjacent lots, including condominium, cooperative and townhome projects), a property owners association or a private club, and to doors and windows of rental units opening into such a pool yard. A single-family home that is not part of such a project is outside it. Covered owners must enclose the pool yard (at least 48 inches high, with opening and material limits), fit gates with self-closing, self-latching, lockable hardware that opens outward, meet door and window rules for units facing the pool yard, inspect enclosures, gates and latches at least every 31 days, and repair window and sliding-door devices after a tenant reports a problem. These duties cannot be waived. Enclosures built before July 1, 2012 are largely grandfathered. A tenant may sue for compliance and damages. No lease notice is required. The chapter also excludes complexes that bar residents under 12; do not treat that as a way out, because federal fair housing law protects families with children.

title: Lease Terms Mississippi Law Forbids
bodyText: Mississippi's prohibited-terms section is short. In any oral or written agreement to rent a home, a lease may not: (1) waive or give up any right, duty or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, except where the Act allows; (2) authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease; or (3) exculpate or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct or its costs. Other statutes add: (4) any waiver of a cosigner's right to end the lease when the tenant dies is void; and (5) pool-safety inspection and repair duties at covered complexes cannot be waived. Written rules bind a tenant only if they meet the Act's fairness tests. Mississippi has no statutory penalty for knowingly using a prohibited term. General contract limits on penalties and on exculpating ordinary negligence are case law, not searched. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Questions About Protected Traits: No Mississippi Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute barring a landlord from asking rental applicants about, or keeping records of, race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability or family status; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none, and the state has no general fair housing act for private rentals. The federal Fair Housing Act does bar statements that indicate a preference, limitation or discrimination, and asking about protected traits invites the inference that the answer was used (federal law not reviewed). So keep protected traits off your application and out of interviews: do not ask about religion, national origin or citizenship, pregnancy or plans for children, or whether an applicant has a disability. Ask every applicant the same questions about rental history, income and the number of occupants. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Severability and Void Terms in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi's statutes knock out offending lease terms one at a time rather than voiding the whole lease: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act forbids specific terms (waivers of the Act, confession of judgment, release of your willful misconduct), and a waiver of a cosigner's death-termination right is void and unenforceable, while the rest of the lease stands. No statute makes an entire residential lease void because it contains a prohibited term. A lease does become void by law in two situations unrelated to its wording: when a tenant uses the premises as a prostitution or drug nuisance, and at the end of the deserted-premises procedure. The library's shared severability clause is consistent with Mississippi law, but it cannot save a forbidden term, so leave such terms out. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Registered Sex Offenders as Tenants in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi places residency limits on registered sex offenders, not on landlords. A person required to register may not reside within 3,000 feet of the real property of a public or nonpublic elementary or secondary school, a child care facility, a residential child-caring agency, a children's group care home, or any playground, ballpark or other recreational facility used by people under 18. There are exceptions, including a residence established before July 1, 2006 (schools and child care) or July 1, 2008 (the other places), a facility that opened nearby later, a residence set up by January 1, 2014 at least 1,500 feet away, and minors or wards. A separate law bars registrants from being present in or loitering near schools while minors are there; it is not a residency rule. No statute found requires a landlord to check the registry, refuse or evict an offender, or put an offender statement in the lease, or bars renting to two offenders who live together. You may screen for registry status under a written policy applied to every applicant. If a tenant's residence appears unlawful, get legal advice before acting. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that limits renting a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or caps the number of rentals in a neighborhood; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Local zoning, subdivision covenants and homeowners association rules may still restrict leasing, and a tenant in a condominium or cooperative must follow its bylaws, so check them before you buy or rent out a home (local ordinances and covenants were not searched). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Steam Radiators: No Mississippi Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring a landlord to install radiator covers or guards on steam or hot-water radiators, to offer them on request, or to add a radiator rider to the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Your general duty applies: maintain the unit and its heating system in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease and comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. If a unit has exposed steam radiators, especially where young children live, consider covers as a safety measure. Local housing codes were not searched. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Voucher Program Inspections: No Mississippi Statute
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute on housing choice voucher (Section 8) inspections: nothing lets a landlord refuse or delay a program inspection, sets inspection deadlines for a housing authority, or lets a landlord reject a voucher holder because of a failed or late inspection; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi does not require landlords to accept vouchers, so taking part is your choice; if you do, the housing assistance payments contract and federal program rules control inspections and repairs (not searched). Mississippi has no statutory entry-notice rule, so give the notice of entry your lease promises before an inspection. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Sharing Tenant Information in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute that bars a residential landlord from disclosing information about a tenant or applicant, such as rental history, payment records or contact details, or that requires the tenant's consent before you share it; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What does apply is the data-breach law: if you do business in Mississippi and own or maintain residents' personal information (a name with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code), you must notify affected people of a breach without unreasonable delay unless an investigation shows harm is unlikely; the Attorney General enforces it. Good practice: share tenant information only to run the tenancy or with the tenant's written authorization, and keep identity and payment data secure. Federal consumer-report rules apply to screening reports (not reviewed). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Housing Your Employees: Mississippi Has No Employee Exclusion
bodyText: Unlike many states, Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no exclusion for an employee whose housing depends on the job, such as a resident manager or maintenance worker. Its exclusions cover institutions, buyers under a contract of sale, fraternal and social organizations, transient hotel, motel or lodging stays, condominium and cooperative owners, and premises used mainly for agriculture or rented for less than fair rental value to someone doing agricultural labor for the owner. So if you rent a home to an employee, the Act's notices, deposit rules and court eviction process apply. State in a lease or employment agreement how the occupancy ends, but end it with the Act's 7-day, 30-day or 14-day breach notice and, if needed, an eviction. No statute requires a separate disclosure or an offer of a lease when the job ends. The rules apply to every tenancy type.

title: Tenant Organizing: No Mississippi Right, One Public-Housing Provision
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving tenants of private housing a right to form or join a tenants' association, meet in common areas or distribute materials, and none barring retaliation for organizing; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does recognize qualified tenant management organizations, nonprofit corporations a majority of whose directors are tenants of a housing project, which public housing authorities may contract with to manage that project. The Act's only retaliation rule limits post-expiration rent increases aimed at a tenant's actions under the Act, and every termination or nonrenewal must be in good faith. Apply your rules on common-area use, signs and solicitation neutrally to every resident. Federal rules for subsidized housing may protect organizing (not searched). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Screening Applicants in Mississippi
bodyText: Mississippi has no tenant-screening statute: no limit on criminal-history look-back periods, no rule that criminal history be checked only after a conditional offer, no cap on income multiples, no duty to give written reasons for a denial, and no statutory negligence shield for renting to someone with a record; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. What does apply: (1) expunged records: a person whose record was expunged is not to be held to have given a false statement by failing to disclose it, so do not treat that silence as a lie; (2) age: anyone 18 or older can sign a binding lease for the home they will live in; (3) data security: protect applicants' identity and account numbers under the breach-notice law; and (4) federal fair housing and consumer-report rules (not reviewed). Use written criteria applied the same way to every applicant. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Unconscionability Statute for Mississippi Home Leases
bodyText: Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no unconscionability section, and no Mississippi statute lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term in a lease of a home; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The statutory unconscionability rule Mississippi does have is in the Uniform Commercial Code article on leases of goods, such as furniture or equipment rentals, not real property. Courts may still refuse unconscionable contract terms under general contract law, and the Consumer Protection Act bars unfair or deceptive practices (case law on both not searched). Keep fees, penalties, waivers and remedies balanced, act in good faith as the Act requires, and leave out terms the Act forbids. No Mississippi statute declares any particular lease clause enforceable notwithstanding unconscionability. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute giving landlords a tax credit, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans, and no rule requiring or forbidding a preference for veterans in private rentals; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The veterans housing statutes found deal with state programs, such as homes acquired for resale to veterans and quarters for veterans' organizations. Veteran status is not a protected class under any Mississippi housing law, but a preference for veterans must not be used to screen out people for a federally protected trait such as disability or familial status. Federal programs such as HUD-VASH vouchers and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act were not reviewed here. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute setting a minimum or maximum water heater temperature for rentals or requiring you to reset a unit's water heater before each new tenant; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. Mississippi does require every water heater installed in a dwelling to have an approved self-closing (levered) pressure relief valve and temperature relief valve, or a combination valve, set to open at no more than 210 degrees Fahrenheit, with no shut-off or check valve between it and the heater; anyone installing, reinstalling or relocating a tank heater of 120 gallons or less must fit an approved relief valve. Those are safety-valve rules, not a setting for the water. To reduce scald risk, set tank heaters to a moderate temperature at turnover, make sure the relief valve works, and tell tenants not to raise the setting. Keep the plumbing in substantially the same condition as at the start of the lease. Local plumbing codes may add rules (not searched). The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Mississippi Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Mississippi has no statute requiring window guards, window stops or other fall-prevention devices in rentals, or a window-guard notice in the lease; a search of the Mississippi Code and Constitution found none. The only window rule found for rentals is in the pool-safety chapter: at a covered multiunit rental complex, windows in a building wall that forms part of a pool yard enclosure must be latched (or, in newer buildings, ground-floor windows permanently closed) to keep children out of the pool yard. Where young children live above the ground floor, consider window stops that limit openings, keep furniture away from windows, and make sure any guard still lets windows serve as emergency exits where codes require. Local codes were not searched. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Mississippi follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Miss. Code Ann. § 75-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Miss. Code Ann. § 75-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Mississippi's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, including your ending a tenancy, not renewing a rental agreement or removing a tenant from the premises, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Miss. Code Ann. § 89-8-9). The act also says you have a good-faith obligation to accept full payment of everything owed under an eviction money judgment if it is offered on or before the court-ordered move-out date (Miss. Code Ann. § 89-8-39(4)(b)). In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No Communal or Tribal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires a government officer to approve a residential lease, or voids it, because the land is communal, tribal or native land. A search of the whole Mississippi Code for Choctaw, tribe, tribal and Indian land near lease, lessee or rent found only statutes on mineral leases and sales of state land. If land is held in trust by the United States for a tribe or a tribal member, federal law, not searched here, governs its leasing.

title: Recording a Lease Is Optional
bodyText: No Mississippi statute requires you to record a residential lease or register it with a state or local office. Recording matters for priority. Every conveyance, covenant, agreement, bond, mortgage and deed of trust takes effect against creditors and later buyers for value without notice only from the time it is delivered to the clerk to be recorded, and an unrecorded one does not take precedence over a similar recorded instrument affecting the same property, absent actual notice (Miss. Code Ann. § 89-5-5). Whether a residential lease falls in that list, and whether a tenant's possession is notice, are questions of case law this library has not reviewed. For a long lease, the cautious course is to record it, and to tell any buyer or lender about it in writing.

title: Public Improvement District Statement
bodyText: After a county public improvement district is established, each contract and instrument of conveyance of a parcel of real property within the district must include, just before the purchaser's signature space, a boldfaced, conspicuous statement in larger type that the named district may impose and levy assessments on the property, that they pay for the district's public facilities and services and are set each year by its board, and that they are in addition to other taxes and assessments (Miss. Code Ann. § 19-31-45). Leaving the statement out does not invalidate any assessment or the contract or instrument (Miss. Code Ann. § 19-31-45). The statute speaks of the purchaser, and whether a lease is an instrument of conveyance for this purpose is a question of case law this library has not reviewed. If your property is in a public improvement district, the cautious course is to put the statement, with the district's name, in the lease just above the tenant's signature, especially if the lease passes any assessment to the tenant. No other Mississippi statute found requires a lease to disclose a special district or gives a tenant a vote in one. The library's clause `special-district-disclosure-ms` carries the statement for a property in a district.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: No Mississippi statute sets special rules for renting a house or apartment to students: no student-housing license, no rule on academic-year leases or parent guarantors. A whole-Code search for student, dormitory and residence hall near landlord, lessor, tenant or lessee found only statutes letting school boards lease facilities for students' industrial training. A student renting from you is an ordinary tenant under Mississippi's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and the same lease applies.
